research.consensus:
SURVEY: 9 real input/microphone preset files were fetched and parsed (MateusRodCosta gist, jtrv gist, azmarifdev podcast v1, MorrisAboveThis Microphone.json, aeolyus fedora-magazine.json, LuixBits luix-voice.json, dzervas rode_nt-usb.json, Obscurely "Discord and Record", Barisozyurek rampage noiseclean). Negative result worth knowing: the two repos named in the task, JackHack96/EasyEffects-Presets and Digitalone1/EasyEffects-Presets, contain ONLY output presets — no microphone presets exist in either. There is no curated, high-authority input-preset collection in this ecosystem; mic presets live in gists and dotfiles.

STAGE ORDER — where they agree:
- Gate before compressor: 9/9. Unanimous.
- Limiter last: 8/9 (rode_nt-usb puts a mid/side→stereo upmix after it, which is a routing fix, not processing).
- De-esser AFTER the compressor: 7/8 of the presets that have both. Only azmarifdev's podcast preset de-esses first.
- A single-band LSP compressor: 8/9 (only MorrisAboveThis uses a multiband, and it sets ratio 1.0 on all 8 bands, so it isn't really compressing).

STAGE ORDER — where they disagree, and where the planned chain diverges:
1. De-esser position. The planned chain is `EQ → de-esser → compressor`. The community default is `compressor → de-esser`. The reasoning behind the majority is sound: the compressor raises the level of quiet passages and therefore raises sibilants too, so de-essing before it lets the compressor re-amplify what you just removed. A careful engineer would move the de-esser after the compressor (or after makeup), i.e. `HPF → gate → EQ → compressor → makeup → de-esser → limiter`. If the fixed order must stay, expect to de-ess harder than these numbers suggest.
2. RNNoise position. The planned chain puts optional RNNoise AFTER the limiter. Zero presets do this. 5/9 put denoise FIRST (before the gate), 3/9 put it just before the limiter. Nothing should follow the brick-wall limiter. Put RNNoise first — it makes the gate's threshold decision far easier — or at worst immediately before the limiter.
3. HPF position. Only 3 presets have a dedicated HPF stage, and all 3 place it after the compressor (MateusRodCosta, aeolyus, dzervas). The other 3 with an EQ fold the high-pass into EQ band 0 (jtrv 80 Hz, luix 75 Hz, azmarif 50 Hz). The planned chain's HPF-first is defensible and arguably better (it stops rumble from driving the gate and compressor detectors), it just isn't what these files do.
4. EQ position: split. jtrv and luix-voice put EQ before the compressor; azmarif and Obscurely put it after. No consensus.

EQ — the important caveat: NOT ONE of the surveyed presets uses a fixed graphic-EQ ladder. All use the LSP parametric equalizer with arbitrary centres, arbitrary Q, and band types that a fixed 10-band ladder cannot express (Hi-pass, Lo-shelf, Hi-shelf). None of these curves can be copied onto 62.5/115.7/214.3/396.9/734.9/1360.8/2519.8/4666.1/8640.5/16000 Hz directly. What CAN be copied is the shape, and the three real voice curves (jtrv, azmarifdev, luix-voice) agree on a recognisable four-move shape:
  - high-pass at 50–80 Hz (handled by the dedicated HPF stage, not by the EQ);
  - optional warmth: +2 to +3 dB somewhere in 90–130 Hz (azmarif as a low shelf, luix as a bell);
  - mud/box cut: -1 to -2 dB somewhere in 220–425 Hz (all three);
  - presence lift: +2 to +3 dB at 3.2–3.5 kHz (all three);
  - air shelf: +2 dB from 9–10 kHz (all three).
Mapped onto the fixed ladder, that becomes roughly: 62.5 → 0 or slightly negative (the HPF already handles it), 115.7 → +1.5 to +3, 214.3 → -1 to -2, 396.9 → -1 to -2, 734.9 → 0, 1360.8 → 0, 2519.8 → +1 to +2, 4666.1 → +1.5 to +2.5, 8640.5 → +2, 16000 → +1 to +2. That is a legitimate "Clean Voice"/"Streaming" starting curve derived from three independent presets, and it fits comfortably inside ±12 dB — the ladder's range is not a constraint here, none of these curves exceeds ±3 dB.

DEFAULTS A CAREFUL ENGINEER WOULD TAKE (modal/median across the presets, cross-checked against Fedora Magazine and the LSP/Calf ranges):
  HPF: 80 Hz, 12 dB/oct (unanimous where present; 75 Hz and 50 Hz are the only variants).
  Gate: attack 5 ms; release 180–250 ms; threshold -48 to -55 dB for a tuned preset (the -24 dB EasyEffects default is far too high and will chop speech); zone/soft-knee -2 dB; reduction -12 to -16 dB (never a full mute); hysteresis on, -3 dB offset, -1 dB zone; RMS detection, reactivity 10 ms.
  Compressor: threshold -18 dB (range seen -12…-26); ratio 3:1 (3–4 is the whole observed range and Fedora Magazine says the same); knee -6 dB (every single preset); attack 5–20 ms, 10–15 ms is the tuned middle; release 100–200 ms; RMS sidechain, reactivity 10 ms, feed-forward; makeup +3 to +6 dB.
  De-esser: threshold -20 dB (range -18…-26); ratio 3:1; split f1 5–6 kHz; laxity 15; Split mode if you want only the sibilant band ducked, Wide if you want the Calf-recommended behaviour for a single voice.
  Limiter: ceiling -1.0 dB (6 of 7 presets; jtrv uses -1.5). Herm Thin, lookahead 5 ms, attack 5 ms, release 5 ms. Turn gain-boost OFF.
  Makeup gain as a separate stage: no preset has one. Treat the planned makeup stage as the compressor's makeup moved out — budget it at +3 to +6 dB and put it before the limiter, which the planned chain already does.

SIX-PRESET MAPPING suggested by the evidence: Studio/Natural ≈ Fedora-Magazine numbers with the EQ flat and unity gain throughout; Clean Voice ≈ MateusRodCosta/Fedora numbers plus the four-move EQ at half strength; Streaming ≈ jtrv (gate -50/-12, comp -18/3:1/15/200/+3, de-ess -22 Split 4k, limiter -1.5); Podcast ≈ azmarifdev (comp -20/4:1/5/75, warmth shelf, de-ess harder); Discord/Calls ≈ luix-voice's heavier compression (-26/3:1/+6 makeup) with a tighter gate, since call codecs punish dynamic range; Warm Voice ≈ azmarifdev's low-shelf idea, i.e. +3 at 115.7 Hz, -2 at 396.9, softer presence.
research.warnings:
1. MOST OF THESE "PRESETS" ARE BARELY EDITED DEFAULTS. The de-esser block `threshold -18 / ratio 3 / f1 6000 / f2 4500 / f1-level 0 / f2-level +12 / Q 1.0 / Wide / RMS / laxity 15` is EasyEffects' factory default (verified against easyeffects_db_deesser.kcfg), and it appears verbatim in MateusRodCosta, aeolyus, dzervas (ratio 4 the only change) and near-verbatim in MorrisAboveThis. Frequency-of-occurrence in this corpus is NOT evidence of tuning. Only jtrv, azmarifdev and luix-voice actually moved the de-esser. Same trap on the compressor: `-12 / 4:1 / -6 knee / 20 ms / 100 ms` is the factory default and appears untouched in three presets.

2. THE PLANNED RNNOISE POSITION IS WRONG. Putting optional RNNoise after the brick-wall limiter means the last thing the user hears is not limited. RNNoise is a neural denoiser operating on 480-sample frames at 48 kHz; it changes level and can add gain artefacts, so peaks can exceed the ceiling you just enforced. No preset in the survey does this. Put it first (before the gate) or immediately before the limiter.

3. DON'T MAP "KNEE" NAIVELY. LSP's compressor knee is NEGATIVE, range -24…0 dB, and means the width of the soft knee below the threshold. -6 dB is the default and is used by every preset in the survey. If your UI exposes a positive knee number, or a hard/soft toggle, do the conversion explicitly. Likewise the LSP gate has NO ratio — it has curve-threshold, curve-zone (soft knee) and reduction (attenuation depth). Presets showing "gate ratio 2.0, knee 9.0, range -12" (MateusRodCosta, Obscurely) are from the old Calf-gate era and those numbers are not interchangeable with the LSP ones.

4. f2-LEVEL IS A SIDECHAIN CONTROL, NOT A TONE CONTROL. The default +12 dB at 4500 Hz boosts the DETECTOR, not the audio. If you implement your de-esser with a plain sidechain band-pass, +12 dB at f2 with Q 1.0 is what you are emulating. Copying +12 dB into an output EQ band would be badly wrong.

5. GATE REDUCTION DEEPER THAN ~-20 dB IS A MISTAKE FOR SPEECH. MorrisAboveThis uses -48 dB, which is effectively a hard mute and will audibly chop breaths and word tails. Fedora Magazine explicitly recommends -12 or -18 dB, and the tuned presets sit at -12 to -16. Also run hysteresis on (jtrv, azmarifdev, luix, Barisozyurek all do: -3/-4 dB threshold offset, -1 dB zone) or the gate will chatter on a breath at the threshold.

6. GATE ATTACK OF 20 ms CLIPS WORD ONSETS. That is EasyEffects' default and Obscurely's value. Every tuned preset uses 1–5 ms. Use 5 ms, and if you want a "safe" preset use 1 ms (azmarifdev).

7. TWO SURVEYED PRESETS HAVE BROKEN GAIN STAGING — DO NOT COPY THEM. Obscurely "Discord and Record" sets the limiter threshold to -14 dB and then applies +5 dB of limiter OUTPUT gain plus +5 dB of EQ output gain, so the limiter is not the last gain stage and the ceiling means nothing. MorrisAboveThis sets the limiter threshold to 0.0 dBFS with gain-boost ON and then -1.1 dB of post-limiter output gain — a 0 dBFS ceiling invites inter-sample overs and, again, the trim is applied after the limiter. Rule for your implementation: the limiter must be the last gain-affecting stage, its ceiling must be ≤ -1.0 dB, and no makeup or output trim may come after it.

8. `gain-boost` (LSP limiter) DEFAULTS TO TRUE AND SHOULD BE OFF FOR A MIC. It lets the limiter apply upward gain; combined with a -1 dB ceiling it quietly adds loudness you did not ask for and makes an A/B against the unprocessed signal dishonest. jtrv, luix-voice and Obscurely turn it off; the untuned presets leave it on.

9. THE "STUDIO/NATURAL" REFERENCE MUST BE UNITY GAIN END TO END. Several presets bake in net gain (azmarifdev's EQ is ~+4 dB of boost with no compensating trim; MorrisAboveThis adds +7.3 dB before the gate and +2.8 dB in the multiband; Obscurely adds +10 dB total). If the reference preset is even 1–2 dB louder than bypass, users will report "processed sounds better" when they are only hearing level. Level-match it.

10. DON'T FAKE THE HIGH-PASS IN THE 10-BAND EQ. A 12 dB/oct high-pass at 80 Hz cannot be produced by a bell at 62.5 Hz on a fixed ladder — the lowest band's -12 dB floor is nowhere near a filter slope, and you would drag 115 Hz down with it. Keep the HPF as its own stage, as the planned chain already does. The same applies to the +2 dB high shelf from 9–10 kHz that all three voice presets use: on the fixed ladder you can only approximate it with 8640.5 and 16000 both lifted, which loses the shelf's flat top. Say so in the UI rather than pretending the ladder is parametric.

11. AUTOGAIN AT -23 LUFS IS A TRAP. aeolyus' preset chains EBU R128 autogain (target -23 LUFS) in front of a gate and a compressor. -23 LUFS is a broadcast programme-loudness target for finished mixes; on a live mic it fights the compressor's own levelling, and it is far too quiet for Discord or a stream. If you ever add auto-level, put it after the compressor and target something near -16 LUFS, and never let it and the compressor both chase the same thing.

12. COMMUNITY PRESETS CONTAIN DEAD SETTINGS. azmarifdev's podcast preset configures Speex `noise-suppression -70` while `enable-denoise` is false; luix-voice ships an RNNoise block with `bypass: true`; aeolyus' gate has `reduction 0.0` (the gate is inert). When you read a number out of one of these files, check that the stage it belongs to is actually enabled before treating it as a considered choice.

13. CALF'S OWN DOCS CONTRADICT COMMON DE-ESSING ADVICE. Calf recommends Wide mode for a single vocal track ("sounds much cleaner"), while typical studio practice and jtrv/luix-voice prefer Split so only the sibilant band ducks. Wide ducks the whole signal on every "s", which on a fixed chain with a compressor after it produces audible full-band pumping. Default to Split for a mic chain and expose Wide as an option; don't pick Wide just because four presets have it (they have it because it's the default).

research.consensus:
WHERE EVERYONE AGREES

1. -1 dBTP is the universal peak ceiling for anything about to hit a lossy encoder. EBU R128 §m ("shall be -1 dBTP"), AES TD1008 §4 ("not exceed -1 dBTP at the codec input"), Spotify ("below -1dB TP max... best for lossy formats"), Apple Podcasts ("true-peak value doesn't exceed -1 dB FS"). This is a genuine standard, not folklore.

2. WHY -1 and not 0: two independent reasons, both documented.
   (a) Inter-sample peaks. A digital signal whose SAMPLES all sit at or below 0 dBFS reconstructs, after the D/A or an SRC, to a continuous waveform that can exceed 0 dBFS. BS.1770-5 Annex 2 defines true-peak measurement precisely because sample-peak metering cannot see this. dBTP is "the maximum value of the audio signal waveform... in the continuous time domain" (EBU R128, Definitions).
   (b) Codec overshoot. A lossy encode/decode round trip does not preserve sample values; the decoder's output peak is generally higher than the encoder's input peak. TD1008 §7B is explicit and quantitative: 256 kbps coders may tolerate -0.5 dBTP, and "peak overshoot increases as the bit rate decreases, so the limiting threshold may need to be reduced below the recommended -1.0 dBTP". libopus concedes the same point structurally by shipping opus_pcm_soft_clip().
   So -1 dBTP is an engineering margin against reconstruction + coding, not a superstition. It is also not a large margin: TD1008 notes true-peak meters themselves carry up to 0.6 dB error.

3. Loudness target and peak ceiling are independent controls. Loudness is set by gain (and by compression), peak by the limiter. Every source insists the limiter must not be used to create loudness: TD1008 recommends ~1 dB of limiting as a starting point and warns that more "may produce more audible artifacts than simply letting the audio material clip on occasional transients".

4. Voice targets cluster at -16 to -19 LUFS depending on channel count, not at -23 and not at -14.
   - AES TD1008: speech -18 LUFS (the only figure in any standards document aimed at speech in a stream).
   - Apple Podcasts: -16 LKFS ±1.
   - Google (speech, for Assistant): -16 LUFS stereo / -19 LUFS mono.
   These agree once you apply the 3.01 LU mono/stereo offset: a mono voice file at -19 LUFS mono IS -16 LUFS once dual-monoed. TD1008's -18 sits deliberately ~2 LU below music because speech at equal BS.1770 loudness is perceived 2-3 dB louder than music.

WHERE THEY DISAGREE, AND WHY IT DOESN'T MATTER HERE

- -23/-24 LUFS (EBU R128, ATSC A/85) vs -16/-18 (AES TD1008, Apple, Google) vs -14 (Spotify/YouTube playback normalisation). This is not a contradiction; they are different layers. -23 LUFS is a delivery target for a broadcast chain with 23 dB of headroom and a downstream device that will turn it up. -14 LUFS is a playback normaliser's operating point at a service that also applies upward gain. -18 LUFS is a distribution loudness chosen, in TD1008's own words, "to accommodate the gain of current player devices". TD1008 §3 even states its intent to lower its numbers by 6 LU later to harmonise with R128 once device metadata support arrives. None of these is a microphone target.

- -1 vs -2 dBTP. Spotify says -1, or -2 if the master is above -14 LUFS. FFmpeg's loudnorm defaults to -2. TD1008 says -1 at the codec input but below -1 at low bitrates. The disagreement is entirely about how much codec overshoot you expect, and everyone reasons the same way: lower bitrate or higher loudness => lower ceiling.

WHAT A CAREFUL ENGINEER SHOULD TAKE AS THE DEFAULT FOR THIS CHAIN

Framing: a virtual microphone is NOT a delivery format. It is an intermediate feed into a consumer that will (a) run its own AGC/noise suppression, (b) encode to Opus or AAC at an unknown and possibly very low bitrate, (c) apply its own limiter. The standards' -1 dBTP assumes you are the LAST processing stage before one known encoder. Here you are neither.

Limiter ceiling:
- Do not ship -1 dBFS sample-peak as the ceiling. That is the number people quote, but it is the wrong quantity (sample peak, not true peak) at the wrong point in the chain (not the last stage).
- Recommended default: -3.0 dBFS true-peak-aware ceiling, exposed as a setting with a range roughly -6.0 .. -1.0 dBFS. Justification, all citable: -1 dBTP is the floor of the standards' requirement for ONE encoder; TD1008 says to go below -1 for lower bitrates; Discord's Opus can drop to tens of kbps; TD1008 documents up to 3 dB of downstream limiter gain reduction when headroom is insufficient; and OBS's own limiter already defaults to -6.0 dB threshold, so a streamer's chain will re-limit you anyway. -3 dBFS costs nothing perceptually (the receiver normalises) and buys margin against all three.
- Make the limiter actually true-peak aware if affordable: 4x oversampled peak detection per BS.1770 Annex 2, with ~1.5-5 ms lookahead. If you ship a non-lookahead, non-oversampled brick wall (the cheap real-time option), add ~1 dB extra margin, because such a limiter at -1 dBFS sample peak routinely leaks above 0 dBTP, and document that the number in the UI is dBFS sample peak, not dBTP.
- Target ≤ ~1 dB of gain reduction in normal speech. If a preset drives the limiter harder than that habitually, the compressor/makeup gain above it is set wrong.

Makeup gain:
- Set makeup gain so the chain lands at -18 LUFS short-term for normal speech. That is AES TD1008's published speech distribution loudness, it is 2 LU below the music figure for the documented perceptual reason, and against a -3 dBFS ceiling it leaves ~15 dB peak-to-loudness ratio — a natural, uncompressed-sounding voice with room for a laugh or a raised voice.
- Give the podcast/Studio-Natural presets -19 LUFS mono / -16 LUFS stereo, matching Apple and Google exactly, and be explicit in the UI/code about which one is measured. Getting the mono/stereo reference wrong is a silent 3 dB error.
- Keep the integrated result above -20 LUFS (TD1008 §5) so a user on a low-gain client isn't inaudible.
- Makeup gain must be computed net of the EQ's contribution. With ±12 dB bands, a bright preset can add 4-6 dB of peak before the limiter; if makeup gain is a fixed per-preset constant chosen without accounting for the EQ, presets will not be loudness-matched to each other and A/B against Studio/Natural becomes meaningless. Measure each factory preset's output loudness on the same speech reference and trim its makeup gain to hit the target — do not hand-pick the dB values.
- Do not attempt to servo makeup gain from an integrated (BS.1770-gated, whole-programme) loudness measurement in real time. Integrated loudness is defined over a programme; it is not a control signal. Use short-term (3 s) loudness for the meter, and keep makeup gain static per preset. If you ever want adaptive gain, that is an AGC and belongs before the compressor, not in makeup.

High-pass cutoff:
- 80 Hz default for the voice chain; 100 Hz for the Discord/Calls and Streaming presets; expose 60-150 Hz. 2nd-order Butterworth (12 dB/oct) is the well-trodden choice; it is literally what WebRTC ships on every VoIP mic path, with the shipped 48 kHz coefficients measuring -3.54 dB @100 Hz, -6.21 dB @80 Hz, -1.01 dB @150 Hz.
- Rationale, not folklore: male speaking fundamentals run down to ~85 Hz, so 80 Hz preserves the voice while removing desk rumble, HVAC, handling noise, DC offset and the low-frequency energy of plosives; the proximity effect of a cardioid close to the mouth also piles energy below ~150 Hz. Removing that energy is mostly a headroom and compressor-behaviour win — LF rumble is inaudible on laptop speakers but drives the compressor and eats limiter headroom.
- 300 Hz is the wrong answer for a modern mic chain, for a documented reason: G.712's 300-3400 Hz band exists because analog/PCM telephone channels were allocated that way, and the industry moved the low edge back down to 50-100 Hz (G.722 50-7000 Hz, P.341 ~100-8000 Hz) the moment bandwidth allowed. Do not cite POTS as an intelligibility optimum.
research.warnings:
THINGS IN THE BRIEF THAT ARE WRONG OR NEED CORRECTING

1. "-16 LUFS mono / -19 LUFS stereo" is INVERTED. It is -16 LUFS STEREO and -19 LUFS MONO. Confirmed twice independently: Podnews ("To achieve -16 LUFS stereo, your editing program should output -16 LUFS stereo... or -19 LUFS mono") and Google's Assistant guideline ("-16 LUFS for stereo... For mono audio content, the average loudness should be -19 LUFS"). Mechanism: duplicating a mono track into two channels adds 3.01 LU under BS.1770's RMS channel summation. If this gets into the code the wrong way round, every mono preset ships 3 dB hot or 3 dB quiet. Given this is a microphone chain feeding a mono-or-stereo virtual source, this is the single highest-risk number in the whole task.

2. RNNoise is placed AFTER the brick-wall limiter in the fixed stage order. This is a real defect, not a style point. AES TD1008 §7B: "Lowpass, highpass, and bandpass filtering can all add overshoots by removing program energy and if not linear-phase, by introducing group delay distortion. Hence, filtering (if used) should ideally occur before the peak limiter." RNNoise is spectral gain modification — exactly this class of operation — and will reintroduce peaks above the ceiling the limiter just enforced. Either move RNNoise before the limiter (ideally right after the high-pass, before the gate, where it also helps the gate), or accept that the limiter is no longer the last word and add margin. TD1008 quantifies how badly filtering can betray a limiter with the square-wave case: removing harmonics raises the peak by 2.1 dB.

3. "Twitch = -14 LUFS" is FOLKLORE. Twitch publishes no loudness target anywhere and applies no loudness normalisation to live streams or VODs. Their Broadcasting Guidelines cover codec (AAC-LC) and bitrate (96 kbps recommended, 160 kbps max) and are silent on LUFS and peak. The -14 figure circulating in streaming blogs is borrowed from Spotify/YouTube and has no Twitch provenance. Practical consequence for this chain: because Twitch does NOT normalise, a Twitch preset should be loud enough to sit in the pack (-18 to -16 LUFS), and there is no platform safety net if it is quiet.

4. "YouTube = -14 LUFS" is EMPIRICAL, not published. Google has never published a numeric LUFS spec for YouTube video audio (the -16/-19 LUFS figures are from the Assistant guideline, a different product). The behaviour is consistent and well-measured, but note YouTube only ATTENUATES — it will not raise a quiet upload. Do not design a preset that relies on being turned up.

5. Do not apply EBU R128's -23 LUFS to a microphone chain. It is a broadcast programme delivery target with a downstream chain that will amplify it. A Discord mic at -23 LUFS integrated is simply quiet, and neither Discord nor Twitch will fix it. TD1008 §5 explicitly warns: content below ~-20 LUFS "can cause content to be unsatisfyingly quiet on some player devices with insufficient gain, particularly when environmental noise is present."

OTHER BAD IDEAS TO AVOID

6. Labelling a sample-peak limiter's threshold "dBTP". If the limiter detects peaks at the native rate without oversampling, it is a dBFS sample-peak limiter. Setting it to -1.0 and calling the result "-1 dBTP compliant" is false; such a limiter regularly passes inter-sample peaks above 0 dBTP. Either oversample 4x per BS.1770 Annex 2, or label the control dBFS and give it more margin.

7. Using the limiter for loudness. TD1008: "A maximum of 1 dB of limiting prior to final encoding is recommended as a starting point... limiting more than about 1 dB may produce more audible artifacts than simply letting the audio material clip on occasional transients." The compressor + makeup gain make the voice loud; the limiter only catches the door slam.

8. Chasing -1 dBFS exactly "because that's the standard", when the downstream will compress again. Discord's Opus, OBS's own -6 dB limiter, Krisp/AGC, and the receiving client's decoder all sit after you. TD1008 documents up to 3 dB of gain reduction in a decode-side OS limiter when the encode side left insufficient headroom. -1 dBFS is not wrong, but it is the minimum defensible margin in a chain where you ARE the last stage — which you are not. -3 dBFS is the better default for a virtual source and costs nothing.

9. A 300 Hz high-pass on a music-capable mic chain. Kills male fundamentals (85-180 Hz) outright and makes every voice sound like a phone call. It is a legacy channel-bandwidth figure from G.712-era telephony, not an intelligibility finding. Even ITU moved on (G.722 50-7000 Hz, P.341 ~100-8000 Hz).

10. Putting the high-pass after the EQ or after the compressor. It belongs first (as the brief has it) both because rumble should never reach the gate/compressor detector, and because of the filters-before-limiter rule above. The brief's stage order is correct on this point — the only ordering problem is RNNoise.

11. Assuming "-1 dBTP" scales down to low bitrates. It does not. TD1008 is explicit that the threshold must go below -1.0 dBTP as bitrate falls. Discord voice negotiates Opus down to tens of kbps on poor connections; that is precisely the regime where the standard tells you to be MORE conservative, not less.

12. Trying to be "compliant" with a single number across all six presets. The presets have different jobs: Discord/Calls faces AGC + low-bitrate Opus (most headroom, tightest band-limiting), Podcast faces an offline editor and Apple's -16/-19 spec (most headroom-preserving, least limiting), Studio/Natural must be near-unity so the A/B against bypass is honest — a Studio/Natural preset with hidden makeup gain makes the processed version sound better purely because it is louder, which is the oldest trap in audio demos. Loudness-match Studio/Natural to the dry signal within ~0.5 LU or the comparison is worthless.

research.consensus:
WHERE SOURCES AGREE

1. High-pass belongs at 70–100 Hz, not higher, for a seated speaker. Shure says 70–90 Hz; RODE and essentially every podcast guide say 80 Hz; BOYA says start at 75 Hz and only climb to 100/150 Hz when the room forces it. Nobody credible recommends a default high-pass at or above 115 Hz for a male voice.

2. Proximity effect lives below roughly 100–250 Hz and appears inside about 30 cm of a cardioid. Shure's own hardware answer to it (SM7B bass-rolloff switch) is a gentle shelf that is only about -3 dB at 200 Hz and reaches its full depth below 100 Hz — a broad tilt, not a notch.

3. The presence region is 2–10 kHz (Shure's own glossary), and the useful part for speech intelligibility is 2–5 kHz. Manufacturers implement presence boosts at +3 to +4 dB maximum (SM7B). Guides recommend +1 to +3 dB. ISO 226 explains why: the ear is most sensitive at 2–5 kHz, so this is the region where a few dB of error is most audible.

4. Sibilance is higher than people assume. RODE says 4–7 kHz, FabFilter says s-sounds are "usually around 8 to 10 kHz", and the male/female split is roughly 5–6 kHz vs 7–8 kHz. A single fixed de-esser must therefore straddle both.

5. Mud is 250–500 Hz and the correction is small: -2 to -4 dB. Both independent open-source presets landed on exactly -2 dB.

6. Compression for speech is 2:1 to 4:1 (RODE states this explicitly), with attack slow enough to pass consonant transients (5–15 ms) and release 75–250 ms.

7. Limiter ceiling -1 dBFS/-1 dBTP. Apple specifies -1 dBTP per ITU-R BS.1770-5; both open-source presets set -1.0 / -1.5 dB.

WHERE SOURCES DISAGREE

- De-esser centre. The Fifine-targeted EasyEffects preset sits at 3000–5000 Hz; the NPR-voice preset at 4000–8000 Hz; FabFilter points at 8–10 kHz. This is the single biggest disagreement found. The 3 kHz end is inside the intelligibility region and will lisp the voice.
- EQ position in the chain. Elgato says EQ before the de-esser and compressor; the Fifine preset puts EQ after the compressor.
- Low-mid direction. Generic vocal guides cut 100–250 Hz as "boomy"; the one preset actually tuned for a Fifine *boosts* 90 Hz by +3 dB, because that class of mic is thin rather than boomy. Both are right for their source — this is mic-dependent, not universal.
- Mono loudness target: Apple's page states -16 LKFS without distinguishing mono; third-party summaries claim -19 LUFS for mono. Apple's own text does not say that, so treat the -19 figure as unsourced.

WHAT A CAREFUL ENGINEER WOULD TAKE AS THE DEFAULT, MAPPED TO THE FIXED LADDER

The decision the task actually asks for: the low cut belongs at 62.5 Hz, not 115.734 Hz. A male fundamental runs 85–180 Hz and a female 165–255 Hz, so 115.734 Hz sits squarely on the male fundamental; a -12 dB band there would hollow out half the users' voices. The correct division of labour is: the dedicated high-pass stage at 75–85 Hz does the rumble/plosive work (this is what every manufacturer recommends), the 62.5 Hz band trims whatever the high-pass left, and proximity/boom is handled with a modest -1 to -3 dB at 214.311 Hz — which is precisely where Shure put the SM7B's own bass rolloff (-3 dB @ 200 Hz). 115.734 Hz should stay near 0, or go slightly positive on a thin mic.

Band-by-band defaults that the sources support:
- 62.5 Hz: 0 to -6 (below all speech; safe to cut hard, but the HPF has usually already done it)
- 115.734 Hz: -1 to +2 (male fundamental — do not cut aggressively; a thin USB condenser wants +2)
- 214.311 Hz: -1 to -3 (proximity/boom; Shure's own -3 dB @ 200 Hz is the precedent)
- 396.85 Hz: -2 to -4 (mud, 250–500 Hz; both open-source presets chose -2)
- 734.867 Hz: -1 to 0 (boxiness; leave mostly alone)
- 1360.79 Hz: 0 to +1 (lower consonant region, RODE's 1.5–4 kHz)
- 2519.84 Hz: +1 to +3 (core intelligibility; SM7B presence boost peaks here)
- 4666.12 Hz: +1 to +2 (upper presence; also the low edge of male sibilance, so restrain)
- 8640.48 Hz: -1 to +2 (sibilance and hiss live here; boost only on a dull mic)
- 16000 Hz: -2 to 0 on a cheap USB condenser (mostly self-noise), 0 to +1 on a good mic

De-esser: a single fixed centre at 6–7 kHz with a wide band covering roughly 4–9 kHz serves both male (5–6 kHz) and female (7–8 kHz) sibilance without touching 2519.84 Hz intelligibility. If the de-esser can be split, 4–8 kHz (the NPR preset's choice) is the better-supported default than 3–5 kHz.

Preset-by-preset, the sources point to: Studio/Natural = all ten bands at 0.0, compressor at 2:1 or bypassed, limiter only (this is the honest reference); Clean Voice = the band defaults above at their mild end, 3:1, -18 dB; Podcast = mud cut at its deeper end plus +2/+3 presence, 3:1 with 15 ms attack / 200 ms release (the NPR preset, which is the best-documented open-source chain); Streaming = Podcast plus a touch more 4666 and a tighter gate; Discord/Calls = the most restrained EQ of all (the platform runs its own AGC and noise suppression on top) with a hard-working gate and limiter; Warm Voice = +2 at 115.734 and 214.311, -1 at 2519.84 and 4666.12, 8640/16000 negative. Every factory preset should stay inside about ±4 dB even though the range allows ±12.
research.warnings:
THINGS COMMONLY RECOMMENDED THAT ARE ACTUALLY A BAD IDEA HERE

1. Putting the low cut at 115.734 Hz. This is the trap in the stated design question. The adult male speech fundamental is 85–180 Hz. A cut at 115.734 Hz — especially anywhere near the -12 dB the range allows — removes the fundamental of half the user base and produces a thin, telephone-like voice. Manufacturers cut *below* this (Shure 70–90 Hz, RODE 80 Hz, BOYA 75 Hz) and treat 200 Hz as a shelf, not a notch.

2. Treating "proximity effect" as an EQ band. Proximity is distance-dependent and can be +16 dB — no fixed preset can track it. It is fixed by mic technique and by the high-pass/low-shelf stage. Baking a deep 115 Hz or 214 Hz cut into a preset to "handle proximity" makes the preset wrong for anyone sitting at a normal distance.

3. De-essing at 3–5 kHz. One of the two open-source presets found does this (f1 3000 / f2 5000 Hz, ratio 5:1). That band is the intelligibility/presence region, not the sibilance region — RODE says sibilance starts at 4 kHz, FabFilter puts s-sounds at 8–10 kHz. A de-esser centred there ducks the consonants that make speech legible and produces an audible lisp on every "s". Do not copy that value just because it appears in a Fifine-branded preset.

4. Boosting 8640.48 and 16000 Hz for "air" on a cheap USB condenser. The Fifine class already has an onboard top-end lift (reviewers describe it as bright/brittle and note apparent built-in EQ), its equivalent noise is -80 dBFS with 78 dB S/N, and the hiss is concentrated up there. An "air" boost on this mic raises hiss and sibilance simultaneously, and the gate then has to work harder, which causes breathing artefacts. On this mic class those two bands should default to 0 or negative.

5. Hard gating. A gate with a fast release and infinite reduction chops word tails and breath, which sounds worse than the noise it removes. The better-designed open-source preset limits reduction to -15 dB (an expander, not a mute), uses hysteresis, and releases over 200 ms. Since the planned stage is called "noise gate/expander", it should behave as an expander by default.

6. Targeting -16 LUFS in the real-time chain. That is Apple's *delivery* spec for a finished file, measured over a whole programme. A live mic chain cannot meaningfully hit an integrated loudness target, and chasing it with makeup gain will pump. Take only the -1 dBTP ceiling from that spec.

7. Trusting the vocal-EQ "cheat sheets". The numbers 250–500 Hz mud / 3–5 kHz harsh / 4.5–9 kHz presence are repeated identically across dozens of SEO sites with no measurement behind any of them. They happen to agree with Shure's and RODE's published ranges, which is why they are usable — but cite Shure and RODE, not the cheat sheets, and do not take their more specific claims (exact dB amounts, gendered "female voices need X") as fact.

8. Using the full ±12 dB range in factory presets. Manufacturers' own voicing switches move 3–4 dB. A factory preset that moves a band 8 or 10 dB will sound broken on a mic whose response already differs from the one it was tuned on. Reserve the outer range for user editing.

9. Making "Studio/Natural" not actually flat. Its stated purpose is an honest processed-vs-unprocessed A/B. If it applies any makeup gain or compression, the user will hear a loudness difference and conclude the processing "sounds better" when it is simply louder. It should be ten zeros with the dynamics stages bypassed or unity, and the A/B should be loudness-matched.

10. Assuming the platform is not already processing. Discord, Zoom and Teams run their own AGC, noise suppression and limiting. Stacking an aggressive local compressor plus RNNoise under a platform AGC causes pumping and noise-floor modulation. The Discord/Calls preset should be the *least* processed of the six, not the most.

11. One caveat on sourcing: no independent measured frequency-response curve for the FIFINE K669/K669B could be found from any measurement lab (RTINGS has not tested it; Podcastage reviews it by ear only). Everything about that mic's tonal balance in this report is either FIFINE's own published spec or subjective reviewer description. The Fifine-specific EQ values come from a single community preset author, not from a measurement — treat them as a starting point to verify by ear on the actual test machine, not as ground truth.

research.consensus:
WHERE SOURCES AGREE (safe defaults a careful engineer would take)

1. Compressor for speech: 2:1–4:1, soft knee ~6 dB, threshold set so normal speech shows 3–6 dB gain reduction, attack 15–30 ms, release 100–250 ms. Rane Note 155 (manufacturer/engineering), Sound On Sound, and both shipped Linux mic presets land inside this box independently. Default: ratio 3:1, knee 6 dB soft, attack 20 ms, release 150 ms, threshold set for 4 dB GR at normal speaking level.

2. Attack must be SLOW relative to music-vocal lore. Rane's stated vocal attack is 25–100 ms; the two open-source mic presets use 15 ms and 20 ms. All of them are far from the "1–5 ms" that consumer blogs repeat. The reason is mechanical: a stop-consonant burst is a transient of a few ms up to ~35 ms (Jackson). An attack of 1–5 ms lands the gain reduction ON the burst, so /p/ /t/ /k/ lose their release energy and /s/ /f/ loses its onset — speech becomes dull and mushy at exactly the frequencies that carry intelligibility. An attack of 15–30 ms lets the consonant through and only then clamps the vowel that follows, which is the part that actually carries the loudness.

3. Release must be tied to syllable rate, not picked freely. The speech envelope's modulation spectrum peaks at 4–8 Hz across languages with a dominant rate near 4.5–5 Hz (Neurosci. Biobehav. Rev.), i.e. one syllable every ~125–250 ms. If release is much shorter than a syllable the compressor recovers inside each syllable and you hear breathing/pumping on the noise floor between words; if it is much longer than a phrase, the compressor rides down a loud sentence and the following quiet one is buried. 100–250 ms sits in the syllable window and is what both Rane (100–500 ms for vocals) and both presets converge on. Also note Rane's definition: release is specified in dB/second, so actual recovery time = (gain reduction × release setting)/10 dB — a "200 ms" release constant is not 200 ms of wall clock when 8 dB of reduction has to unwind.

4. Expander, not gate, for speech. Everyone agrees. A gate is an expander with an ∞:1 ratio (Rane). The ∞:1 cliff produces two specific artefacts: (a) CHATTERING — when the signal hovers at the threshold the gain slams between 0 and −∞ repeatedly, audible as a fluttering/stuttering noise floor (Wikipedia Noise gate, SOS); (b) CLIPPED CONSONANTS — voiceless fricatives (/s/, /f/, /th/) and the tail of plosives are low-level broadband noise, often only a few dB above room tone, so a gate set to kill the room also kills the front of "see" and the end of "stop"; the word arrives with its consonant amputated. A 2:1 expander with a −12 dB reduction floor and a −6 dB soft knee zone attenuates the room without ever muting, so a quiet fricative is only pulled down a few dB rather than erased.

5. Two independent anti-chatter mechanisms, and a real preset uses both. HOLD (defer release until the signal has been below threshold for N ms — 70–150 ms for speech, which spans the inter-word gaps) and HYSTERESIS (close at a threshold 3 dB below the open threshold, so the signal must fall further to close than it needed to open). Wikipedia, SOS and LSP's gate manual all describe both; the NPR preset ships −3 dB hysteresis. Default: hold 100 ms, hysteresis −3 dB, attack 5 ms, release 200 ms.

6. De-esser must be split-band/sidechain, not wideband. Wikipedia and iZotope both describe the split-band form: the sidechain is high-pass/band-pass filtered so the detector only sees sibilant energy, and only the HF band is attenuated. Centre 5–6 kHz for male, 7–8 kHz for female, 3–10 kHz overall; the two-band 4 kHz + 8 kHz arrangement in the NPR preset and the dbx 286s' 4 kHz default are the pragmatic compromises for a preset that does not know the speaker. Ratio 3:1, threshold set so a hard S produces 2–4 dB reduction, range capped at 6 dB, attack fast (0.1–1 ms), release 40–150 ms.

7. Limiter: ceiling −1 dBTP (EBU R 128), −1.5 to −2 dB if a lossy codec follows (Discord/Opus, browser WebRTC). Lookahead 2 ms is enough for a plosive in this chain and costs exactly 2 ms of latency; there is no reason to spend 5–10 ms in a live mic path.

WHERE SOURCES DISAGREE

- Compressor attack: Rane says 25–100 ms for vocals, the open-source presets say 15–20 ms, consumer blogs say 1–5 ms. Rane's figures are from analogue hardware where the knee and the detector are slower anyway; 15–25 ms is the honest modern middle and I would default to 20 ms.
- De-esser attack: mastering-guide sources say 0.1–1 ms, LedgerNote says 10–20 ms "smoothing". These are different controls — a true attack vs an envelope-smoothing constant in de-essers that auto-set their own attack. Implement attack (fast) and expose release; do not expose both.
- Gate thresholds: −50 dB vs −24 dB between the two presets. This is NOT a technical disagreement, it is gain staging. Threshold must be referenced to the measured noise floor, which is why a fixed factory number is fragile.
- Makeup gain: Rane treats it as a manual ±12 dB output trim; Waves documents auto-makeup from threshold+ratio. See below.

WHICH PARAMETERS INTERACT (why a preset cannot be assembled number by number)

A. Threshold ↔ ratio ↔ makeup. These three are one parameter set, not three. Gain reduction at a given input = (input − threshold) × (1 − 1/ratio). Halving the ratio roughly halves the reduction, so the same threshold gives a completely different result. This is why the correct spec for a factory preset is a TARGET (3–6 dB GR at normal speech, per Rane) and the numbers are solved backwards from it. Consequence: expose "amount" in the UI and derive threshold internally, or the preset breaks the moment the user changes their mic gain.

B. Makeup gain ↔ limiter ceiling ↔ EQ gains. The makeup stage sets how hard the limiter works. Ten EQ bands at up to +12 dB each can add 10+ dB of broadband gain before the makeup stage even sees the signal. So makeup CANNOT be a hard-coded per-preset dB value chosen independently — it must be auto-derived (0.5 × |threshold| × (1 − 1/ratio), the TASCAM/Waves rule) and then offset by the preset's net EQ gain, otherwise the Streaming and Warm Voice presets will sit on the limiter permanently while Studio/Natural is 8 dB quieter, and users will perceive the louder preset as "better" for reasons that have nothing to do with the processing.

C. Attack ↔ release ↔ ratio (the "squashed" axis). Fast attack + fast release + high ratio is the combination that produces the squashed, lifeless, pumping sound — not any one of them alone. SOS makes this explicit: fast attack with fast release suppresses transients; fast attack with slow release keeps hits consistent without changing the transient-to-sustain balance. A 6:1 ratio with a 30 ms attack and a 200 ms release is still natural; a 3:1 ratio with a 2 ms attack and a 20 ms release is not. Any preset that raises the ratio must also lengthen the attack and release, or it changes character rather than just amount.

D. High-pass cutoff ↔ limiter lookahead ↔ compressor threshold. The high-pass is what actually defuses plosives. With an 80–100 Hz HPF the plosive no longer produces a huge LF excursion, so the limiter needs far less lookahead (2 ms rather than 10) and the compressor's threshold is not being triggered by inaudible sub-100 Hz energy. Move the HPF down to 40 Hz for a "warm" preset and both the lookahead and the compressor threshold need re-tuning.

E. De-esser ↔ EQ bands at 4666 Hz and 8640 Hz ↔ compressor attack. All three touch the same sibilant energy, and they fight. A +4 dB lift at 4666/8640 Hz for "air"/presence drives the de-esser harder at a fixed threshold, so the de-esser cancels the EQ move — dynamically, which sounds worse than not making the move. And a compressor attack fast enough to catch consonants is itself a crude wideband de-esser, so it changes how much the real de-esser has to do. Fixed rule for the preset set: de-esser threshold must be offset by the preset's own gain at the 4666/8640 Hz bands, and presets with HF lift (Streaming, Clean Voice) need the de-esser proportionally more sensitive than presets with flat HF (Studio/Natural).

F. Expander threshold ↔ compressor makeup ↔ perceived noise. The compressor raises the noise floor by exactly the makeup gain plus the reduction applied to loud passages — typically 6–10 dB. So the expander must be set AFTER the downstream gain is known, or a preset that sounds quiet in the gaps in testing will hiss in use. In the fixed stage order (gate before compressor) the expander cannot see the noise it is ultimately responsible for; the threshold therefore has to be chosen against the post-compressor floor, not the raw input.

G. Optional RNNoise ↔ expander. RNNoise already suppresses stationary noise. Running an aggressive expander in front of it is redundant and makes RNNoise's job harder (it sees a non-stationary, gated floor). Presets with RNNoise on should use a gentler expander (higher reduction floor, e.g. −6 dB rather than −12 dB), not the same one.

SUGGESTED PER-PRESET DIFFERENTIATION (all six share the same topology; only amount changes)
- Studio/Natural: HPF 60 Hz, expander −6 dB floor, EQ all 0, de-esser off/minimal, comp 2:1 @ 25 ms/200 ms, makeup auto, limiter −1 dB. The A/B reference.
- Clean Voice: HPF 80 Hz, comp 3:1 @ 20 ms/150 ms, de-esser 3:1 @ 5–6 kHz cap 4 dB, mild presence lift.
- Podcast: HPF 80 Hz, comp 3:1 @ 25 ms/200 ms (longer release for conversational pacing), gentle 200–400 Hz cut, warm HF.
- Streaming: HPF 100 Hz, comp 4:1 @ 15 ms/120 ms, more HF lift, de-esser correspondingly more sensitive, limiter −1.5 dB.
- Discord/Calls: HPF 100 Hz, comp 4:1 @ 20 ms/120 ms, strongest expander, presence lift at 2519 Hz for intelligibility over a codec, limiter −2 dB (Opus headroom).
- Warm Voice: HPF 62.5 Hz band left flat or +1, LF/low-mid retained, HF lift minimal, comp 2.5:1 @ 25 ms/200 ms, de-esser light.
research.warnings:
COMMONLY RECOMMENDED, ACTUALLY A BAD IDEA

1. "Attack 1–5 ms for vocals." This is the single most repeated piece of bad advice in the search results, and it is wrong for SPEECH specifically. It compresses the plosive burst and fricative onset — exactly the 2–8 kHz transient energy that carries consonant identity — and produces dull, mushy, slightly lisping speech that people then try to fix with MORE EQ lift at 4666/8640 Hz, which drives the de-esser harder, which makes it duller. Use 15–30 ms. (Rane Note 155 gives 25–100 ms for vocals.)

2. A hard gate (∞:1) on a voice path. Produces chattering when the signal hovers at threshold, and amputates the low-level voiceless fricatives and plosive tails that sit barely above room tone. Use a downward expander (2:1, −12 dB reduction floor, −6 dB soft zone) with hold 100 ms and −3 dB hysteresis. Never ship a gate preset with hold = 0.

3. Auto-makeup gain left permanently on with no visible value. Sound On Sound's explicit warning: auto makeup "encourages inexperienced users to dial in more compression than is necessary" because the loudness increase reads as improvement. In a consumer product this is worse — users will A/B the preset against bypass, hear it louder, and conclude the processing is good. If you auto-derive makeup (recommended, see the TASCAM/Waves formula), loudness-match the bypass path too, or the comparison is dishonest.

4. Wideband de-essing. Ducking the whole signal when the detector sees sibilance dips the vowel underneath the S. On a fixed-topology product, implement the split-band form (filtered sidechain, HF-band-only attenuation).

5. Over-de-essing → lisping. This is the named failure mode. Threshold too low or range uncapped means the de-esser reduces every S, not just the harsh ones, and the /s/ collapses toward /th/ — the speaker sounds like they have a lisp. Two guards: cap maximum gain reduction at 6 dB (not unlimited), and keep release short enough (40–150 ms) that the band recovers before the following vowel. Symptom to test for: read a sentence full of S's ("she sells sea shells") and check that the S's are still identifiable as S.

6. A fixed de-esser centre frequency for all speakers. Male sibilance centres 5–6 kHz, female 7–8 kHz — a 4 kHz preset set for a male voice will barely touch a female voice's sibilance, and a 7 kHz preset will make a male voice sound hollow without fixing the S. Either use the two-band 4 + 8 kHz arrangement the NPR preset uses, or expose one frequency control.

7. Large limiter lookahead in a live mic path. Lookahead is added latency 1:1, and true-peak/oversampled limiting adds ~5 ms more (FabFilter). A 10 ms lookahead plus RNNoise's 10 ms frame plus PipeWire's own buffer will put self-monitoring latency into the range where speakers start stuttering. 2 ms lookahead is enough here because the 80–100 Hz high-pass has already removed most plosive energy. Budget the whole chain: target under ~15 ms added.

8. Ceiling at 0 dBFS. Inter-sample peaks will clip downstream, and anything that re-encodes (Discord/Opus, browser, OBS to AAC) will clip audibly. EBU R 128 uses −1 dBTP for linear programme and −2 dBTP ahead of data-reduction codecs. Use −1 dB generally, −2 dB for the Discord/Calls preset.

9. Hard-coded factory threshold values in dB. Every threshold in this chain (expander, compressor, de-esser) is meaningless without gain staging — this is why two reputable open-source mic presets differ by 26 dB on the gate threshold. Either normalise the input to a known reference level before the chain, or derive thresholds from a short noise-floor/speech-level measurement, or the presets will behave completely differently on a Fifine at +40 dB gain vs an interface at +20 dB.

10. Running an aggressive expander in front of RNNoise. Redundant, and it hands RNNoise a non-stationary gated noise floor that it is not trained on. If RNNoise is enabled, soften the expander.

11. Treating the near-flat "Studio/Natural" preset as bypass. It is not — it still has the HPF, a gentle expander and a limiter, so it will be quieter or brighter than true bypass. If the point is "hear processed vs unprocessed", give users an actual bypass toggle, loudness-matched, rather than relying on a flat preset.

12. Sources caveat. I could not verify Izhaki's "Mixing Audio" or Katz's "Mastering Audio" directly — the full-text host (dokumen.pub) was down during this research and no legitimate excerpt surfaced. Everything above is sourced from Rane Note 155, Sound On Sound, manufacturer docs (dbx, FabFilter, iZotope, Waves), open-source DSP documentation (LSP, Calf), two real EasyEffects mic preset files, and peer-reviewed speech-science literature for the syllable-rate and plosive-duration claims. Where a number comes only from a low-authority mixing blog (de-esser attack/release, max gain reduction) I have flagged it as such in the per-number source field and cross-checked it against the shipped presets.

research.consensus:
WHERE SOURCES AGREE

1) Gate depth converges on about -24 dB, not -inf. LSP's REDUCTION_DFL is -24 dB (gate.h:47) and Calf's "Max Gain Reduction" default is 0.06125 = -24.26 dB (metadata.cpp:593). Two independent projects landing within 0.3 dB is the strongest single agreement in this whole survey. A hard mute is NOT the default anybody ships.

2) Compressor threshold converges on -18 dBFS. OBS -18.0 (compressor-filter.c:441), Calf 0.125 = -18.06 dB (metadata.cpp:447). LSP is 6 dB hotter at -12 dB (compressor.h:37).

3) Detector is RMS everywhere by default. LSP SC_MODE_DFL = 1 = RMS in gate, compressor, expander and de-esser; Calf "detection" default 0 = RMS; OBS expander default detector string is "RMS". Peak detection is nobody's default.

4) Compressor attack/release cluster at 20 ms / 100-250 ms. LSP 20/100, Calf 20/250. OBS is the outlier at 6/60 — fast and grabby, tuned for a live stream rather than for transparency.

5) Makeup gain default is 0 dB in every single source (LSP MAKEUP_DFL = GAIN_AMP_0_DB in gate/compressor/expander; Calf makeup 1.0; OBS output gain 0.0). No project ships makeup baked in.

6) Knee is soft by default, 6-9 dB: LSP KNEE_DFL = -6 dB (compressor, expander, de-esser all identical), Calf 2.828427125 = +9.03 dB.

7) De-essing lives at 4-6 kHz. Calf's split is 6000 Hz with a +12 dB detector bell at 4500 Hz; LSP's detector band is HPF 2000 / LPF 10000 with peaks at 4000 and 6000 Hz. De-esser timing is uniformly faster than the main compressor: LSP 10 ms attack / 30 ms release vs 20/100 for its compressor.

8) RNNoise is immovably 480 samples at 48 kHz = 10 ms, in every wrapper (OBS, werman, Re-Nooice, upstream). Re-Nooice reports exactly 10 ms fixed latency.

WHERE SOURCES DISAGREE

a) Compression ratio: Calf 2:1, LSP 4:1, OBS 10:1. OBS's 10:1 at -18 dB is effectively a soft limiter, not a compressor — but it is what millions of streamers run untouched, so it is the honest prior for "Streaming", not for anything else.

b) Gate threshold: OBS -26 open / -32 close (with 6 dB hysteresis and a 200 ms hold), LSP -24 with 12 dB hysteresis and 0 ms hold, Calf -18 with no hysteresis concept at all. Calf's -18 is plainly wrong for a microphone and is a generic default, not a voice one. OBS is the only source whose gate defaults were actually tuned for a speaking human.

c) RNNoise VAD threshold: the LADSPA build has no explicit default at all — it uses LADSPA_HINT_DEFAULT_LOW, which the spec defines as 0.75·lower + 0.25·upper, giving ≈25 % on a 0…99 range. The JUCE build hard-codes 60 %. Re-Nooice hard-codes 60 %. The README recommends 85-95 %. The README's own copy-paste PipeWire config uses 50 %. That is five different numbers from one author. The two values the author actually wrote down as choices (JUCE 60, PipeWire snippet 50) are the ones to trust; the LADSPA ≈25 % is an artefact of a hint, not a decision.

d) Limiter ceiling: OBS -6 dBFS, LSP 0 dBFS. LSP also ships 5 ms of lookahead (real added latency); OBS ships none.

WHAT A CAREFUL ENGINEER WOULD TAKE AS THE DEFAULT

- Gate/expander: open ≈ -26 dBFS, close ≈ -32 dBFS (6 dB hysteresis), attack 10-25 ms, hold 150-200 ms, release 100-150 ms, depth -24 dB (not -inf), RMS detection. This is OBS's gate with LSP's and Calf's agreed -24 dB depth.
- Compressor: threshold -18 dBFS, ratio 2:1 (Studio/Natural, Warm) to 3-4:1 (Clean Voice, Podcast, Discord), 10 (fast, Streaming) to 20 ms attack, 60-100 ms release, 6 dB soft knee, RMS, makeup 0 dB shipped and set per preset only where you have measured it.
- De-esser: detector centred 5-6 kHz (split at ~6 kHz per Calf; LSP's 4/6 kHz peaks agree), threshold -12 to -18 dBFS, ratio 3-4:1, attack ≤10 ms, release 30-50 ms.
- Limiter: ceiling -3 to -1 dBFS for a virtual source feeding apps (OBS's -6 is over-conservative once your own makeup gain is in the chain and LSP's 0 dBFS leaves nothing for downstream Opus encoding), release ~60 ms, no oversampling, no dither — LSP ships OVS_NONE and DITHER_NONE.
- RNNoise stage: threshold 50-60 %, grace 200 ms, retroactive grace 0 ms. Off by default for Studio/Natural; off by default for Discord too (see warnings).

TWO GAPS THIS RESEARCH DOES NOT CLOSE

- The high-pass. NOT ONE of these projects ships a voice high-pass default. LSP's sidechain HPF defaults to 10 Hz, i.e. off (gate.h:92, compressor.h:102); Calf and OBS have no high-pass filter in these filters at all. So the 70-100 Hz figure everyone "knows" is not sourced from any of these — it needs its own pass (EBU/broadcast practice, or a specific mic manufacturer's guidance) before it goes into a preset.
- The ten EQ gains. No open-source project ships a 10-band graphic preset on FxSound's fixed centres (62.5 / 115.734 / 214.311 / 396.85 / 734.867 / 1360.79 / 2519.84 / 4666.12 / 8640.48 / 16000 Hz — these are the FxSound/DFX band set). The only band-shaping evidence available here is indirect: the de-essing region is 4-6 kHz (so 4666.12 Hz is the band to cut for sibilance), and Calf's detector bell has Q 1.0 at 4.5 kHz. The EQ curves will have to be justified from voice-EQ practice, not from shipped plugin defaults, and that should be stated honestly rather than dressed up as sourced.

research.warnings:
1. DO NOT run a gate and RNNoise's VAD gating at the same time with both tight. They are two independent gates in series; a word start has to survive both. RNNoise's retroactive grace exists precisely to un-chop word starts, and it buys that at the cost of latency. If RNNoise is on, loosen the gate (or drop it to an expander) rather than stacking.

2. Retroactive VAD grace is pure added latency, 10 ms per block, on top of RNNoise's own fixed 10 ms. The LADSPA default hint resolves to 50 ms of it — so a user who loads the LADSPA plugin and touches nothing may be paying ~60 ms before your chain's limiter lookahead is even counted. werman's own JUCE default and PipeWire snippet both set it to 0. Ship 0.

3. The Discord preset should process LESS, not more. Discord runs Krisp noise suppression, echo cancellation and AGC on your stream by default. A WebRTC-class AGC targets -3 dBFS, applies up to 9 dB of digital compression gain, and hard-limits (audio_processing.h:314/319/323). Two consequences: (a) heavy upstream compression raises your noise floor, and the client's AGC then amplifies that floor during pauses — classic pumping/breathing that users blame on Discord; (b) your makeup gain is largely wasted because the AGC renormalises anyway. Keep Discord's preset gentle: shallow ratio, modest makeup, ceiling around -3 dBFS so the client's limiter never engages.

4. Do not run RNNoise by default in the Discord preset. Krisp is already a neural suppressor with its own VAD. Two neural suppressors in series produce artefacts neither produces alone, and Krisp resamples to its model's operational rate (often 32 kHz) and back, so anything you carefully preserved above ~16 kHz is discarded downstream anyway. That also makes a 16 kHz EQ boost in a Discord preset actively pointless.

5. Do not copy OBS's compressor ratio of 10:1 into anything except the Streaming preset. It is defensible as "what streamers use", but at a -18 dB threshold it is a limiter wearing a compressor's name. For Clean Voice / Podcast / Warm, LSP's 4:1 and Calf's 2:1 are the better-founded priors.

6. Do not copy Calf's gate threshold (-18 dBFS). It is a generic dynamics default that happens to sit in the gate's port table; at -18 dBFS a gate will chop the tails and quiet consonants of normal speech. Calf's gate and Calf's compressor share an identical parameter block, which is itself the tell that neither was tuned for microphones.

7. Do not copy LSP's de-esser SPLIT_FREQ_DFL of 1500 Hz as a de-essing frequency. It is a crossover default with a 500-4000 Hz range, i.e. it cannot even reach the sibilance region. LSP's actual sibilance detection is the 2-10 kHz sidechain band with peaks at 4 and 6 kHz (deesser.h:76-93). Calf's 6000 Hz split is the number that means what you want it to mean.

8. Do not ship LSP's limiter threshold of 0 dBFS. A 0 dBFS ceiling leaves zero headroom for the Opus encoder downstream (Discord, Zoom, OBS's own encoder), and inter-sample peaks will clip after encoding. LSP also defaults to no oversampling and no true-peak detection, so its 0 dBFS is a sample-peak ceiling, not a true-peak one.

9. Limiter lookahead is not free. LSP's 5 ms lookahead default is 5 ms of microphone latency. For a live mic chain, either accept and document the total (HPF 0 + gate 0 + EQ ~0 + limiter 5 ms + RNNoise 10 ms ≈ 15 ms) or use a zero-lookahead limiter and accept slightly worse transient control. Do not let it accumulate silently across stages.

10. RNNoise will not work at anything but 48 kHz. werman's README is emphatic: "use ONLY 48000 Hz". If the virtual source can be opened at 44.1 kHz, the RNNoise stage must resample (as OBS does) or be disabled, not run at the wrong rate.

11. Treat the Discord claims in this report as the weakest link. Discord's own Krisp FAQ is behind a Cloudflare bot-check that I did not bypass, so the "on by default" statement is second-hand. The structural claim — that a VoIP client applies AEC + NS + AGC with a limiter, and that this is what your preset is feeding — is solidly grounded in the WebRTC APM source; the Discord-specific UI wording and any per-level numbers are not. Verify manually before writing them into user-facing preset descriptions.

12. The LADSPA "defaults" in werman's plugin are not authored defaults. They are LADSPA_HINT_DEFAULT_LOW, which hosts compute as 0.75·min + 0.25·max. Different hosts round integers differently, so users on different hosts get different starting points for the same plugin. If you expose these parameters, set them explicitly rather than inheriting the hint.

research.consensus:
WHAT THE SOURCES AGREE ON (region names)

Every source consulted — iZotope (manufacturer), Sound On Sound (trade press), and the community cheat-sheets — uses effectively the same map, so the region names can be treated as settled: below ~100 Hz rumble (high-pass territory, not EQ); 100-400 Hz body/warmth, turning into boom and proximity effect when excessive; 250-500 Hz mud, densest at 250-350 Hz; 400-800 Hz boxy/papery/throaty; 800 Hz-1.5 kHz nasal/honky; 1.5-5 kHz presence and intelligibility with the core at 2-4 kHz; 4-10 kHz sibilance; 8-20 kHz air/sparkle. The only meaningful disagreement is the sibilance boundary: Sound On Sound gives one wide 4-10 kHz range and declines to split it by gender, while the popular guides split it into male 4-7 kHz and female 6-9 kHz. For our purposes the wide range is the safer engineering assumption.

MAPPING ONTO OUR TEN CENTRES

Each band owns 0.889 octave at Q = 1.5976. The -3 dB spans and the perceptual content:

- Band 0, 62.5 Hz (46-85 Hz) — pure rumble: HVAC, desk thump, footfall, the tail of plosives. Below essentially every speech fundamental. Raising it re-imports exactly what the high-pass removed and eats limiter headroom; lowering it is nearly a no-op (see the high-pass analysis below). Sane maximum: 0 dB. Use 0.0 in all six presets.
- Band 1, 115.734 Hz (85-157 Hz) — the male fundamental and chest/proximity boom. This is the real low-end control of the chain. Raising: weight and authority, but boom and plosive energy first. Lowering: removes close-mic boom cleanly. Sane range -3..+2 dB; past -4 dB a male voice goes hollow.
- Band 2, 214.311 Hz (157-292 Hz) — female fundamental, male second harmonic, the "body" a voice is judged warm or thin by. Its top edge is already in mud. Sane range -3..+2 dB.
- Band 3, 396.85 Hz (292-540 Hz) — the mud/boxiness core and the single most useful cut on the ladder for a close mic in an untreated room. Sane range -4..+1 dB; below -5 dB the voice goes thin and telephone-like.
- Band 4, 734.867 Hz (540-1000 Hz) — boxy, papery, throaty; the lower edge of nasality. Almost always a cut or zero. Sane range -3..+1 dB. Boosting here is what makes a preset sound like a cheap conference speaker.
- Band 5, 1360.79 Hz (1000-1852 Hz) — nasal/honky upper half, and the start of real intelligibility. Two-sided and touchy. Sane range ±2 dB; a boost beyond +3 dB is the "megaphone" sound.
- Band 6, 2519.84 Hz (1852-3429 Hz) — the presence and intelligibility core, the highest-value band on the ladder for speech. iZotope's explicit guidance for this region is that 1-2 dB is the normal move. Sane range -2..+3 dB; past +4 dB it is harsh and edgy, and it drives consonant peaks into the compressor and de-esser that follow.
- Band 7, 4666.12 Hz (3429-6350 Hz) — upper presence, consonant definition, and the lower half of sibilance. The most dangerous band we have: it cannot add clarity without also adding esses. Sane range ±2 dB, and treat +2 dB as the ceiling for any shipped preset.
- Band 8, 8640.48 Hz (6350-11758 Hz) — air and brightness, but also the top of female sibilance, breath noise, and microphone hiss. Sane range -2..+2 dB; +2 dB is already audible as extra hiss on a cheap mic once the makeup gain is applied.
- Band 9, 16000 Hz (11758-21773 Hz) — for speech this is almost entirely noise, breath and codec artifacts; there is little vocal harmonic content left up there. Sane range -3..+1 dB; recommend 0 or a small cut, never a "sparkle" boost on a microphone chain.

WHAT FALLS BETWEEN OUR CENTRES (and therefore cannot be addressed)

The crossover points are 85, 157, 292, 540, 1000, 1852, 3429, 6350 and 11758 Hz. Four collisions matter:

1. Sibilance. The 5-9 kHz core lands almost exactly on the 6350 Hz crossover between band 7 and band 8. Neither band can reach it cleanly: pulling band 7 down takes 3.4-5 kHz presence and consonant definition with it, making the voice dull rather than de-essed; pulling band 8 down takes the air with it and still only catches the upper half of the ess. Using both is worse — it cuts a full octave and a half out of the top. Conclusion: sibilance is structurally out of reach of this EQ and must be the de-esser's job. Both open-source Linux mic presets confirm this by bracketing 4 kHz and 8 kHz in the de-esser rather than in the EQ, and Sound On Sound's detector recipe (high-pass at 4 kHz, peak at 7.5 kHz) sits in exactly the hole our ladder leaves.
2. Nasality at ~1 kHz sits precisely on the band 4 / band 5 crossover. A 1 kHz notch has to be made by cutting both bands by a smaller amount each, not by one band.
3. Mud at 250-350 Hz straddles the 292 Hz crossover between bands 2 and 3. Band 3 catches most of it; band 2 catches the rest but also takes body.
4. The 3400 Hz top of the telephony band sits on the band 6 / band 7 crossover — which is convenient rather than a problem, because it means a "cut everything above the voice band" preset for Discord/Calls has a natural hinge there.

GRAPHIC-EQ PRACTICE ON A FIXED LADDER

Rane's overview (Bohn) sets out the two schools: with proportional-Q the bandwidth varies inversely with slider position, whereas a constant-Q design keeps bandwidth fixed at all boost/cut levels. Our EQ is constant-Q in practice: the port does contain a small-gain Q-widening rule, but it only bites below about 0.42 dB, so at any usable preset value the band is always 0.889 octave. That contradicts the common intuition that small slider moves are automatically broad — on this ladder they are not, so a broad gentle curve must be built by moving several adjacent bands a little, never one band a lot.

Two quantitative facts a preset author has to internalise:
- Bands overlap heavily, so gains add. Two neighbours at +3 dB each produce a +3.6 dB plateau (not +6), and three at +3 dB each produce +4.12 dB in the middle. The nominal slider values understate the resulting curve by roughly 20% per added neighbour. Author the curve, then check the composite, then scale back.
- A single band already bleeds ~0.5-0.6 dB into each neighbouring centre at +3 dB. Nothing on this ladder is surgical, which is precisely why narrow large moves fail: a -6 dB attempt at a resonance takes most of an octave and a half with it and reads as a hole, whereas -2 dB on two adjacent bands reads as tone.

On cutting versus boosting, Rane is deliberately even-handed — boosting costs headroom, and cut-only designs need makeup gain that costs the same headroom. But our chain settles the argument in favour of cutting, because the EQ sits before the de-esser, compressor, makeup gain and limiter. An EQ boost is not just a level change: it changes what the compressor's and de-esser's detectors see. A +3 dB presence boost makes the compressor pump on consonants and the de-esser over-trigger; the same tonal result reached by cutting the neighbours and letting the makeup gain restore the level leaves the detectors seeing a flatter signal. The vendor's own presets agree in spirit: 11 of the 13 shipped FxSound presets on this exact ladder stay inside -4..+5 dB and most moves are ±1 to ±3 dB. The ±12 dB range is a limit, not a working range.

THE HIGH-PASS / BAND 0 / BAND 1 QUESTION — RECOMMENDATION

With the planned high-pass at 75-100 Hz, band 0 and band 1 end up in completely different situations, and this is the clearest single conclusion of this research.

Band 0 at 62.5 Hz covers 46-85 Hz — the entire band sits inside the high-pass's stopband. Measured for a Butterworth response: a 4th-order high-pass at 80 Hz already gives -9.1 dB at 62.5 Hz, and at 100 Hz it gives -16.4 dB. There is essentially nothing left there for the band to act on. Cutting it is close to a no-op for its stated purpose and is actively harmful for a reason that is easy to miss: because the bell is 0.889 octave wide, a -3 dB move at 62.5 Hz also produces -1.83 dB at 80 Hz and -0.88 dB at 100 Hz — it thins the bottom of the voice you just decided to keep, while removing rumble that is already gone. Boosting it is worse: it fights the high-pass, re-introduces the rumble and plosive energy the high-pass was installed to remove, and spends limiter headroom on inaudible content.

Recommendation: set band 0 to exactly 0.0 dB in all six presets, and pair it with a 4th-order (24 dB/oct) high-pass at 80 Hz as the default, 75 Hz for the Warm Voice and Studio/Natural presets, and 100 Hz for Discord/Calls where narrowband intelligibility matters more than weight. This matches the vendor: band 0 is 0 dB in all 13 shipped FxSound factory presets, including the extreme one. Consider exposing band 0 in the UI as disabled or annotated ("handled by the high-pass") rather than as a live control, so users do not spend it on a phantom problem.

Band 1 at 115.734 Hz is the opposite case. Its span is 85-157 Hz and the same 80 Hz 4th-order high-pass leaves it at -0.2 dB — untouched. It contains the male fundamental (90-155 Hz), which means it is the only genuinely effective low-frequency control in the chain and the band that decides whether a voice sounds boomy or thin. Give it the full working range. Suggested per-preset starting values for the two bands: Clean Voice 0 / -1; Streaming 0 / -2; Podcast 0 / 0 (or +1 for warmth); Discord/Calls 0 / -3 with the 100 Hz high-pass; Warm Voice 0 / +2 with the 75 Hz high-pass; Studio/Natural 0 / 0.

FACTUAL CORRECTION TO THE TASK'S PREMISE

The centres are not actually immovable. The .fac format stores a centre frequency per band, the port applies preset centres verbatim (`app.rs:409`), and shipped preset 6.fac already uses 13500 Hz for band 10 instead of 16000 Hz. So a microphone preset could legitimately place band 8 at 6.3-7 kHz and cover the sibilance gap in the EQ itself. Two costs come with that, and they are why I would still not do it: the derived Q is computed from band count and the min/max band frequencies, not from the actual centres, so the band would still be 0.889 octave wide and would still take presence or air with it; and the GUI slider labels and the user's mental model of "my ten bands" would stop matching between the music and microphone chains. Better to keep the ladder fixed as planned and let the de-esser own 4-10 kHz — but the parent agent should know the option exists rather than believing the ladder is a hard constraint.

WHAT I COULD NOT VERIFY

I could not obtain the actual ANSI/ASA S3.5-1997 band-importance numbers — the standard is paywalled and the open mirrors I tried were unreachable. So the claim that 1-4 kHz dominates intelligibility rests here on the engineering literature and on the 300-3400 Hz telephony band, not on the standard's own weights. If exact per-band importance weights are wanted to justify the presence-band choices numerically, that needs a copy of the standard.
research.warnings:
1. Do NOT cut band 0 (62.5 Hz) to "remove rumble". The high-pass in front of the EQ has already removed it (-9.1 dB at 62.5 Hz for an 80 Hz 4th-order, -16.4 dB at 100 Hz). All a band-0 cut achieves is -1.8 dB at 80 Hz and -0.9 dB at 100 Hz from the bell's skirt, i.e. it thins the voice's real bottom end while doing nothing about the rumble. This is the most likely mistake in a hand-authored preset and it looks completely reasonable on the slider.

2. Do NOT try to de-ess with bands 7 and 8. Sibilance centres on 5-9 kHz, which lands on the 6350 Hz crossover between them. Any EQ attempt costs either presence (band 7 also covers 3.4-5 kHz consonant definition) or air (band 8 also covers 6.3-11.7 kHz), it is static where sibilance is intermittent, and it will make the preset sound dull rather than clean. This is what the de-esser stage exists for.

3. Do NOT boost band 7 (4666 Hz) for "clarity". It is the single most damaging boost available: it adds sibilance and harshness, and because the EQ sits before the de-esser and the compressor, it also makes the de-esser over-trigger and the compressor pump on consonants. If a preset needs more intelligibility, use band 6 (2519 Hz) at +1..+3 dB, which is where the presence core actually is.

4. Do NOT boost band 9 (16 kHz) for "air" on a microphone chain. There is almost no speech harmonic content above 12 kHz — what is there is mic self-noise, breath and codec artifacts, and the gate and makeup gain downstream will make the added hiss more audible, not less. If a preset wants air, band 8 at +1..+2 dB is the honest place.

5. Beware the sample rate. On a Bluetooth headset using HFP/mSBC the capture rate is 16 kHz (Nyquist 8 kHz) and with CVSD it is 8 kHz. Band 9 and most of band 8 are then at or above Nyquist. A preset that relies on them will do nothing on exactly the devices whose users most want help, and the biquad design should be checked for what it produces when f0 approaches or exceeds Nyquist. Consider clamping or bypassing bands above ~0.4 x sample rate.

6. The ±12 dB range is a trap. FxSound's own 13 shipped presets on this exact ladder almost all live inside ±3 dB, and the one that uses ±12 is a novelty effect. A ±12 dB voice preset will sound processed, will collapse under the compressor, and will not survive a listener's codec.

7. Slider dB is not resulting dB. Bands overlap at 0.889 octave and Q 1.598, so neighbours sum: three adjacent bands at +3 dB each give +4.1 dB, not +3 or +9. Always evaluate the composite response of a candidate preset, not the individual values. Conversely, do not expect two neighbours at +3 to give +6 and then push them to +6 each to compensate — that gives +8.3 dB.

8. Small slider moves are NOT automatically wide here. The intuition from proportional-Q graphics does not apply: the port's Q-widening rule only engages below about 0.42 dB, so a -1 dB move is just as narrow as a -12 dB move. Broadness has to be authored by spreading the move across adjacent bands.

9. Do not reuse music-EQ shapes. A "smiley" curve, a bass boost, or anything borrowed from the playback chain's presets is wrong for a microphone: it amplifies exactly the proximity boom, room mud and hiss that the mic chain is there to remove.

10. Do not cut band 3 (396 Hz) hard to "clean up mud". Past about -5 dB the voice loses the body that 292-540 Hz carries and starts sounding like a telephone. Mud is better handled by -2..-3 dB across bands 3 and 4 together, plus getting the speaker's mic distance right, than by one deep cut.

11. Studio/Natural must be genuinely flat. Its stated purpose is an A/B reference for processed versus unprocessed. If it carries even ±1 dB of EQ the comparison is dishonest and users will not trust the other presets. Ship it as all-zero gains with the rest of the chain at its gentlest (high-pass 75 Hz, minimal gate, low-ratio compressor), and be explicit in the UI that it is not bypass.

12. One premise in the task is not quite right: the centres are per-preset in the file format and the port applies them (see consensus, final section). Treat "fixed ladder" as a product decision to uphold, not as a technical limit — and do not let a future contributor silently move a centre, because the derived Q will not follow it.

preset.intent: The universal default for anyone who plugs in a microphone and does not want to think about it: rumble and desk noise removed, room tone eased down rather than gated shut, a small amount of mud taken out and a small amount of presence added, levelled by about 4 dB so the voice stops ducking in and out — and nothing that a listener could name as an effect.
preset.name: Clean Voice
preset.rationale:
GOVERNING IDEA. Clean Voice is the first thing a user hears, on an unknown microphone, at an unknown gain, in an unknown room, feeding an app that will very likely process again (Discord runs Krisp + AEC + AGC; OBS's own limiter defaults to -6 dBFS). Two constraints follow and they set every number below: (a) every move must be small enough that it cannot make a good microphone worse, and (b) no stage may depend on a level assumption I cannot verify. Where the dossier offers a tuned-but-aggressive number and a conservative one, I take the conservative one and say so.

HIGH-PASS — 80 Hz, 2nd-order Butterworth (12 dB/oct).
80 Hz is the one number every independent source agrees on: Shure says 70-90 Hz for speech, RODE says 80, BOYA says start at 75, and 80 Hz appears in every surveyed Linux mic preset that has a dedicated filter (MateusRodCosta, aeolyus, dzervas) and as EQ band 0 in jtrv's. The floor is set by the adult male fundamental, 85-180 Hz: 100 Hz costs a deep male voice ~3.5 dB of fundamental (measured from WebRTC's shipped coefficients), 120-150 Hz audibly thins it. 80 Hz leaves it alone — computed for a 2nd-order Butterworth at 80 Hz, the residual is -5.66 dB at 62.5 Hz, -0.89 dB at 115.734 Hz, -0.08 dB at 214.311 Hz. I chose 2nd order rather than the 4th order one researcher preferred because Clean Voice's job is to sound untouched: 12 dB/oct is the topology every VoIP stack ships on the capture path (WebRTC's filter is literally `butter(2,100/fs,'high')`), it costs no meaningful latency, and its phase behaviour around the fundamental is gentler. 300 Hz is not considered: that is G.712 telephone-channel allocation, and ITU itself moved the low edge back down (G.722 50-7000, P.341 ~100-8000).
This filter is also the chain's plosive defence, which is what lets the limiter run a short lookahead later, and it is deliberately first so rumble never reaches the expander or compressor detector. It is also, per AES TD1008 §7B, on the correct side of the limiter ("filtering, if used, should ideally occur before the peak limiter").

EQ — [0.0, 0.0, -1.0, -1.5, -0.5, 0.0, +1.5, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] dB.
I verified the ladder in this repo rather than trusting the brief: crates/fxsound-dsp/src/eq.rs gives r = 1.85175 between centres (exactly 8/9 octave) and Q = sqrt(r)/(r-1) = 1.5976, and biquad.rs only widens Q below ~0.42 dB of gain — so these bands are constant-Q and each one is nearly a full octave wide. Nothing here is surgical, so the curve is authored as a shape and then checked as a composite. Computed composite of the ten values above: -0.05 dB at 62.5, -0.25 at 115.7, -1.29 at 214.3, -1.76 at 396.9, -0.76 at 734.9, +0.12 at 1360.8, +1.46 at 2519.8, +0.27 at 4666.1, +0.05 at 8640.5. In between: -0.17 dB at 100 Hz, -1.31 at 300, -1.23 at 500, +1.12 at 3 kHz. Net: a broad ~1.5 dB scoop from 200 to 700 Hz and a ~3.2 dB tilt from 400 Hz to 3 kHz. Log-mean over 100-8000 Hz is -0.27 dB, i.e. essentially no broadband gain for the makeup stage to compensate.
- 62.5 Hz = 0.0. Deliberate, per the hard constraint. The band spans 46-85 Hz and the high-pass has already put -5.7 dB there; cutting it would add only skirt (-1.8 dB at 80 Hz for a -3 dB slider move) and thin the voice I just decided to keep, while boosting it would re-import exactly what the filter removed and spend limiter headroom on inaudible content. FxSound's own 13 shipped factory presets on this ladder leave 62.5 Hz at 0 dB without exception.
- 115.734 Hz = 0.0. This is the only genuinely effective low control in the chain (85-157 Hz, HPF residual only -0.89 dB) and the sources point both ways for good reasons: generic vocal practice cuts 100-250 Hz as boomy, while the one preset tuned for a cheap USB condenser boosts 90 Hz by +3 dB because that class of mic is thin, not boomy. Proximity effect is worth up to +16 dB and depends entirely on how close the speaker sits — no fixed preset can track it. Since I cannot know the mic or the distance, and since either sign is audibly wrong for half the users, 0.0 is the only defensible universal value. Warm Voice and Discord/Calls are where this band should move.
- 214.3 / 396.9 / 734.9 = -1.0 / -1.5 / -0.5. The mud cut, and the only correction all three real voice presets agree on (jtrv -2 at 220 and 350; azmarifdev -2 at 425; luix -1 at 300).
