Their -2 dB is spread across two overlapping octave-wide bands here, so I scaled back: the composite still reaches -1.8 dB at 396.9 Hz and holds ~-1.3 dB from 250 to 500 Hz, which is the region iZotope, Shure and RODE all name. Spreading it across three bands rather than cutting one hard is the explicit recommendation for this ladder and avoids the "telephone" failure mode that starts around -5 dB at 396.9.
- 1360.8 = 0.0. Nasal/honk region; two-sided and touchy, nothing in the dossier asks for a move.
- 2519.8 = +1.5. The presence and intelligibility core (1852-3429 Hz), and the highest-value band available. iZotope's explicit limit for this region is "no more than 1 or 2 dB"; Shure's own SM7B presence switch — a manufacturer's deliberate voicing, i.e. the ceiling — is about +3 to +4 dB. +1.5 slider (+1.46 composite, +1.12 at 3 kHz) is comfortably below both, and it is where the other presets' +2 to +3 dB at 3.2-3.5 kHz actually lands on this ladder.
- 4666.1 = 0.0. The strongest single "do not" in the dossier, and I agree with it: this band covers 3429-6350 Hz, so it cannot add clarity without adding sibilance, and because the EQ sits ahead of the de-esser it would make the de-esser over-trigger and then cancel the move dynamically — worse than not making it. The +0.27 dB it receives from band 6's skirt is already as much lift as this region should get.
- 8640.5 and 16000 = 0.0. This is where I depart from the three community presets, which all add +2 dB of "air" from 9-10 kHz. Three reasons: (1) on a budget USB condenser this region is mostly self-noise (FIFINE publishes 78 dB S/N and -80 dBFS equivalent noise) and the +6 dB makeup downstream amplifies it; (2) an air lift feeds the de-esser's detector; (3) on an HFP/mSBC Bluetooth headset, 16 kHz is at or above Nyquist and 8640 Hz is near it, so the boost does nothing on exactly the devices whose users most need help. A Streaming or Podcast preset on a known-good mic can take the air; the universal default should not.
Everything stays inside ±1.5 dB. That is not timidity, it is the vendor's own practice: 11 of 13 shipped FxSound presets on this ladder live inside -4..+5 dB with typical moves of ±1-3 dB, and the only one using ±12 is a novelty.
Honest gap: no source measures the FIFINE-class response, and no open-source project ships a preset on these centres. The shape above is transferred from three parametric voice curves; the exact dB values on these ten centres are my mapping, checked against the composite, not something anybody published.

EXPANDER ("gate") — threshold -45 dBFS, ratio 2.0:1, attack 5 ms, hold 120 ms, release 200 ms.
Ratio 2.0 (not a hard gate) is Rane Note 155's stated figure for expansion used as noise reduction, and every source in the dossier warns that an infinite-ratio gate on speech chatters at the threshold and amputates voiceless fricatives (/s/, /f/, /th/) and plosive tails, which sit only a few dB above room tone. At 2:1 a signal 10 dB under the threshold is pulled down 10 dB and a signal 20 dB under is pulled down 20 dB — room tone is pushed well below audibility while a quiet consonant onset loses only a few dB. LSP and Calf independently ship a -24 dB depth floor rather than a mute; if the implementation exposes a reduction floor, set it to -16 dB (Fedora Magazine's -12/-18 recommendation; the tuned presets sit at -12 to -16) — the schema here has no field for it, so I am naming it rather than silently assuming it.
Threshold -45 dBFS is the weakest number in this preset and I will say so plainly: the dossier's two best-tuned presets differ by 26 dB on this control (-50 vs -24), which is a gain-staging difference, not a disagreement, and it means a fixed dBFS threshold cannot be right for every mic. -45 is chosen as the safe side of the tutorial consensus (-40 to -50 dBFS) — low enough that normal speech, including trailing consonants, never approaches it on a correctly-gained mic, high enough to sit above a cheap condenser's floor. It should be replaced by a measured noise-floor offset (floor + ~8 dB) as soon as the product can measure one.
Attack 5 ms: both shipped Linux presets use it; 20 ms (the LSP/Calf default and OBS's 25 ms) lands the gain change on the word onset. Hold 120 ms: the speech envelope peaks at 4-8 Hz, i.e. a syllable every 125-250 ms, so a hold near 120 ms spans inter-syllable gaps and is the direct cure for chattering; OBS ships 200 ms, the tutorials say 100-200. Release 200 ms sits mid-range of the 100-250 ms consensus and fades under a word tail instead of chopping it. If the optional RNNoise stage is enabled, soften this stage rather than stacking two gates in series.
Note on chain order: because the expander sits ahead of the compressor and +6 dB of makeup, it cannot see the noise floor it is ultimately responsible for. That is a property of the fixed stage order, not of these numbers, and it is another reason to keep the ratio gentle rather than chase silence here.

DE-ESSER — split 5500 Hz, threshold -22 dBFS, ratio 3:1, max reduction 4 dB, attack 1 ms, release 80 ms.
Split-band, not wideband: Wikipedia, iZotope and the practical argument all agree that ducking the whole signal on every "s" dips the vowel underneath it, and on this chain a wideband duck would then be re-levelled by the compressor immediately downstream — audible full-band pumping. Calf's own manual recommends Wide for a single voice, and four surveyed presets use it; I am siding against Calf here because in those four presets Wide is simply the untouched factory default, while both presets whose authors actually retuned the de-esser (jtrv, luix-voice) chose Split.
5500 Hz splits the difference between the male centre (5-6 kHz) and the female (7-8 kHz), which a single fixed preset has to straddle: Sound On Sound gives 4-10 kHz and declines to split it by gender, RODE says 4-7 kHz, FabFilter says s-sounds are usually 8-10 kHz, Calf's split default is 6000 Hz, LSP's detector peaks sit at 4 and 6 kHz. It also covers the hole this EQ structurally cannot reach: sibilance centres almost exactly on the 6350 Hz crossover between bands 7 and 8, so the de-esser, not the EQ, must own it. I did not take azmarifdev's 3000 Hz — that is inside the intelligibility region and produces a lisp.
Threshold -22 dBFS is jtrv's value and 3-4 dB below the -18/-20 modal, chosen deliberately because of a defect in the fixed stage order: the de-esser here runs BEFORE the compressor, so anything it removes gets partially re-amplified downstream, and the compressor's slow 20 ms attack passes sibilant transients while clamping vowels, which raises sibilance relative to the rest by roughly the amount of gain reduction. The dossier's conclusion is explicit — with this order you must de-ess somewhat harder. The safety against over-de-essing is not a high threshold but the 4 dB reduction cap: mastering practice puts typical reduction at 2-4 dB and warns that uncapped reduction collapses /s/ toward /th/. 4 dB cannot lisp; it can only fail to be enough, which is the right failure direction for a default. Ratio 3:1 is unanimous across every tuned preset and guide.
Attack 1 ms because sibilance is a short noisy burst that must be caught, not passed (LSP's de-esser ships 10 ms attack / 30 ms release, far faster than its own compressor; mastering guides say 0.1-1 ms). Release 80 ms is mid-range of the 40-150 ms window — long enough not to modulate, short enough that the band recovers before the following vowel, which is what stops the dull/lisping sound.
Test criterion, per dbx's own manual: on "she sells sea shells" the detector should flicker on hard S's and the S's must still be identifiable as S.

COMPRESSOR — threshold -18 dBFS, ratio 3:1, knee 6 dB soft, attack 20 ms, release 150 ms.
-18 dBFS is the strongest convergence in the whole dossier: OBS ships -18.0, Calf ships 0.125 linear = -18.06 dB, jtrv tuned to -18. With ratio 3:1 a speech peak at -12 dBFS gets exactly 4 dB of gain reduction ((-12 - -18) x (1 - 1/3)), landing in the middle of Rane Note 155's stated target of 3-6 dB on normal speech and ~0 dB on quiet passages — which is how a threshold should be justified, rather than by quoting a dB number. Ratio 3:1 is RODE's stated vocal range (2:1-4:1), Rane's "gentle" band, and the value both careful researchers assigned to Clean Voice. I explicitly do not take OBS's default 10:1, which at -18 dB is a limiter wearing a compressor's name.
Attack 20 ms is the single most important number here and it contradicts the common "1-5 ms for vocals" advice. A stop-consonant burst is a transient of a few ms up to ~35 ms; an attack of 1-5 ms clamps the burst itself, so /p/ /t/ /k/ lose their release and /s/ /f/ lose their onset, and the voice goes dull and mushy in exactly the band that carries intelligibility. Rane gives 25-100 ms for vocals, jtrv uses 15, MateusRodCosta 20; 20 ms is the honest middle and passes the consonant while still clamping the vowel behind it.
Release 150 ms is tied to syllable rate, not picked freely: the speech envelope's modulation spectrum peaks at 4-8 Hz (dominant ~4.5-5 Hz), one syllable per 125-250 ms. Shorter and the compressor recovers inside each syllable, which is audible as breathing on the noise floor between words; much longer and it rides down a loud sentence and buries the next quiet one. 150 ms sits inside that window and between the two shipped presets (100 and 200 ms). Note Rane's caveat: release is specified in dB/second in some implementations, so actual recovery scales with the amount of reduction — if this engine works that way, 150 ms is the constant, not the wall-clock recovery.
Knee 6 dB, expressed here as a positive width. Every surveyed plugin uses a 6-9 dB soft knee (LSP -6 dB, Calf +9.03 dB) and it is what makes the transition between compressed and uncompressed syllables inaudible. LSP writes this same knee as -6 dB, meaning "6 dB of knee below the threshold" — if the FxSound implementation follows LSP's sign convention, this value must be stored as -6.0, not 6.0. This conversion must be done explicitly in the code, not assumed.

MAKEUP — +6.0 dB, and it must be measured before shipping.
Derived, not picked: the TASCAM/Waves auto-makeup rule gives 0.5 x |threshold| x (1 - 1/ratio) = 0.5 x 18 x 0.667 = 6.0 dB. The EQ contributes essentially nothing to correct for — the computed log-mean of my curve over 100-8000 Hz is -0.27 dB — which is one of the reasons the curve was kept net-neutral. Result: about +2 dB net versus dry on loud speech (6 dB makeup less 4 dB of gain reduction) and about +6 dB on quiet passages, which is the levelling the preset exists to do.
The honest caveat, which the dossier is emphatic about: a hand-picked makeup constant makes the six factory presets mutually unmatched, and users then prefer whichever is loudest. 6.0 dB is the correct starting value from the formula; it must then be verified by metering the chain on one fixed speech reference and trimmed so short-term (3 s) loudness lands near -18 LUFS measured on the stereo virtual source — equivalently -21 LUFS if the meter is fed the single channel, because duplicating mono into two channels adds 3.01 LU under BS.1770's channel summation. That mono/stereo direction is the single highest-risk number in this task: the brief's "-16 mono / -19 stereo" is inverted, it is -16 LUFS stereo and -19 LUFS mono (Google's speech guideline and Podnews both state it that way). The -18 LUFS figure is AES TD1008's published distribution loudness for speech, which sits ~2 LU below the music figure because speech at equal BS.1770 loudness is perceived 2-3 dB louder. Do not use EBU R128's -23 LUFS (a broadcast programme target with a downstream amplifier), do not use -14 (a playback normaliser's operating point), and keep the integrated result above -20 LUFS (TD1008 §5) so a low-gain client is not inaudible. Do not servo this from an integrated measurement in real time — integrated loudness is defined over a programme, it is not a control signal.

LIMITER CEILING — -3.0 dBFS.
-1 dBTP is the published ceiling (EBU R128 §m, AES TD1008 §4, Spotify, Apple) and it assumes you are the last processing stage before one known encoder. This chain is neither. Four documented reasons to take more margin: (1) TD1008 §7B states outright that the limiting threshold must go below -1.0 dBTP as bitrate falls, and Discord's Opus negotiates down to tens of kbps; (2) a cheap real-time brick wall detects sample peaks, not true peaks, and the two differ — that is the whole reason BS.1770-5 Annex 2 defines 4x-oversampled true-peak measurement, and libopus concedes the point structurally by shipping opus_pcm_soft_clip(); (3) TD1008 documents up to 3 dB of gain reduction in a decode-side OS limiter when the encode side left insufficient headroom; (4) OBS's own limiter already defaults to a -6 dBFS threshold and a WebRTC-class client AGC targets -3 dBFS with its own limiter, so something downstream will re-limit this signal anyway. -3 dBFS costs nothing perceptually and buys margin against all four. The label is dBFS sample peak, not dBTP, and should say so in the UI unless the limiter oversamples.
Companion settings the schema has no field for, stated so they are not left to chance: lookahead 2 ms, release ~60 ms, and gain-boost/upward gain OFF. 2 ms is enough here precisely because the 80 Hz high-pass already defused the plosive, and lookahead is added latency 1:1 (LSP's 5 ms default is 5 ms of microphone latency for no benefit in this chain). Target no more than ~1 dB of gain reduction on normal speech — TD1008 warns that more than about 1 dB of limiting produces more audible artefacts than the occasional transient would; if this preset habitually sits on the limiter, the makeup gain above it is wrong. Nothing may apply gain after this stage: two surveyed presets are broken in exactly that way and are not to be copied.

LATENCY BUDGET. HPF ~0 + expander 0 + EQ ~0 + de-esser 0 + limiter lookahead 2 ms = ~2 ms, plus 10 ms if the optional RNNoise stage is on (it is fixed at 480 samples / 48 kHz and cannot be shortened). That stays well under the ~15 ms where self-monitoring starts to interfere with speaking.

ONE DEFECT IN THE PLANNED CHAIN THAT THIS PRESET CANNOT FIX. RNNoise is placed after the brick-wall limiter. No surveyed preset does this, and AES TD1008 §7B is explicit that filtering belongs before the peak limiter because removing programme energy raises peaks (their square-wave example gains 2.1 dB). RNNoise is spectral gain modification of exactly that class and also has its own VAD gate, so with it enabled the last thing the listener hears is not limited and can exceed the ceiling this preset just enforced. It should move to immediately after the high-pass, where it also makes the expander's job easier, or at worst immediately before the limiter. Until it moves, the -3 dBFS ceiling is the only thing absorbing the error, which is a further argument for it over -1.

WHAT THIS PRESET DELIBERATELY DOES NOT DO: no air lift, no 4666 Hz "clarity" boost, no low-end shaping, no gate deep enough to silence a room, no 4:1 or 10:1 ratio, no fast attack. Those are levers for Streaming, Podcast, Warm Voice and Discord/Calls, whose users have opted into a character. Clean Voice's success condition is that a user with a good microphone switches it on and cannot immediately tell it is on — only that the quiet parts stopped disappearing.

critiques.overall:
TONE VERDICT: SOUND. I recomputed the whole curve with this repo's own filter design (crates/fxsound-dsp/src/biquad.rs::calc_parametric, Q = sqrt(r)/(r-1) = 1.59764, fs = 48 kHz) rather than a textbook bell, and summed it with the 80 Hz 2nd-order Butterworth. Every number in the rationale reproduces to 0.01 dB, including the two claims I expected to be hand-waved: a -3 dB move on the 62.5 band really does put -1.83 dB at 80 Hz, and -5 on 396.85 really does reach -5.26 dB composite.

MEASURED TOTAL CONTOUR (EQ + HPF): -5.72 @62.5, -3.11 @80, -1.66 @100, -1.14 @115.7, -0.87 @144 (local max), -1.38 @214.3, -1.33 @300, -1.77 @392 (global min), -1.23 @500, -0.76 @734.9, -0.27 @1k, +0.12 @1360.8, +1.46 @2519.8, +1.12 @3k, +0.43 @4k, +0.26 @4666, +0.16 @5.5k, +0.06 @8k, +0.05 @8640, +0.01 @16k. Peak-to-peak excluding the HPF is 3.2 dB. Log-mean over 100-8000 Hz is -0.27 dB, so the +6 dB makeup has essentially nothing to correct for — that checks out too.

DOES IT FIGHT THE HPF? No, and the reason is structural rather than lucky. The HPF and the EQ overlap only across roughly 115-210 Hz, and in that window the EQ is the junior partner: at 115.7 Hz the HPF contributes -0.89 dB and the entire EQ contributes -0.25 dB (of which the 214 band is -0.19). The two combine to at most -1.4 dB anywhere below 214 Hz. The one move that would have fought the filter is a cut at 62.5, because that band's skirt lands -1.83 dB at 80 Hz and would drag the effective corner up to ~105 Hz while doubling the attenuation at the crossover; leaving it at 0.0 is the correct call and the stated reason for it is the right one. There is a 0.5 dB shelf-like ripple between the HPF skirt and the 214 cut, peaking at -0.87 dB around 144 Hz — that is the only place the two stages visibly meet, it is a ~0.5 dB feature spread over a third of an octave, and it is below the audibility threshold for a broad tilt. Not worth a slider.

HONKY / BOXY / THIN / BOOMY / HARSH / LISPY, each checked against its own band:
- Honk (800-1500 Hz): the composite rises monotonically from -0.62 @800 through -0.27 @1k to +0.12 @1360.8 with no local bump. 1360.79 at 0.0 is right; a boost there is the classic honk and a cut there hollows the voice. Not honky.
- Box (400-800): -1.77 falling to -0.76. Correct direction, correct magnitude.
- Thin: the only stage touching a male fundamental (85-180 Hz) is the HPF; the EQ adds -0.19 dB at 115.7. A female fundamental (165-255) sees -0.2 to -1.4 dB, centred near -1.0. Neither fundamental is meaningfully reduced. Not thin.
- Boomy: the chain will not rescue a close-talker with 6-16 dB of proximity lift — total low-end reduction is only about -1.3 dB at 150-300 Hz. That is a deliberate consequence of leaving 115.734 at 0.0, and for a preset that must not thin a distant or already-thin mic it is the only defensible choice. The lever exists and is correctly deferred to Warm Voice / Discord.
- Harsh: maximum gain anywhere in 4-8 kHz is +0.43 dB (at 4 kHz, entirely skirt from the 2520 band). Cannot read as harsh.
- Lispy: nothing is cut in 4-10 kHz, so the EQ cannot cause a lisp. Its only interaction with the de-esser is +0.17 dB of pre-emphasis at the 5500 Hz detector split — negligible. Had 4666 been set to +1.5 as the community presets imply, it would have put +1.17 dB at 5.5 kHz and +0.74 at 6.35 kHz straight into that detector; declining it is the single best decision in the curve.

IS ANY BAND DOING TOO MUCH? No. At the scoop minimum (392 Hz) the 396.85 band supplies -1.50 of the -1.76 dB, with -0.19 and -0.09 from its neighbours — the three cuts overlap without stacking into an unintended trough, which on an 8/9-octave constant-Q ladder is the thing that usually goes wrong. Largest single move is 1.5 dB, comfortably under iZotope's 1-2 dB rule for the presence region and well under the SM7B presence switch's +3-4 dB. The 734.867 band at -0.5 earns its slot: without it the composite would flatten abruptly (-0.26 @735, -0.02 @1k) and the scoop would end in a step instead of ramping monotonically from -1.77 @392 to +1.46 @2520 across 2.7 octaves.

ONE IMPLEMENTATION NOTE, NOT A TONE PROBLEM: calc_parametric's Rule B warps Q down whenever |gain| < 0.4235 dB (max_q = 3.3*|g| + 0.2 must exceed 1.59764). Every value in this preset is >= 0.5 dB, so all bands run at the nominal Q and the curve above is what ships. But it means 0.4 dB is the smallest honest step on this ladder — anything below it silently becomes a wider, lower-Q filter. Worth knowing before anyone "fine-tunes" this curve in 0.25 dB increments.

I looked for an objection and did not find one worth a slider move. This is a well-judged curve for a universal default: it is a tilt, not a set of corrections, it stays out of every two-sided region (62.5, 115.7, 1360.8, 4666, 8640, 16k all at 0.0), and its success condition — that a good mic sounds untouched — is met, because the largest thing a listener could hear is a 3.2 dB tilt spread over three octaves.

The chain is well-reasoned and most of it survives scrutiny. Specifically, these are NOT problems and I am not going to invent objections to them: compressor 3:1 at −18 dBFS with a 6 dB soft knee gives 3.5 dB of GR on a −12 dBFS peak and recovers over 150 ms — 3.5 dB of GR with a 150 ms release cannot pump, and 150 ms is correctly inside the 125–250 ms syllable window; the 20 ms attack is the right call against the 1–5 ms folk wisdom and does pass the 5–35 ms plosive burst; gate ratio 2.0 with hold 120 ms will not chatter (the hold alone spans an inter-syllable gap, and re-triggering on every stressed vowel keeps it open through a word); the de-esser will not lisp — the 4 dB cap makes that arithmetically impossible; and the −3 dBFS ceiling is correctly argued. The compressor also self-protects: a hot mic peaking at −3 dBFS gets 9.5 dB of GR, so makeup + compression can never drive the limiter into constant reduction.

The defects are all one kind of error: three absolute dBFS thresholds were copied from source chains with different gain staging or different stage order, and they do not mean what they meant there. The gate is the dangerous one (fails by chopping speech, not by leaving noise), the de-esser is inert where it sits, and the makeup misses the preset's own loudness target and so starves the limiter of the ~1 dB of work the rationale assumes it does.

Repo-verified and worth flagging before any of this is implemented: there is no gate, compressor, de-esser or de-esser-class stage in this tree at all (`crates/fxsound-dsp/src/effects/`), and the only limiter is Dynamic Boost, whose ceiling is a hard-coded constant. All four stages are new code.

With the four corrections applied the set is self-consistent on a −12 dBFS-peak reference: peaks land at −6 dBFS with 3 dB of margin, transients faster than the 20 ms compressor attack arrive at −2.5 dBFS for ~0.5 dB of limiting (inside AES TD1008's ≤1 dB), short-term loudness lands near −17.5 LUFS, and the output noise floor sits ~28 dB below speech peaks.

Per CLAUDE.md, anything landing in `dsp/` equivalents is higher-risk by default; these are four new real-time stages, so watch for allocation/locking in the detector paths when they are written.

problems.problem: −45 dBFS is too high for a preset that claims to be safe on an unknown microphone at an unknown gain. Speech crest factor is 12–18 dB, so a correctly-gained mic peaking at −12 dBFS has an RMS near −26 dBFS, unstressed syllables at −36 to −41 dBFS, and weak fricatives (/f/, /θ/, /h/) and word tails at −45 to −55 dBFS — i.e. sitting on or under the threshold. At 2:1 a word tail at −52 takes 7 dB of reduction and a /θ/ at −55 takes 10 dB. On the very common case of a user who gained 6–10 dB low to avoid clipping, unstressed syllables themselves cross the threshold and the expander modulates at syllable rate: it will not chatter (hold=120 ms prevents that), it will breathe 3–8 dB on every word, which is harder to notice and much harder for a user to diagnose. The failure is asymmetric — too high amputates speech, too low merely leaves room tone, and the preset's own stated philosophy is 'eased down rather than gated shut'.
problems.corrected_value: gate.threshold_db: -55 (ratio 2.0, attack 5 ms, hold 120 ms, release 200 ms unchanged; reduction floor −12 dB rather than the −16 dB named in the rationale — at 2:1 a −12 dB floor is only reached 12 dB below threshold, i.e. −67 dBFS, so it stays out of the way)
problems.why: −55 dBFS is ~29 dB below the RMS of a nominally-gained voice and ~14 dB below the weakest fricative, so nothing in speech can approach it, while a typical cheap-condenser floor at −55 to −65 dBFS still gets 0–10 dB of expansion. It also preserves the design's intent under the 10 dB gain-staging error that a fixed-dBFS threshold cannot otherwise survive. The rationale already concedes this control is the weakest number in the preset; the consensus window it cites (−40 to −50) is drawn from chains where the gate sits after makeup gain.

problems.problem: −22 dBFS makes the de-esser very nearly inert in the position it occupies. The threshold is measured on the split band above 5500 Hz, and on a source peaking at −12 dBFS full-band, a hard /s/ peaks roughly 8–15 dB below vowel peaks, with a further ~2 dB lost because part of /s/ energy sits below the 5.5 kHz split — so the band level of the loudest sibilant is about −22 to −29 dBFS. Against a −22 dBFS threshold at 3:1 that is 0 to ~0.5 dB of gain reduction; the 4 dB cap is never approached and the stage does nothing. The value is borrowed from jtrv, where the de-esser is not sitting ahead of the compressor and its +3 dB makeup, so it saw a signal roughly 6–9 dB hotter. The rationale's own test criterion (dbx: the detector should flicker on hard S's) would fail at −22 in this position.
problems.corrected_value: deesser.threshold_db: -30 (split_hz 5500, ratio 3, max_reduction_db 4, attack_ms 1, release_ms 80 all unchanged)
problems.why: At −30 dBFS a sibilant band peak of −26 dBFS gets 2.7 dB of reduction and the 4 dB cap is reached at −24 dBFS band level — exactly the 2–4 dB typical-reduction window from mastering.com, and the cap still makes lisping arithmetically impossible. This preserves every argument the rationale makes for de-essing harder because of the pre-compressor position, while actually engaging. Note also that the rationale's justification is partly wrong: a sustained /s/ runs 100–150 ms, far longer than the 20 ms compressor attack, so the compressor does clamp sibilants — only the first ~20 ms escapes. The threshold still needs lowering, but for the level-reference reason, not the transient-escape reason.

problems.problem: The repo has no input-chain limiter, and the only limiter that exists — Dynamic Boost in crates/fxsound-dsp/src/effects/dynamic_boost.rs — cannot honour this field and would wreck the dynamics if reused. MAX_OUTPUT is a compile-time const 0.966051 = −0.30 dBFS that the parameter layer never writes (the doc comment says so explicitly), LOOK_AHEAD_SECONDS is 0.00075 (0.75 ms, not the 2 ms the rationale budgets), the envelope release is τ ≈ 10.18 ms (not ~60 ms), and — the real problem — the block is not a limiter but a maximizer: it carries a slow auto-gain off a 0.1 Hz / τ ≈ 1.59 s RMS estimator with a TARGET_LEVEL of 0.32 and a MIN_BACKOFF_GAIN anti-pumping floor of 1.06 (+0.5 dB). Putting that in series with a 150 ms-release compressor gives two level servos an order of magnitude apart in time constant — the textbook breathing generator — and the +0.5 dB floor means the stage applies gain after the point where the rationale states 'nothing may apply gain after this stage'.
problems.corrected_value: Implement a separate input-only limiter stage: ceiling as a parameter (default −3.0 dBFS), lookahead 2 ms, release ~60 ms, no auto-gain. Do not reuse DynamicBoost. If it is reused, gain_boost must be pinned to 1.0, the `gain_boost·rms > 0.32` back-off branch bypassed, and MAX_OUTPUT promoted from a const to a per-instance parameter.
problems.why: Otherwise limiter_ceiling_db: -3 is silently ignored — the signal is ceilinged at −0.3 dBFS, which destroys the entire four-part headroom argument the rationale builds (Opus overshoot, sample-peak vs true-peak, decode-side limiting, downstream OBS/WebRTC re-limiting) — and a 1.59 s AGC is added that no line of the preset accounts for. Per CLAUDE.md this is exactly the class of change that needs flagging for human review before merge.

problems.problem: +6.0 dB is internally inconsistent with the preset's own loudness targets and leaves the limiter with nothing to do. On the −12 dBFS-peak reference the rationale uses, speech short-term loudness is about −25 LUFS (PLR ≈ 13 LU). The chain adds roughly +7 dB on quiet passages and +2.5 dB on loud ones, averaging near +4.5, so output short-term lands near −20.5 LUFS and integrated below that — under the −20 LUFS floor the preset itself cites from TD1008 §5, and 3+ dB short of its stated −18 LUFS speech target. Peaks land at −12 − 3.5 + 6 = −9.5 dBFS, i.e. 6.5 dB of unused headroom below the −3 dBFS ceiling, so the limiter never reaches even the ~1 dB of gain reduction the rationale describes as the operating point. Secondary arithmetic error feeding this: the derivation states 'exactly 4 dB of gain reduction' from (−12 − −18)×(1 − 1/3), but that is the hard-knee result; with the 6 dB soft knee this same preset specifies, GR at −12 dBFS is 3.5 dB and gain reduction does not begin until −21 dBFS, not −18.
problems.corrected_value: makeup_db: 9.5 (with compressor.threshold_db −18 and knee 6 unchanged; and correct the rationale's GR figure from 4.0 dB to 3.5 dB, net +2.5 dB rather than +2 dB versus dry on loud speech)
problems.why: At +9.5 dB the set becomes self-consistent on the reference: sustained peaks −6.0 dBFS (3 dB under the ceiling), transients faster than the 20 ms compressor attack arrive at −2.5 dBFS for ~0.5 dB of limiting — inside TD1008's ≤1 dB inaudibility guidance and the first value at which the limiter does the job the rationale assigns it — and short-term loudness lands near −17.5 LUFS, on the −18 LUFS target with the margin above −20 LUFS intact. The auto-makeup formula 0.5×|T|×(1 − 1/R) restores what the compressor removed; it was never a loudness target, so it is the floor for this number, not the answer. The cost is 3.5 dB more noise floor (−45.5 dBFS out from a −55 dBFS input floor, ~28 dB under speech peaks), which is acceptable and is the reason the final value must still be trimmed by metering one fixed speech reference, as the rationale already requires.

preset.name: Streaming
preset.intent: For someone talking over game audio into OBS or a voice channel: a forward, consistently-levelled voice that stays intelligible after Twitch's AAC or a chat client's Opus has re-encoded it, without sounding obviously processed.
preset.rationale:
REFERENCE LEVEL (everything below depends on it). All three threshold numbers assume the chain input is gain-staged so normal speech peaks near -12 dBFS. The dossier's single most repeated structural warning is that a fixed dB threshold is meaningless without gain staging — two reputable open-source mic presets differ by 26 dB on the gate threshold for exactly this reason. These values are a starting point at that reference, not a universal truth, and the product should eventually derive thresholds from a measured noise-floor/speech-level calibration rather than ship them hard-coded.

HPF = 100 Hz, 2nd-order Butterworth (12 dB/oct). The sources split: Shure says 70-90 Hz and RODE says 80 Hz for voice generally, while two of the six researchers independently recommend 100 Hz specifically for Streaming and Discord. I take the 100 Hz side for this preset for three reasons. (1) WebRTC's shipped capture high-pass is literally `butter(2,100/fs,'high')` — every Chrome, Discord, Teams and Jitsi mic path runs it, measuring -3.54 dB @100 Hz and -1.01 dB @150 Hz, and nobody reports thin voices from it. That is the largest deployed empirical sample available. (2) A streaming desk has fans, a mechanical keyboard and a chair within a metre of the mic; that LF energy is inaudible on the listener's laptop speakers but it drives the compressor detector and eats limiter headroom, and this preset compresses harder than Clean Voice. (3) Twitch AAC-LC at 96 kbps and game-chat Opus spend bits on whatever you send; sub-100 Hz content is pure cost. I choose 2nd order rather than 4th deliberately: at 2nd order the residual at band 1 (115.734 Hz) is -1.9 dB, a gentle trim of the male fundamental region; 4th order would be near-cliff behaviour just below the fundamentals of deep male voices (85-180 Hz adult male range).

EQ BAND 0 (62.5 Hz) = 0.0, on purpose. The constraint is right and the reasoning is quantified in the dossier: a 100 Hz 2nd-order HPF already leaves -8.8 dB at 62.5 Hz, so there is nothing there to cut. Worse, because this ladder is effectively constant-Q at Q≈1.598 (0.889 octave; the port's Q-widening rule only engages below 0.42 dB of gain), a -3 dB move at 62.5 Hz would also produce about -1.8 dB at 80 Hz and -0.9 dB at 100 Hz — it would thin the bottom of the voice while removing rumble that is already gone. FxSound's own 13 shipped factory presets on this exact ladder use 0 dB at 62.5 Hz in 13 of 13 cases, including the extreme one.

EQ BAND 1 (115.734 Hz) = 0.0. One researcher suggests -2 here for Streaming, but that recommendation was made against an 80 Hz high-pass. With the 100 Hz HPF I chose, this band already sits at -1.9 dB. Adding -2 dB of slider on top would be the same doubling-up the brief warns about at 62.5 Hz, just one band higher, and it would land on the male fundamental (90-155 Hz sits inside this band's 85-157 Hz span). The HPF owns proximity/boom control in this preset; the slider stays out of it.

EQ SHAPE, 214.3 / 396.9 / 734.9 = -1.5 / -2.0 / -1.0. Three independent tuned voice presets (jtrv, azmarifdev, luix-voice) all cut the mud region, all landing at -1 to -2 dB, at 220/350, 425 and 300 Hz respectively. On this ladder those parametric moves fall across bands 2, 3 and 4. Three adjacent bands sum: with ~19% bleed per neighbour the composite is about -1.9 dB at 214.3, -2.5 dB at 396.9 and -1.5 dB at 734.9 — a broad tilt rather than a notch, which is the only way to author breadth on a constant-Q ladder. The composite stays well clear of the ~-5 dB point where the dossier says the voice starts sounding like a telephone. This mud cut, not a boost, is what makes the preset "forward": it increases the presence-to-low-mid ratio without spending limiter headroom.

EQ 1360.79 = 0.0 (nasal/honk region, two-sided and touchy; nothing to gain). 2519.84 = +2.0. This is the presence and intelligibility core (band span 1852-3429 Hz) and it is where Shure's own SM7B presence switch peaks at about +3-4 dB — a manufacturer's ceiling, not a starting point. iZotope's explicit limit for 1.5-5 kHz is "no more than 1 or 2 dB is common". +2.0 slider composites to about +2.1 dB, which is at that limit and is the largest move in the preset; it is where forwardness is bought most cheaply.

EQ 4666.12 = +0.5, deliberately small. The intuitive "clarity" move is to boost this band, and one researcher suggests Streaming should be "Podcast plus a touch more 4666". I go against that. This band spans 3429-6350 Hz — it is half consonant definition and half male sibilance — and in this fixed chain the EQ sits *before* the de-esser, so every dB here goes straight into the de-esser's detector and makes it over-trigger, dynamically cancelling the move. The dossier's interaction analysis states this explicitly. +0.5 slider still composites to about +1.07 dB because of bleed from the +2.0 at 2519.84 and the +1.0 at 8640.48 — a good illustration that slider dB is not resulting dB on this ladder, and the number the de-esser threshold is offset against below.

EQ 8640.48 = +1.0, 16000 = -1.0. +1 dB of air is the honest half of the +2 dB high shelf that all three tuned voice presets use; the fixed ladder cannot make a shelf's flat top, so I take the lower band only. 16 kHz gets a small cut rather than the "sparkle" boost: there is essentially no speech harmonic content above 12 kHz, what is there is mic self-noise and breath, the +12 dB of makeup gain below will lift that floor, and Twitch's 96 kbps AAC and low-bitrate Opus discard or badly reproduce that octave anyway. Spending encoder bits and hiss on it is a net loss.

Whole EQ stays inside -2..+2 on the sliders. FxSound's own factory presets on this ladder live inside about ±3 dB and only one novelty preset uses ±12; manufacturers' own voicing switches move 3-4 dB. A ±12 dB voice preset will not survive the listener's codec.

GATE — downward expander, ratio 2.0, threshold -42 dBFS. Ratio 2.0 is Rane Note 155's stated ratio for noise reduction by expansion and is OBS's own "expander" preset value; it is an expander, not a gate, so low-level voiceless fricatives (/s/, /f/) and plosive tails — which sit only a few dB above room tone — are attenuated rather than amputated. Threshold -42 dBFS sits between the tuned Linux presets (-48 to -55, which assume a quiet room and conservative gain) and OBS's -26 (which assumes a hot streamer mic); a gaming desk's noise floor is genuinely higher than a podcast booth's. Note honestly: this schema has no reduction-depth/range parameter, so ratio is the only depth control. Fedora Magazine and all four tuned presets cap depth at -12 to -18 dB rather than muting; the implementation should cap expansion depth around -18 dB, and I am flagging the missing parameter rather than pretending ratio alone expresses it. Attack 5 ms: four independently tuned presets use 1-5 ms, and I reject OBS's 25 ms default and EasyEffects' 20 ms default because a 20-25 ms gate attack demonstrably clips word onsets — that default was never tuned for consonants. Hold 150 ms and release 200 ms: the speech envelope's modulation spectrum peaks at 4-8 Hz, i.e. one syllable every 125-250 ms, so a 150 ms hold spans inter-word gaps without holding through a real pause, and 200 ms is the median of the four tuned presets (180/200/220/250). Hold plus the expander's soft behaviour is the anti-chatter mechanism here; if the implementation also offers hysteresis, -3 dB is the value all four tuned presets use.

DE-ESSER — split 5500 Hz. Sources disagree hard: 3000 Hz (azmarifdev), 4000 (jtrv), 4500/6000 (Calf default), 8-10 kHz (FabFilter). I reject the 3-5 kHz end outright — that is the intelligibility region and de-essing there produces an audible lisp on every "s". 5500 Hz is luix-voice's tuned Split value and is the defensible compromise: above the 5 kHz upper edge of the presence region that must not be ducked, inside the male sibilance band (4-7 kHz, centre 5-6), and it catches all of the female band (7-8 kHz). It also sits in the 6350 Hz hole between EQ bands 7 and 8 that the fixed ladder structurally cannot reach — de-essing is the only tool for that region, which is why the EQ does not attempt it. Threshold -25 dBFS is derived, not copied: start from jtrv's tuned -22, subtract ~1 dB for this preset's composite HF lift at 4666/8640 (the dossier is explicit that the de-esser threshold must be offset by the preset's own gain in the sibilant bands), and subtract ~2 dB more because the fixed stage order puts the de-esser *before* the compressor — the majority of surveyed presets de-ess after it, precisely because a downstream compressor re-amplifies the sibilance you just removed. That lands at -25, independently close to luix-voice's tuned -26. Ratio 3.0 is the consensus value across every tuned preset. max_reduction 6.0 dB is the guard that makes the lower threshold safe: typical sibilant reduction should be 3-6 dB, and capping the range is what prevents one harsh syllable becoming a lisp. Attack 1.0 ms (sibilance is a short burst and must be caught, unlike the main compressor); release 60 ms, inside the 40-150 ms window and comfortably shorter than a 125-250 ms syllable so the band recovers before the following vowel.

COMPRESSOR — 4:1 at -20 dBFS, 6 dB soft knee, 15 ms / 150 ms. Ratio 4:1 is the top of RODE's stated 2:1-4:1 voice range and LSP's own default; I explicitly refuse OBS's 10:1 default, which at -18 dB is a limiter wearing a compressor's name — defensible as "what streamers actually run", but the brief asks for a considered product default, not maximum processing. Threshold -20 is solved backwards from Rane Note 155's target rather than picked: at the -12 dBFS reference speech peak, input is 8 dB over threshold, so gain reduction = 8 × (1 - 1/4) = 6 dB, the top of Rane's 3-6 dB target window — appropriate for a preset that is meant to be denser than Clean Voice, while quiet passages see ~0 dB. Knee 6.0 dB means a 6 dB-wide *soft knee below* the threshold: that is LSP's -6 dB with the sign flipped, used by literally every preset in the survey, and the sign convention is a documented trap worth stating in the code. Attack 15 ms: the common "1-5 ms for vocals" advice is wrong for speech specifically — a stop-consonant burst is a transient of a few ms up to ~35 ms, so a 1-5 ms attack clamps the burst itself and produces dull, mushy, slightly lisping speech. Rane gives 25-100 ms for vocals; jtrv's tuned preset uses 15 ms; 15 ms is the fast end of the defensible window, chosen because this preset wants level consistency. Release 150 ms sits mid-way in the 125-250 ms syllable window: long enough that the compressor does not recover inside a syllable (which is what produces audible breathing on the noise floor, and AAC/Opus exaggerate it), short enough to recover between phrases. Note Rane's definition — release is specified in dB/second, so wall-clock recovery scales with the amount of reduction; 150 ms is a constant, not a measured recovery time.

MAKEUP +12.0 dB. Arithmetic from the stated reference: speech peaks -12 dBFS in, minus 6 dB of gain reduction = -18 dBFS after the compressor; +12 dB puts peaks near -6 dBFS. Compressed speech carries a peak-to-loudness ratio of roughly 12 dB, which lands short-term loudness near -18 LUFS — AES TD1008's published distribution loudness for speech, and comfortably above the -20 LUFS floor below which TD1008 warns content is "unsatisfyingly quiet on some player devices". Loudness matters more for this preset than for any other in the set, because Twitch publishes no loudness target and applies no normalisation to live or VOD — there is no platform safety net if the preset is quiet, and the streamer sits in a pack that is not normalised either. I do not use the 0.5 × |threshold| × (1 - 1/ratio) auto-makeup rule (which would give 7.5 dB) because that rule is referenced to a 0 dBFS input that speech never reaches. Two caveats stated rather than hidden: the 12 dB PLR figure is an estimate, not a measurement, so this value MUST be re-trimmed after measuring this preset's short-term loudness on the same speech reference used for the other five presets — the makeup value is the only thing that makes the six presets A/B-comparable, and hand-picked makeup is what makes users conclude the louder preset is the better one. And +12 dB of makeup raises the noise floor by 12 dB, which is why the expander threshold above was chosen against the post-makeup floor rather than the raw input.

LIMITER CEILING -3.0 dBFS. The reflex answer is -1 dBTP (EBU R128, AES TD1008, Spotify, Apple all say it), and one researcher recommends -1.5 for Streaming. I take -3.0 dBFS instead, for four citable reasons. (1) -1 dBTP is specified for the last processing stage before one known encoder. A virtual microphone is neither: OBS's own limiter filter defaults to a -6.0 dBFS threshold, so a streamer's chain will re-limit whatever we send. (2) TD1008 is explicit that the threshold must go *below* -1.0 dBTP as bitrate falls; Twitch AAC-LC runs at 96 kbps recommended and game-chat Opus negotiates down to tens of kbps — exactly that regime. (3) A real-time limiter without 4x oversampled peak detection is a sample-peak limiter, not a true-peak one; at -1.0 dBFS it routinely passes inter-sample peaks above 0 dBTP, and true-peak meters themselves carry up to 0.6 dB of error. The label on this field is dBFS sample peak and should say so in the UI. (4) It costs nothing: loudness here is set by makeup gain, not by the ceiling. With peaks landing near -6 dBFS, the limiter sees ~0 dB of reduction on normal speech and 1-3 dB on a laugh or a desk hit — which is TD1008's guidance that ~1 dB of limiting is the sensible maximum and the limiter is a safety net, not a loudness tool. One chain-level note that bears on this number: the planned stage order puts optional RNNoise *after* the brick-wall limiter. No preset in the nine-file survey does that, and TD1008 documents that filtering removes programme energy and can raise peaks (up to 2.1 dB in its square-wave example), so anything spectral placed after the limiter defeats it. -3.0 dBFS gives margin for that defect, but the defect should be fixed by moving RNNoise ahead of the limiter rather than relying on the margin.

WHAT THE DOSSIER DOES NOT COVER. No open-source project ships a 10-band graphic preset on these exact centres, so the ten gains are justified from voice-EQ practice mapped onto the ladder plus the port's own Q and summation behaviour, not from any shipped preset — that is stated rather than dressed up. The composite dB figures above are computed from Q≈1.598 and the ~19%-per-neighbour bleed figure in the dossier; they should be confirmed against the engine's actual response before shipping. And no source in the dossier measures the FIFINE-class USB condenser this will be tested on, so the 8640/16000 choices reflect that mic class's reported bright, hissy top end by reputation only and should be verified by ear.

problems.problem: The +1.0 dB air band sits ENTIRELY inside the de-esser's sidechain and so is dynamically cancelled on every sibilant. Verified against the engine: band 8's span is 6358-11758 Hz (band_frequency_range, eq.rs:88-117), and the de-esser split is 5500 Hz. 100% of this band is above the split. The rationale uses exactly this argument to hold band 7 down to +0.5 - but band 7 spans 3434-6348 Hz, so only its top ~15% is above 5500. The argument applies four to six times more strongly to the band that got twice the gain. Tonal consequence: composite is +0.99 dB at 8640 and +0.59 dB at 10 kHz on vowels, then up to 6 dB lower on every /s/ and /f/ because max_reduction_db is 6. Air present on vowels, absent on fricatives, at a 125-250 ms syllable rate is an audible brightness flutter, and it is the same defect as a lisp approached from the other side. Offsetting the de-esser threshold by -1 dB (as the rationale does) does not fix this - it makes the de-esser trigger MORE often, so the lift is removed more of the time. Secondary: this is also the self-noise octave of a bright USB condenser, lifted a further 12 dB by makeup, which contradicts the preset's own stated reason for cutting 16 kHz.
problems.corrected_value: eq_boost_db[8] = 0.5, and eq_boost_db[9] (16000) = -0.5
problems.why: At +0.5 the composite is +0.58 dB at 8640 and +0.35 dB at 10 kHz - still audible openness, but now smaller than the de-esser's own action so the modulation is not the dominant HF event. Band 9 comes up to -0.5 in the same move because -1.0 was sized to rein in a +1.0 neighbour; with the neighbour halved, -1.0 over-trims (composite would fall to -0.87 at 16 kHz and -0.26 at 12 kHz, i.e. a dull top). The pair +0.5/-0.5 gives -0.37 at 16 kHz and +0.005 at 12 kHz, keeping the air centred at 8.6 kHz and flat above 11 kHz, which is what the rationale actually wanted.

problems.problem: This band turns a mud cut into a 1.7-octave mid scoop and works against the preset's stated 'denser' intent. Band 4's span is 541-1000 Hz - that is not mud, it is the first-formant/chest region (male F1 on open vowels sits at 600-750 Hz). None of the three tuned presets the rationale cites cut there: jtrv is at 220/350, luix-voice at 300, azmarifdev at 425, all at or below 425 Hz. The -2.0 at 396.85 already bleeds -0.37 dB into 735 on its own. Adding -1.0 of slider makes the composite -1.35 dB at 735, so the run 300-900 Hz is continuously down 1.4-2.4 dB. On the playback devices this preset is explicitly designed for - a laptop speaker or a phone, which have essentially nothing below 300 Hz - that region IS the body of the voice, and scooping it reads as thin and papery rather than forward. Forwardness is already bought by the +2.08 at 2520; this band only subtracts weight.
problems.corrected_value: eq_boost_db[4] = -0.5
problems.why: Composite at 735 becomes -0.83 dB, which still removes boxiness without touching F1, and the scoop collapses to a proper bell centred on 400 Hz (397 stays at -2.20, 735 at -0.83, 1361 rises to +0.23) - i.e. the shape a parametric at 350-425 Hz with Q ~1 would draw, which is what every cited source actually uses. It also widens the presence-to-body contrast less abruptly, so the 4 dB tilt from low-mid to 2.5 kHz becomes a smooth ramp rather than a step across one octave.

problems.problem: The only band in the preset that lands on a fundamental rather than on harmonic mud, and the preset is voice-class-agnostic. Band 2's span is 158-292 Hz; adult female F0 (165-255 Hz) falls entirely inside it, and so does the male second harmonic. At -1.5 slider the composite is -1.89 dB at 214 Hz, so for a female or higher-pitched male speaker the preset attenuates the fundamental by ~1.9 dB while lifting 2.5 kHz by +2.08 - a 4 dB tilt against the voice's own root, which is the classic recipe for 'thin and a bit brittle'. For that voice class the mud is at 300-500 Hz, not 214. The dossier's own evidence supports this: only jtrv's 220 Hz node is this low, and that is a narrow parametric, not a 0.889-octave constant-Q bell that reaches from 158 to 292 Hz.
problems.corrected_value: eq_boost_db[2] = -1.0
problems.why: Composite at 214 becomes -1.37 dB - still a clear cut for the male chest harmonics it is aimed at, but no longer eating the female fundamental. Combined with the band 4 change above, the scoop's centre of mass shifts from roughly 300 Hz to roughly 360 Hz, landing where all three tuned reference presets actually put theirs, and the final curve reads 214 -1.37 / 397 -2.20 / 735 -0.83 / 1361 +0.23 / 2520 +2.06 - a symmetric mud bell plus a presence plateau, with total span 4.26 dB.

critiques.overall: The skeleton is right and the best part of it is the part most presets get wrong: the HPF/EQ coordination. Bands 0 and 1 at 0.0 is the correct call, quantitatively - a 100 Hz 2nd-order Butterworth already leaves -8.78 dB at 62.5 and -1.92 at 115.7, and I confirmed the constant-Q claim in the engine (derive_q gives exactly 1.598; calc_parametric's Rule B only widens Q below 0.424 dB of gain, so every band here runs at full Q). There is no fight with the high-pass, and the resulting low end has a small local maximum at 150 Hz (-1.59 dB) that actually preserves the male fundamental rather than tilting continuously into the HPF corner. Nothing here is honky (1361 Hz composite +0.14), boomy, or harsh - 2 kHz is +1.27 and 3.5 kHz +1.23, a smooth plateau rather than a 2.5 kHz spike, and +2.08 dB composite at 2520 is at iZotope's stated 1-2 dB limit and below Shure's 3-4 dB presence switch, so no single band is doing too much. Total curve span is 4.46 dB, which will survive 96 kbps AAC intact. The three problems are all sub-1.5 dB refinements of the same two ideas: the mud cut is drawn 1.7 octaves wide (bands 2, 3, 4 all negative) when the sources it cites all sit inside one octave around 350-425 Hz, so it leans on the female fundamental at one end and the male first formant at the other; and the air band at 8640 sits wholly inside the de-esser's sidechain, which makes it a dynamic brightness modulation rather than a static lift. With [0, 0, -1.0, -2.0, -0.5, 0, +2.0, +0.5, +0.5, -0.5] the composite reads -0.05 / -0.28 / -1.37 / -2.20 / -0.83 / +0.23 / +2.06 / +0.94 / +0.58 / -0.37, which is the same design intent executed with a tighter mud bell and an air lift the de-esser will not chew on. Two things I could not check and that should be measured rather than argued: these composites come from a dB-additive peaking cascade at Q=1.598 with 18.6% first-neighbour bleed, and should be confirmed against the engine's actual magnitude response (eq.rs exposes a magnitude helper at line ~370); and the 8640/16000 pair really does need a listen on the target FIFINE-class capsule, since no source in the dossier measures one.

problems.problem: At the preset's own -12 dBFS reference, a -20 dBFS threshold puts only the top 8 dB of the speech range above the knee, so the stage does not deliver the "consistent level" the intent promises. Work the transfer curve across a realistic conversational range: quiet passage peaking -26 dBFS -> 0 dB GR (it is at the very bottom of the 6 dB below-threshold knee) -> -14 dBFS after +12 makeup. Reference speech -12 -> 6 dB GR -> -6 dBFS. Emphatic word -6 -> 10.5 dB GR -> -3.5 dBFS. A 20 dB input span comes out as a 10.5 dB output span: the whole chain is acting as a ~2:1 leveller despite the 4:1 label, and the quiet-to-loud residual is still audible as level drift on stream. Lowering the threshold and backing the ratio off is the standard fix and is strictly better here, because deeper, gentler compression is what "denser than Clean Voice" actually means.
problems.corrected_value: threshold_db: -26.0, ratio: 3.0 (keep knee_db 6, attack 15). New curve at the same reference: -26 in -> ~0 dB GR; -12 in -> 14 dB over -> 14*(1-1/3) = 9.3 dB GR -> -21.3 dBFS; -6 in -> 13.3 dB GR -> -19.3 dBFS. A 20 dB input span becomes a 6.7 dB output span.
problems.why: The stated goal is level consistency, and consistency is set by how much of the signal sits above the threshold, not by the ratio number. -20 leaves half the usable speech range untouched. -26/3:1 gives more levelling with less per-dB squeeze than -20/4:1, and it does not change the makeup arithmetic much (peak lands -21.3 instead of -18).

problems.problem: The 12 dB makeup is solved from steady-state gain reduction, but the compressor's 15 ms attack means fast transients never see that gain reduction, so the limiter (not the compressor) ends up controlling emphasis. For a 4 ms plosive or desk knock the detector has only travelled 1-e^(-4/15) = 23% of the way, so GR is ~23% of steady state. With the preset as written: a -12 dBFS burst gets ~1.4 dB instead of 6 -> -12-1.4+12 = -1.4 dBFS, already 1.6 dB over the -3 ceiling; an emphatic -6 dBFS syllable gets ~2.4 dB instead of 10.5 -> +3.6 dBFS, i.e. 6.6 dB of limiting. The rationale claims "~0 dB on normal speech and 1-3 dB on a laugh or desk hit" and cites TD1008's ~1 dB maximum; the actual chain does 1.5-7 dB on every raised voice, and a fast-release brick wall doing 7 dB is exactly the crunch that 96 kbps AAC and low-rate Opus expose. Only 3 dB separates sustained peaks (-6) from the ceiling (-3), which is less than the within-talker peak variation of a single sentence.
problems.corrected_value: makeup_db: 9.0 if the compressor is left as written (sustained peaks -9 dBFS, 6 dB of transient headroom). If Problem 1 is adopted (-26 / 3:1), keep makeup_db: 12.0 — peaks then land at -9.3 dBFS, a -12 burst arrives at ~-2.1 dBFS for ~1 dB of limiting, which matches the TD1008 figure the rationale cites.
problems.why: Headroom for sub-attack-time transients has to be budgeted separately from steady-state peak arithmetic; the current calculation only accounts for the latter. Note that with makeup 9 the short-term loudness drops to roughly -21 LUFS, below the preset's own -20 floor — which is another reason to take the Problem 1 route (deeper compression raises RMS, landing near -20 LUFS at peaks of -9.3) rather than simply turning the makeup down.

problems.problem: At ratio 2.0 the expander mathematically cannot offset the +12 dB of makeup downstream, so the preset's noise handling is close to a no-op. For a downward expander, attenuation in dB = (ratio-1) x (dB below threshold). A gaming-desk floor of about -50 dBFS post-HPF sits 8 dB below the -42 threshold, so it is attenuated by exactly 8 dB to -58 dBFS. That is far below the compressor threshold, so it passes at unity and then takes the full +12 dB of makeup: the output floor is -46 dBFS, 4 dB HIGHER than the raw input floor. Measured against speech (peaks landing near -6), the chain nets about 2 dB of SNR improvement. The rationale's own framing — "the expander threshold was chosen against the post-makeup floor" — conflates threshold with depth: the gate runs pre-makeup so its threshold lives in the input domain, and makeup can only be answered by depth, which ratio 2 does not supply. The same arithmetic also makes the flagged -18 dB depth cap inert: at 2:1 it would only engage at inputs below -60 dBFS.
problems.corrected_value: ratio: 3.0 (threshold stays -42). Reduction at a -50 dBFS floor becomes 2 x 8 = 16 dB -> -66 dBFS -> -54 dBFS after makeup, 4 dB below the raw floor, and the -18 dB depth cap now engages at inputs at or below -51 dBFS so it does real work. General rule to state in code: (ratio-1) x (floor margin in dB) must be >= makeup_db, which at an 8 dB margin means ratio >= 2.5.
problems.why: Ratio is the only depth control this schema has, so it must be sized against the makeup gain, not picked from a reference that had a separate range parameter. Ratio 3 is still an expander, not a chopper: a voiceless fricative at -40 dBFS (2 dB under threshold) is attenuated 4 dB instead of 2, which stays well inside the soft behaviour the rationale wants. Raising the threshold to -36 at ratio 2 is the alternative but it starts eating /f/ and /th/ tails, so changing ratio is the safer of the two.

problems.problem: -25 dBFS will produce roughly 2 dB of reduction, not the 3-6 dB the rationale says it is targeting, and the 6 dB cap never engages. During a loud /s/ the energy above 5.5 kHz typically runs 8-12 dB below the broadband speech peak, so at a -12 dBFS reference the band peak is about -22 dBFS (lower still with an RMS detector). Against -25 at ratio 3 that is 3 dB over threshold -> 3 x (1-1/3) = 2 dB of reduction. The derivation also mixes domains: jtrv's tuned -22 was measured at a 4000 Hz split, and moving the split up to 5500 Hz discards roughly 4-6 dB of band energy on a typical sibilant, so the same threshold number is already 4-6 dB more conservative before the -1 and -2 offsets are applied. Separately, the schema does not say whether threshold_db is measured on the post-split HF band or on the full-band level, and the two readings differ by more than 20 dB — at full-band level, -25 fires on every vowel and ducks everything above 5.5 kHz by up to 6 dB on all sustained speech, which does not lisp but does dull the whole top octave.
problems.corrected_value: threshold_db: -30.0, and the schema must state explicitly that threshold_db is referenced to the post-split HF band level. At -30 a -22 dBFS sibilant is 8 dB over -> 8 x (1-1/3) = 5.3 dB of reduction, just inside the max_reduction_db 6 cap. Non-sibilant HF is safe: a vowel's energy above 5.5 kHz sits 25-35 dB below the broadband peak (-37 to -47 dBFS), well under the threshold.
problems.why: Lisp risk here is governed by the split frequency and the reduction cap, both of which are already correct (5500 Hz is above the presence region, and 6 dB is bounded), so the threshold can safely be set where it actually catches sibilants. As written the stage is close to bypassed, which matters because the de-esser is the only tool that reaches the 6350 Hz gap in the fixed EQ ladder.

problems.problem: The compressor release and the gate's open window are fighting in exactly the same time slot, which produces the floor breathing the rationale claims to avoid. In an inter-word pause the compressor starts recovering its 6-9 dB of gain reduction with a 150 ms time constant, sweeping the noise floor up by that amount — while the gate is deliberately held open for 150 ms (hold) and only then closes over 200 ms. So every word is followed by a 150-350 ms puff of room tone rising 6-9 dB, amplified by +12 dB of makeup. AAC-LC at 96 kbps and low-rate Opus make this worse, not better, because that floor is where the codec's noise-fill lives. Shortening the hold is not the fix — the rationale correctly argues the hold must span inter-word gaps at the 4-8 Hz modulation rate — so the compressor has to be the slower of the two.
problems.corrected_value: release_ms: 250 (gate hold 150 / release 200 unchanged). 250 ms is the long edge of the 125-250 ms syllable window the rationale itself derives, so the compressor holds level within a phrase and recovers between phrases rather than inside every inter-word gap.
problems.why: Whichever stage recovers faster sets the audible floor behaviour. At 150 ms the compressor recovers fully inside gaps that the gate is intentionally holding open, so the gate cannot mask it. Adopting Problem 1's lower threshold helps independently, since the compressor then sits in 4-9 dB of reduction continuously and has less swing to breathe with.

critiques.overall:
The reasoning quality is high and several choices are correct and well defended — 5500 Hz de-esser split (above the presence region, catches both male and female sibilance), max_reduction 6 dB as the anti-lisp guard, de-esser attack 1 ms / release 60 ms (5.5 kHz is ~5.5 cycles per ms, no band modulation; 60 ms recovers well inside a 125-250 ms syllable), compressor attack 15 ms (the anti-1-5 ms argument for stop consonants is right), gate attack 5 ms, gate hold 150 ms against the 4-8 Hz modulation peak, the 6 dB soft-knee sign-convention warning, limiter ceiling -3 dBFS as a sample-peak field, and the observation that RNNoise after the brick wall defeats it. None of those need changing.

The failures are all in the arithmetic that couples the stages rather than in any single value read in isolation. Three of them compound: the gate at 2:1 delivers 8 dB of reduction against 12 dB of makeup, so the processed noise floor ends up 4 dB above the raw one; the compressor at -26 dB below the reference only touches the top 8 dB of the speech range, so the 4:1 label buys about 2:1 of actual levelling; and the 15 ms attack combined with only 3 dB of peak headroom hands transient control to the limiter, which does 1.5-7 dB rather than the claimed ~1 dB. The de-esser at -25 dBFS delivers about 2 dB and its cap never engages, and the compressor release at 150 ms recovers inside the gate's own hold window and breathes.

The five corrections form one self-consistent set: gate ratio 3.0, compressor -26/3:1 with release 250 ms, makeup held at 12.0, de-esser threshold -30.0 band-referenced, limiter ceiling unchanged at -3.0. At that setting the reference -12 dBFS speech peaks land at -9.3 dBFS with ~1 dB of limiting on plosives, a -50 dBFS room floor ends up at -54 dBFS post-makeup, and 20 dB of input dynamic range comes out as 6.7 dB. Two spec gaps should be closed in the schema rather than in the numbers: threshold_db on the de-esser must be declared as post-split band level (the two readings differ by more than 20 dB), and the gate needs an explicit range/depth parameter so depth stops being a side effect of ratio. The preset's own closing caveat is also correct and should be enforced — every threshold here is meaningless until the product derives them from a measured noise floor and speech level, and the makeup value in particular must be re-trimmed against a measured short-term loudness on the same speech reference as the other five presets.

problems.problem: -42 dBFS sits exactly on top of the quietest speech, not below it, at the preset's own stated reference. The rationale also contradicts itself: it says the threshold 'was chosen against the post-makeup floor rather than the raw input', but the gate is the first stage in the chain and sees pre-makeup levels only. The +12 dB of makeup is four stages downstream and cannot move the gate's operating point — that justification is inoperative, and the number it was used to defend is the most consequential one in the preset.
problems.why: At the stated reference (speech peaks -12 dBFS), long-term speech RMS is ~-24 dBFS, and the standard intelligibility-bearing dynamic range of running speech is ~30 dB below peak (the range ANSI S3.5/SII is built on). That puts the quietest useful segments — unvoiced fricatives /s/ /f/ /th/, plosive tails, the last 100 ms of a trailing word — right at -42 dBFS. A threshold there expands the bottom of live speech, which is the specific failure the author correctly identified as unacceptable and then walked into: 2:1 expansion at the fricative level is exactly the 'amputated /s/' the expander-instead-of-gate choice was made to avoid, and low-bitrate AAC/Opus punish a chopped fricative onset far more than they punish room tone. -50 dBFS is 38 dB below reference peak, i.e. ~8 dB of clearance under the quietest speech, while a gaming-desk floor at this gain staging lands around -60 to -65 dBFS — still 10-15 dB under threshold, so at 2:1 the floor gets 10-15 dB of attenuation (inside the recommended -18 dB depth cap) and the expander still does its job. Keep ratio 2.0, attack 5, hold 150, release 200 and the -3 dB hysteresis note; only the threshold is wrong. This also removes the dependence on the broken post-makeup argument: at -50 the gate is safe whether or not makeup is later re-trimmed.

problems.problem: The compensation for the de-esser sitting BEFORE the compressor is under-scaled by roughly a factor of three, and the 6 dB reduction cap then cancels whatever the de-esser did. The rationale identifies the right hazard and then applies a 2 dB offset to a 6 dB problem.
problems.corrected_value: threshold_db: -28, max_reduction_db: 8
problems.why: Arithmetic from this preset's own numbers. A strong /s/ runs 10-15 dB below vowel peaks broadband, so at the -12 dBFS reference it sits at -22 to -27 dBFS — below the compressor's -20 dBFS threshold. Vowel peaks at -12 dBFS are 8 dB over threshold and take 8 x (1 - 1/4) = 6 dB of gain reduction; the sibilant, below threshold, takes ~0 dB. Both then receive the same +12 dB makeup. Net result: sibilance emerges from the compressor 6 dB louder RELATIVE to vowels than it went in, downstream of the only de-esser in the chain. The author's -2 dB offset covers a third of that, and a 6 dB max_reduction cap means the de-esser's maximum possible action is precisely erased by the compressor's differential gain — the stage becomes decorative on the loudest syllables, which are the ones that lisp through 96 kbps AAC. Correct compensation is the full differential: jtrv's tuned -22, minus ~1 dB for this preset's composite +1.07 dB lift at 4666 Hz, minus the ~6 dB the compressor adds back, rounded up to -28 to allow that not every sibilant fully escapes compression. Raise the cap to 8 dB so the guard sits above the 6 dB the compressor will undo rather than at it; 3-6 dB of NET reduction (the SoundOnSound/typical target the author cites) is then still what reaches the listener, because 6-8 dB applied pre-compressor becomes 0-2 dB net after the compressor's differential gain. Ratio 3.0, split 5500, attack 1.0, release 60 all stay — those are right, and the 5500 Hz split correctly stays clear of the presence region.

problems.problem: The WebRTC evidence is read backwards. That every Chrome/Discord/Teams/Jitsi capture path already runs butter(2, 100/fs, 'high') is an argument that OUR filter is redundant on those destinations, not that 100 Hz is the right value for ours. On the game-voice-chat half of this preset's stated destination the two filters cascade into a 4th-order 100 Hz response — the near-cliff behaviour just below male fundamentals that the rationale explicitly chose 2nd order to avoid.
problems.why: Cascading two 2nd-order 100 Hz Butterworths gives -7.1 dB at 100 Hz and -2.0 dB at 150 Hz (doubling WebRTC's measured -3.54/-1.01), landing 7 dB of attenuation on the fundamental of an adult male voice in the 85-100 Hz part of its range — audible thinning on exactly the Discord/Teams path the preset names. At 80 Hz our filter contributes -1.8 dB at 100 Hz instead of -3.5, so the cascade is -5.4 dB rather than -7.1, while the cost on the OBS path (where nothing else filters) is only 2.3 dB less rejection at 50 Hz: -9.7 dB vs -12.0 dB, still ample for fans, chair and keyboard thump, and still the 80 Hz that RODE states for voice and that sits inside Shure's 70-90 Hz. 80 Hz is the value that is defensible on BOTH destinations rather than optimal on one. Downstream consequences are benign: residual at band 1 (115.734 Hz) becomes -0.9 dB instead of -1.9 dB, which does not change the correct decision to leave eq_boost_db[1] at 0 (the HPF still owns proximity control and a -2 slider there would still land on the male fundamental), and it does not affect eq_boost_db[0], which is correctly 0.

critiques.overall:
The reasoning quality here is unusually high and most of the preset is right. Confirmed against the repo rather than taken on trust: eq.rs:71-82 gives Q = sqrt(r)/(r-1) = 1.598 at r = 1.8517 (0.889 oct), so the constant-Q ladder behaviour, the ~19%-per-neighbour bleed and every composite dB figure in the rationale are structurally sound; the Q-widening floor really does only engage below 0.42 dB. On latency — the thing that normally sinks a live-voice chain — this preset is clean: nothing in it has look-ahead except the limiter, and the existing brick-wall (dynamic_boost.rs:70-71) uses 0.75 ms / 36 frames at 48 kHz. Feed-forward gate, de-esser and compressor add zero. There is no latency objection to make, and I am not going to invent one.

Things I checked and affirm rather than change. The EQ is correct and correctly small: 0 dB at 62.5 Hz (13/13 factory presets agree, and a cut there would bleed -1.8 dB into 80 Hz for no benefit), +2.0 at 2519.84 as the single largest move, and the deliberate +0.5 restraint at 4666 because the EQ precedes the de-esser. Sliders inside ±2 is the right call for a signal that ends up in 96 kbps AAC. The compressor is the strongest part: 4:1 at -20 dBFS is solved backwards from a 6 dB gain-reduction target rather than picked, 15 ms attack correctly refuses the 1-5 ms vocal-tracking folklore that clamps 10-35 ms stop-consonant bursts, and refusing OBS's 10:1 default is right. It also has a property the rationale does not claim: because the ratio absorbs input-level error, a mic running 6 dB hotter than the -12 dBFS reference lands peaks at -4.5 dBFS instead of -6, so the chain degrades gracefully in the loud direction. It does NOT degrade gracefully in the quiet direction — a mic 12 dB under reference exits around -15 dBFS peaks / ~-27 LUFS, 7 LU under TD1008's floor, because most of the speech then falls below the compressor threshold and never gets the 6 dB back. That asymmetry reinforces the author's own (correct) demand for measured calibration and for re-trimming makeup against the same speech reference as the other five presets. -3.0 dBFS ceiling is right and the four reasons given are individually valid; the observation that RNNoise placed after the brick-wall limiter defeats it is correct and should be fixed by reordering, not absorbed by margin.

Three corrections, in severity order. The gate threshold is the one that must change before any listening test: -42 dBFS sits on the quietest speech, not under it, and the argument defending it (post-makeup floor) cannot apply to the first stage in the chain. The de-esser compensation is arithmetically under-scaled — the compressor adds back 6 dB of sibilance-to-vowel ratio downstream of it and the 6 dB cap exactly cancels the stage. The HPF reads its best piece of evidence backwards: WebRTC shipping a 100 Hz butter(2) on every browser capture path means ours is redundant there and merely doubles the slope, so 80 Hz is the value that is safe on both destinations.

Two smaller notes, no value change needed. The claim that 6350 Hz is a hole the ladder 'structurally cannot reach' is false: at 0.889-octave spacing the -3 dB points of bands 7 and 8 fall on each other's centres, so setting both to X dB produces about X dB at 6350 — the ladder can reach it, just not without also moving 4666 and 8640. That does not change the decision to let the de-esser own that region, but the code comment should not assert the stronger claim. And the knee sign convention (6 dB soft knee BELOW threshold, LSP's -6 with the sign flipped) is correctly flagged as a trap but is not yet expressed anywhere in a schema — since crates/fxsound-preset/src/ has no input-preset types at all, define the convention in the type, not in a comment, before six presets are written against an ambiguous field.

preset.name: Podcast
preset.intent: For someone recording spoken word into an editor and mixing for headphone listening: a warm, present, lightly-levelled voice with breaths and word tails intact and plenty of headroom left for the editor's own loudness pass.
preset.rationale:
HPF 80 Hz. Unanimous across the dossier's manufacturer sources: Shure 70–90 Hz, RODE 80 Hz, BOYA "start at 75". Adult male speaking fundamentals run 85–180 Hz, so 80 Hz keeps the voice and removes desk rumble, HVAC and the LF body of plosives before they reach the gate and compressor detectors. 100 Hz (the Streaming/Discord value) is rejected here specifically because Podcast is asked for MORE body and the WebRTC-measured 2nd-order response is already -3.54 dB at 100 Hz — audible thinning on a deep voice through headphones. Assume 2nd/4th-order Butterworth; researcher 5's computed residual for a 4th-order at 80 Hz is -9.1 dB at 62.5 Hz and -0.2 dB at 115.734 Hz, which is exactly the division of labour the EQ below relies on.

GATE (downward expander, not a gate). threshold -45 dBFS, ratio 2.0, attack 5 ms, hold 120 ms, release 250 ms. Ratio 2.0 is Rane Note 155's figure for noise reduction by expansion; the dossier is explicit that an infinite-ratio gate amputates voiceless fricatives (/s/, /f/) and plosive tails, which sit only a few dB above room tone and are the first thing a headphone listener notices. Attack 5 ms is what every *tuned* preset in the survey uses (jtrv, luix-voice, dzervas, Barisozyurek); EasyEffects' 20 ms default clips word onsets and was rejected on that basis. Hold 120 ms sits in the 70–150 ms speech window (Wikipedia/SOS) and spans inter-word gaps, which is the direct cure for chattering. Release 250 ms is jtrv's value and the longest in the survey — deliberate here, because podcast pacing is conversational and a fast release audibly chops breaths, which matters far more on headphones than on a laptop speaker. Threshold -45 dBFS is the weakest number in this preset and I am saying so: the dossier's own tuned presets range from -50 (jtrv, azmarifdev) to -55 (luix) to -24 (untuned default), and researcher 4 states plainly that this spread is gain staging, not disagreement — threshold is only meaningful against a measured noise floor. -45 assumes a nominal chain where normal speech RMS lands near -24 dBFS. It should be derived from a short noise-floor measurement rather than shipped as a constant, and this preset sits at the conservative (low) end on purpose so that a quiet aside is never expanded.

EQ, ten gains on the fixed ladder. Authored as a shape, not as ten independent numbers, because researcher 5 measured the derived Q at 1.5976 (0.889 octave per band, constant-Q above ~0.42 dB of gain) and showed that adjacent bands sum: two neighbours at +3 give +3.6 dB, not +6, and a single band bleeds 0.5–0.6 dB into each neighbouring centre. Every value stays inside ±2 dB, matching FxSound's own shipped presets (11 of 13 live within -4..+5 dB) and iZotope's "no more than 1 or 2 dB is common" for the presence region.
- 62.5 Hz: 0.0. Deliberate, and the single most likely mistake to make here. The 80 Hz high-pass has already put this band 9 dB down; cutting it further would be a no-op on rumble while the bell's 0.889-octave skirt pulls -1.8 dB at 80 Hz and -0.9 dB at 100 Hz out of the voice I just chose to keep. Boosting it would re-import exactly what the HPF removed and spend limiter headroom on inaudible content. FxSound's own 13 factory presets are 0 dB here in 13 of 13 — I confirmed this directly in Installer/Resources/Factsoft/3.fac ("Voice").
- 115.734 Hz: +1.5. This is where the brief's "more body" is actually spent. The band spans 85–157 Hz — the male fundamental — and an 80 Hz 4th-order HPF leaves it untouched (-0.2 dB), so it is the only genuinely effective LF control in the chain. Precedent: azmarifdev's podcast preset lifts +3 dB with a 90 Hz low shelf, luix-voice +2 dB at 130 Hz. +1.5 rather than +3 because a shelf and a 0.889-octave bell are not the same thing, and because proximity effect can already add up to +16 dB below 100 Hz at close distance (Sweetwater/DPA) — a preset cannot track that, so it must not assume it away.
- 214.311 Hz: -1.0. Proximity/chest region. Shure's own hardware answer (SM7B bass rolloff) is about -3 dB at 200 Hz, which is the precedent for cutting here at all; I use a third of it because this preset is explicitly meant to keep body, and a deeper cut would fight the +1.5 one band below.
- 396.85 Hz: -2.0. The mud/box core (250–500 Hz). All three genuinely tuned voice presets in the survey — jtrv (-2 at 220 and 350), azmarifdev (-2 at 425), luix-voice (-1 at 300) — land on about -2 dB. Podcast gets the deeper end of that range because it is the preset carrying the most low-end body and mud is the cost of body.
- 734.867 Hz: -1.0. Boxy/papery/throaty. Paired with the band below rather than deepening a single cut: researcher 5's warning is that -5 dB or more at 396 Hz reads as a telephone hole, whereas -2/-1 across two adjacent bands reads as tone. Composite here is about -2.2 dB at 396.85 and -1.4 dB at 734.9 once summation is accounted for.
- 1360.79 Hz: 0.0. Nasal/honk region, two-sided and touchy, and the 1 kHz honk actually sits on the band 4/5 crossover where neither slider can address it cleanly. Left alone.
- 2519.84 Hz: +2.0. This is where the brief's "more presence" is spent. Band spans 1852–3429 Hz, i.e. the presence and intelligibility core, and it is the closest fixed centre to the +2/+2.5/+3 dB at 3.2–3.5 kHz that jtrv, luix-voice and azmarifdev all independently chose. Shure's own presence switch on the SM7B is about +3–4 dB peaking at 2.5–5 kHz, which is the manufacturer ceiling; +2 dB is inside iZotope's stated 1–2 dB norm.
- 4666.12 Hz: 0.0. This is a considered refusal. It is the most damaging boost on the ladder: it adds sibilance and harshness in the region where ISO 226 says the ear is most sensitive, it drives the de-esser that sits immediately after it, and on headphones that harshness has nowhere to hide. Researcher 3's six-preset mapping explicitly differentiates Streaming as "Podcast plus a touch more 4666" — so Podcast getting its presence from 2519.84 and its extra body from 115.734, while Streaming buys edge up here, is what keeps the two presets distinguishable for the right reason.
- 8640.48 Hz: +1.0. Air. All three tuned presets use a +2 dB shelf from 9–10 kHz; a fixed ladder cannot make a shelf (boosting 8640 and 16000 together loses the shelf's flat top and lifts pure hiss), so I take half the move on the one band that has real content. +1 not +2 because budget USB condensers concentrate their self-noise here (FIFINE publishes -80 dBFS equivalent noise / 78 dB S/N) and the +5 dB makeup below makes any added hiss +5 dB more audible.
- 16000 Hz: 0.0. There is essentially no speech harmonic content above ~12 kHz — what is up there is mic self-noise, breath and codec artefacts. Also at or above Nyquist on an HFP/mSBC Bluetooth headset (16 kHz capture), so a boost here would be a no-op on exactly the devices whose users need help most.
Net: +4.5 dB of boost against -4.0 dB of cut, in non-overlapping regions, so the broadband level change is within a few tenths of a dB. That matters because it keeps the makeup gain below honest and keeps this preset loudness-comparable to Studio/Natural.

DE-ESSER: split 5500 Hz, threshold -24 dB, ratio 3:1, max reduction 5 dB, attack 1 ms, release 60 ms.
