Split-band, not wideband — Wikipedia and iZotope both describe why (wideband ducks the vowel under the S), and Calf's own recommendation of Wide mode is rejected here because with a compressor immediately downstream, full-band ducking on every "s" produces audible pumping. 5500 Hz is luix-voice's split, sitting between Calf's 6000 default and jtrv's 4000: it is above the 4666.12 EQ centre so presence and consonant definition are not ducked, it catches the upper half of male sibilance (5–6 kHz) and all of female (7–8 kHz). I explicitly refuse azmarifdev's 3000 Hz split despite that preset being the closest thing the survey has to a "podcast" preset — 3 kHz is the intelligibility region, and RODE puts sibilance at 4–7 kHz while FabFilter puts s-sounds at 8–10 kHz. Ratio 3:1 is unanimous across the tuned presets and mastering.com. Threshold -24 dB is lower than jtrv's -22 and azmarifdev's -20, for one structural reason: the planned chain puts the de-esser BEFORE the compressor, and researcher 1 is right that the compressor then re-amplifies whatever sibilance survives, so the de-esser has to engage earlier than the community numbers suggest. The safety against the resulting lisp risk is the 5 dB reduction cap (mastering.com and LedgerNote both say 3–6 dB is the working range and that uncapped reduction is what produces a lisp) plus a 60 ms release, inside the 40–150 ms window so the band recovers before the following vowel. Attack 1 ms because a sibilant is a short burst that must be caught, unlike the main compressor which must let transients through. Test criterion from the dbx 286s manual and researcher 4: read a sentence full of S's and confirm the S's are still identifiable as S, not as th.

COMPRESSOR: threshold -20 dB, ratio 3:1, knee -6 dB, attack 20 ms, release 200 ms. Ratio 3:1 is RODE's stated 2:1–4:1 for vocals, Rane's "gentle" band, and jtrv's choice; it is the modal tuned value in the survey. Attack 20 ms is the most consequential choice in this preset and it contradicts the common "1–5 ms for vocals" advice on purpose: a stop-consonant burst runs from a few ms up to ~35 ms (Jackson), so a 1–5 ms attack clamps the burst itself and produces the dull, mushy speech that people then try to fix with more HF lift. Rane Note 155 gives 25–100 ms for vocals, jtrv uses 15, EasyEffects/MateusRodCosta 20; 20 ms is the honest middle. Release 200 ms is chosen against syllable rate, not by feel: the speech envelope's modulation spectrum peaks at 4–8 Hz (mean ~4.5–5 Hz), i.e. one syllable every 125–250 ms, so 200 ms recovers between syllables without breathing inside them — and the longer end of that window suits conversational podcast pacing (researcher 4 recommends exactly 25 ms/200 ms for this preset; I take 20/200). I explicitly do NOT copy azmarifdev's podcast compressor (5 ms attack, 75 ms release) even though it is nominally the closest match, because that combination is the fast-attack/fast-release pairing SOS names as the cause of the squashed sound. Threshold -20 dB assumes normal speech RMS near -24 dBFS and loud syllables near -12: at -12 in, 8 dB over threshold at 3:1 gives about 5.3 dB of reduction, which lands inside Rane's stated target of 3–6 dB gain reduction on normal speech and ~0 dB on quiet passages. That target, not the dB number, is the real spec — the same caveat as the gate threshold applies. Knee -6 dB is written in the LSP/EasyEffects convention (negative = width of the soft knee BELOW threshold) and is the one parameter every single preset in the corpus shares, untouched, across LSP, Calf-era and tuned presets alike. If the implementation's knee control is a positive width, read this as 6 dB, and if it is a hard/soft toggle, it is soft — do the conversion explicitly rather than passing -6 through.

MAKEUP +5.0 dB. Derived, not picked. The TASCAM/Waves auto-makeup rule gives 0.5 × |threshold| × (1 - 1/ratio) = 0.5 × 20 × 0.667 = 6.7 dB for a 0 dBFS signal; real speech sees ~4–5 dB of reduction, so ~5 dB restores the level the compressor took, and the EQ's net broadband contribution is near zero so no further offset is needed (this is the reason the EQ was authored balanced). Target: -19 LUFS mono, equivalently -16 LUFS once dual-monoed into a stereo virtual source — Apple Podcasts' -16 LKFS ±1 and Google's speech guideline agree once the 3.01 LU mono/stereo offset is applied. That offset is the highest-risk number in this whole design and the brief's own framing had it inverted; it is -16 STEREO and -19 MONO, confirmed independently by Podnews and Google. This +5.0 is a starting value and must be trimmed by measuring this preset's short-term loudness on the same speech reference used for the other five, so the six are loudness-matched to each other and to bypass — researcher 2 is right that hand-picked makeup values make the A/B against Studio/Natural meaningless. Do not servo it from an integrated measurement in real time; integrated loudness is defined over a programme and is not a control signal.

LIMITER CEILING -3.0 dBFS. Podcast is the preset that should limit least. Reasoning: (a) this is a virtual microphone, not a delivery format — it is not the last stage, so the standards' -1 dBTP (EBU R128 §m, AES TD1008 §4, Apple) does not apply to it directly; Apple's -1 dBTP is a spec for the finished file, which the user's editor will produce, not for the capture. (b) Whatever follows — Opus at an unknown bitrate, a DAW, OBS's own limiter which defaults to a -6 dB threshold — will re-limit or re-encode, and TD1008 documents up to 3 dB of gain reduction in a decode-side OS limiter when the encode side left insufficient headroom, and says the threshold must go BELOW -1.0 dBTP as bitrate falls. (c) If the implementation detects peaks at the native rate without 4× oversampling then this number is dBFS sample peak, not dBTP, and such a limiter routinely leaks above 0 dBTP at a -1 dBFS setting — label the control dBFS in the UI and do not claim -1 dBTP compliance. With the gain staging above, speech peaks land around -10 dBFS, so the limiter should see roughly 0 dB of reduction on normal speech and only catch a door slam or a laugh — which is TD1008's own guidance that ~1 dB of limiting is the maximum before artefacts beat the occasional clipped transient. -3 dBFS costs nothing perceptually here because the editor will normalise anyway, and it preserves the peak-to-loudness ratio that makes a podcast voice sound uncompressed.

LATENCY. HPF, expander, EQ, de-esser and makeup are all zero-lookahead; the only cost is the limiter's lookahead, for which 2 ms is sufficient because the 80 Hz high-pass has already defused the plosive energy a longer window would exist to catch (FabFilter: lookahead is added latency 1:1; 4× oversampling adds ~5 ms more). Total added latency ~2 ms, well under the ~15 ms budget for self-monitoring.

TWO THINGS THE DOSSIER SAYS ARE WRONG WITH THE FIXED CHAIN, WHICH THIS PRESET CANNOT FIX. First, the de-esser sits before the compressor; 7 of the 8 surveyed presets that have both do the opposite, for the sound reason that the compressor re-amplifies sibilance. I have compensated with a lower de-esser threshold and a reduction cap, but the right fix is to move the de-esser after makeup. Second, optional RNNoise is placed after the brick-wall limiter. Zero presets in the survey do this, and AES TD1008 §7B states that filtering should occur before the peak limiter because removing programme energy raises peaks (up to +2.1 dB in their square-wave example). RNNoise is spectral gain modification and will push peaks back above the ceiling the limiter just enforced. It should run first, before the gate, where it also makes the expander's threshold decision easier. For this preset I would ship RNNoise OFF by default regardless: a podcast is edited afterwards, offline denoising is strictly better than a real-time neural pass, and the 10 ms RNNoise frame would quintuple the chain's latency.

NOT COVERED BY THE DOSSIER, stated rather than invented: the high-pass slope/order (the dossier gives 12 dB/oct as the well-trodden WebRTC choice and researcher 5 computes a 4th-order case, but no source settles it for this product); the gate's sidechain detection mode (RMS is every surveyed project's default, but this schema has no field for it); and any per-band importance weights from ANSI/ASA S3.5 — that standard is paywalled and was not obtained, so the presence-band choices rest on Shure, RODE, iZotope and the 300–3400 Hz telephony band, not on the standard's weights.

critiques.overall:
DYNAMICS VERDICT: the time constants are the strongest part of this preset and I am not going to invent objections to them. What is broken is level referencing — three of the four dynamics stages have thresholds that were imported from other people's presets without being re-referenced to this preset's own stated gain staging (-24 dBFS normal speech RMS, -12 dBFS loud syllables). The de-esser lands in the wrong measurement domain entirely.

Direct answers to the questions asked:

WILL THE GATE CHATTER? Not from hold/release — 120 ms hold spans inter-word gaps (50-200 ms) and 250 ms release is correctly longer than the 125-250 ms syllable period. It will BREATHE, not chatter, and that is problem #2: there is no range/floor cap, so at 2:1 a -60 dBFS room tone is attenuated 15 dB and released over 370 ms, i.e. a 2-3 Hz modulation of the noise floor sitting just under the 4-8 Hz speech envelope band. That is the classic expander artifact and it is worse on headphones, which is this preset's stated target.

WILL IT CLIP CONSONANTS? No. 5 ms attack at 2:1 is correct and the rejection of EasyEffects' 20 ms default is right. The only exposure is a sentence-initial fricative after a >370 ms pause, and at 2:1 that costs a few dB of a 20-50 ms onset ramp — inaudible.

WILL THE COMPRESSOR PUMP OR SQUASH? No, and this is the best-reasoned parameter in the preset. 20 ms attack against a 2-35 ms stop-burst and 200 ms release against a 4-8 Hz (125-250 ms) syllable rate is correct, and the explicit refusal of azmarifdev's 5 ms/75 ms is the right call for exactly the reason given. The only defect is the threshold/knee interaction (problem #3): under the preset's OWN stated knee convention the compression onset is -26 dBFS, 2 dB below average speech, and loud-syllable reduction is 7.3 dB, not the 5.3 dB computed with a hard-knee formula — outside the Rane 3-6 dB target the rationale names as the real spec.

WILL MAKEUP + COMPRESSION DRIVE THE LIMITER INTO CONSTANT REDUCTION? No. Loudest syllables reach ≈-12 dBFS RMS, take 5-7 dB of reduction, peak ≈-12 dBFS after compression (crest ≈15 dB on -24 RMS gives ≈-9 dBFS unprocessed peaks), +5 makeup puts them at ≈-7 dBFS against a -3 dBFS ceiling. The limiter idles, exactly as claimed. It still idles under the hotter loudness reading in problem #5 (peaks ≈-4 dBFS at +8 makeup). The -3 dBFS ceiling is genuinely well-defended: at -3 dBFS sample peak, speech inter-sample overshoot of ~1-1.5 dB lands near -1.5 dBTP, so the no-oversampling caveat in the rationale is honest and the number is true-peak safe without claiming to be.

WILL THE DE-ESSER LISP? No — the opposite, and that is the headline failure. As specified it will barely engage at all (problem #1), which silently voids the whole safety argument for placing a de-esser ahead of the compressor. Once the threshold is corrected, a secondary point: with ratio 3 and a 5 dB cap, a strong /s/ 12 dB over threshold asks for 8 dB and gets clamped to 5, so the de-esser behaves as a switched -5 dB HF shelf rather than a proportional one. Lisp-safe but blunt; ratio 2.5 with max_reduction_db 6 gives the same peak reduction with a proportional response. Not severe enough to list separately.

TWO SCHEMA GAPS worth raising with whoever owns the format, since no preset value can work around them: the gate has no hysteresis and no range/floor field (both are how real expanders avoid the breathing in problem #2), and the limiter has only a ceiling — no lookahead, attack or release — while the rationale asserts a 2 ms lookahead that the preset cannot actually express.

Everything else — HPF at 80 Hz before the detectors, gate ratio 2.0 as expansion rather than an infinite-ratio gate, compressor ratio 3:1, de-esser split at 5500 Hz above the 4666 Hz EQ centre, de-esser attack 1 ms and release 60 ms, the refusal to servo makeup from an integrated measurement, and the chain-order criticisms at the end — I checked and would not change.

problems.problem: The threshold is in the wrong measurement domain relative to this preset's own gain staging, and the rationale's central claim about it is inverted. The rationale argues -24 dB is 'lower than jtrv's -22 and azmarifdev's -20' so the de-esser 'engages earlier than the community numbers suggest' — compensating for sitting ahead of the compressor. But those presets run typical EasyEffects input levels, roughly -18 dBFS broadband speech RMS. This preset explicitly assumes -24 dBFS, i.e. 6 dB colder. Referenced to program level, -24 dB here is EQUIVALENT to about -18 dB in jtrv's chain — 4 dB HIGHER than jtrv, not 2 dB lower. The de-esser therefore engages LESS than every source it cites, and against a >5.5 kHz split band that carries 15-25 dB less energy than broadband, a strong /s/ will sit near or below the threshold and produce zero or near-zero gain reduction. The 5 dB cap and the lisp-safety argument protect a stage that never fires.
problems.corrected_value: -30 (jtrv's -22 shifted 6 dB for the colder gain staging = -28, minus 2 dB for the stated intent to engage earlier than the community values). Ship it as derived, not constant: threshold = measured broadband speech RMS minus 6 dB, evaluated in the >5500 Hz band. Also state in the preset which domain the field is in — LSP/Calf split-band absolute dBFS vs. a level relative to the full-band sidechain — because the two differ by ~20 dB and nothing in the schema disambiguates it.
problems.why: This is the one error that changes what the user hears. The rationale correctly identifies that de-esser-before-compressor is a chain-order defect and correctly says the compensation must be a lower threshold. It then supplies a number that, against this preset's own assumed levels, is higher than the presets it is compensating against. Net result: sibilance passes the de-esser untouched, gets +2 dB at 2519.84 Hz and +1 dB at 8640.48 Hz from the EQ upstream, then +5 dB of makeup — the exact harsh-on-headphones outcome the 4666.12 Hz 'considered refusal' was written to avoid.

problems.problem: Expansion is unbounded. Ratio 2.0 with threshold -45 dBFS applies 2x the under-threshold excursion with no floor: a room tone at -60 dBFS is 15 dB under, so it is pushed to -75 dBFS — 15 dB of attenuation that is applied in 5 ms and removed over a 120 ms hold plus 250 ms release on every phrase boundary. That is a 2-3 Hz amplitude modulation of the noise floor, landing just below the 4-8 Hz speech envelope band where the ear is most sensitive to envelope modulation. Rane Note 155's 2:1 figure is for range-limited expansion; quoting the ratio without the range is what produces breathing. On an untreated room with a condenser at 20 cm — the stated podcast scenario, with RNNoise deliberately OFF — a -55 to -62 dBFS floor is normal, so this is the expected case, not the worst case.
problems.corrected_value: Add "range_db": 10 to the gate block (cap total expander attenuation at 10 dB; LSP/OBS call this range or floor). If the schema cannot be extended, set ratio to 1.5, which caps the same -60 dBFS floor at 7.5 dB of swing. Also add "hysteresis_db": 3 — hold alone does not prevent detector re-triggering when the floor sits near the threshold, which is a live risk at -45 dBFS on a noisy USB interface.
problems.why: The preset's stated priority is headphone listening with breaths and word tails intact. A noise floor that pumps 15 dB in and out over 370 ms is more audible on headphones than the room tone it removes, and it is the specific artifact that makes people distrust expanders. Capping the range keeps every other gate value — the 5 ms attack, the 120 ms hold, the 250 ms release, all of which are correctly chosen — and removes the artifact outright.

problems.problem: The rationale explicitly declares the LSP/EasyEffects knee convention ('negative = width of the soft knee BELOW threshold'), then computes gain reduction with a hard-knee formula. Those are inconsistent. Under the declared convention the knee spans -26 to -20 dBFS and the curve is slope-continuous, so gain reduction at the threshold itself is already (1-1/3) x 6/2 = 2.0 dB and the asymptote above threshold is offset by that 2 dB: at a -12 dBFS loud syllable, GR = 2.0 + 0.667 x 8 = 7.3 dB, not the 5.3 dB stated. That is outside the Rane 3-6 dB window the rationale itself names as 'the real spec'. Separately, compression now begins at -26 dBFS, 2 dB BELOW the stated -24 dBFS average speech RMS, so the compressor is lightly active on all voiced speech rather than the claimed '~0 dB on quiet passages'. The 5.3 dB figure is only correct under a threshold-centred knee, which is not the convention the preset declared.
problems.corrected_value: threshold_db: -18, keeping knee_db -6 in the declared below-threshold convention. The knee foot then lands at -24 dBFS = stated average speech (GR ≈ 0 there, as intended), full ratio from -18, and a -12 dBFS loud syllable gets 2.0 + 0.667 x 6 = 6.0 dB — the top of Rane's 3-6 dB band and the behaviour the rationale describes. If instead the implementation's knee is threshold-centred, keep -20 and correct the rationale's stated convention; do not leave both unresolved.
problems.why: The rationale is right that the gain-reduction target, not the dB number, is the real spec — so an arithmetic slip that puts the actual reduction 2 dB outside that target matters more than usual. It also cascades: the +5 dB makeup was derived from 0.5 x |threshold| x (1-1/ratio) on threshold -20; at -18 that rule gives 6.0 dB and real-speech reduction near 3 dB, so +5 remains a defensible starting value and nothing downstream needs to move.

problems.field: limiter (missing lookahead field; rationale for 2 ms)
problems.problem: The latency section asserts a 2 ms limiter lookahead, but the schema has no lookahead, attack or release field — only limiter_ceiling_db — so the preset cannot express it and an implementer will pick their own. The justification is also wrong: it argues 2 ms suffices because the 80 Hz high-pass 'already defused the plosive energy a longer window would exist to catch'. Lookahead exists for fast broadband transients, not LF pops. The peaks that actually reach this limiter are the stop-consonant bursts of /t/ and /k/ — 2-35 ms, concentrated 2-8 kHz, raised by the +2 dB at 2519.84 Hz and +1 dB at 8640.48 Hz, and deliberately passed by the 20 ms compressor attack. The 80 Hz HPF does nothing to those.
problems.corrected_value: Add "limiter_lookahead_ms": 5 to the schema and the preset (still well inside the ~15 ms self-monitoring budget: total added latency ~5 ms, not ~2 ms). Restate the rationale as: lookahead is sized for 2-35 ms stop-burst transients, which is also why the compressor's 20 ms attack is safe to pass them.
problems.why: Low severity under the stated gain staging, because peaks land near -7 dBFS against a -3 dBFS ceiling and the limiter idles. It becomes real the moment a user's preamp runs 5-6 dB hotter than assumed — then the limiter starts catching exactly those bursts, and a 2 ms window on a broadband click is where a limiter audibly distorts rather than limits. Fixing the stated reason matters as much as the number, because the wrong reason will survive into the next preset.

problems.problem: The -19 LUFS mono target and the +5 dB makeup only reconcile under one reading of '-24 dBFS normal speech RMS', and the rationale uses the other reading elsewhere. If -24 dBFS is the BS.1770-gated energy mean of active speech, active level is ≈-21 LUFS, mean compressor reduction ≈3 dB gives ≈-24 LUFS, and +5 lands on -19 LUFS: correct. But the compressor section treats -24 dBFS as the typical/modal syllable level and calls -12 dBFS 'loud syllables' — under that reading the energy mean sits near -20 dBFS, post-compression loudness near -25 to -26 LUFS, and +5 delivers -21 to -23 LUFS mono, i.e. 2-4 dB short of the stated target. The same symbol is carrying two different meanings across two sections.
problems.corrected_value: Keep makeup_db: 5 and pin the anchor in the rationale: '-24 dBFS = BS.1770-gated energy mean of active speech, not the modal syllable level.' If the intended anchor is the modal level, makeup_db: 8 instead. Either way the -3 dBFS ceiling survives — at +8 makeup, peaks move from ≈-7 to ≈-4 dBFS and the limiter still sees ~0 dB of reduction on speech.
problems.why: The rationale already commits to trimming this by measurement against the other five presets, which is the right process and makes this the least severe item here. But the same -24 dBFS figure is also what sets the gate threshold and, in my first finding, exposes the de-esser threshold error — so an ambiguous level anchor is not a documentation nit in this preset, it is the reference that three thresholds are derived from. Define it once, explicitly, and the other derivations become checkable.

critiques.overall:
The numbers in this preset are, unusually, mostly correct — I checked the load-bearing ones against the code and they hold. `crates/fxsound-dsp/src/eq.rs:derive_q` gives r = 256^(1/9) = 1.85175, i.e. 0.8889 oct/band and Q = 1.5976412 exactly as claimed; `crates/fxsound-dsp/src/biquad.rs:129` warps Q down only below |gain| = (1.5976-0.2)/3.3 = 0.4235 dB, so the "constant-Q above ~0.42 dB" claim is exact and every non-zero gain here (≥1.0 dB) keeps full Q; the Rule-A low-frequency Q cap only bites below 60 Hz so the 62.5 Hz band is unaffected; the 4th-order HPF residuals (-9.14 dB at 62.5, -0.22 dB at 115.734) reproduce to two decimals; and the +3.01 LU dual-mono offset is right. The EQ shape is genuinely well authored and I am not asking for a single band to change.

The problem is not arithmetic, it is dose. This is the one preset in the set whose destination is an offline editor with undo, lookahead and whole-programme knowledge — and it is carrying the second-heaviest dynamics chain in the set. The rationale itself makes exactly the right argument ("a podcast is edited afterwards, offline denoising is strictly better than a real-time neural pass") to switch RNNoise off, and then declines to apply that same argument to the expander, to 4-5 dB of real-time gain reduction, and to 5 dB of irreversible sibilance ducking. Compression and de-essing are the two moves in this chain that cannot be undone downstream; they are the two that should be smallest here, not largest.

Second-order concern: the preset aims the *capture* at a *delivery* loudness (-19 LUFS mono / -16 stereo). That target is defeated by the destination in both likely directions — an editor renormalises it anyway, and a browser-based recorder (Riverside/Zencastr/Zoom in Chromium) runs WebRTC AGC2 plus its own 80 Hz high-pass over the top, which will re-inflate whatever the expander pulled down and re-level whatever the compressor levelled. A capture node's spec is headroom in dBFS, not LUFS.

With the six corrections below the preset still sounds like "Podcast" — it keeps every EQ move, the de-esser, the limiter and the whole tonal identity — but hands the editor a file with ~13-14 dB of crest left instead of ~10-11, and stops making promises (self-monitoring latency, -19 LUFS, "EQ is broadband-neutral") that it cannot keep. Verdict NEEDS_CHANGES rather than BROKEN: nothing here is wrong-sounding, it is over-committed for where the audio goes.

problems.problem: 3:1 at -20 dB with 20 ms attack is the heaviest irreversible move in a chain whose destination is an offline editor. Steady-state: normal speech RMS -24 passes, a -12 dBFS syllable gets 5.3 dB GR, a -9 dBFS peak gets 7.3 dB. Combined with +5 dB makeup that takes the speech crest factor from ~15 dB in to ~10-11 dB out, baked in, before the editor sees a sample. The rationale claims the design 'preserves the peak-to-loudness ratio that makes a podcast voice sound uncompressed' — it says that about the limiter, which never engages, while the compressor is the stage actually destroying 4-5 dB of PLR. An editor can add exactly this compression later with lookahead and undo; it cannot remove it.
problems.corrected_value: {"enabled": true, "threshold_db": -16, "ratio": 2, "knee_db": -6, "attack_ms": 20, "release_ms": 200}
problems.why: 2:1 at -16 dB gives 0 dB GR on normal speech (RMS -24), 2.0 dB on a -12 dBFS syllable and 3.5 dB on a -9 dBFS peak (less in practice, since the 20 ms attack lets short bursts through). Output crest stays ~13-14 dB instead of ~10-11. That is a safety net against a laugh or a table knock — which is all a capture stage owes an editor — while keeping the 20 ms/200 ms envelope choices, which are the best-argued numbers in the whole preset (stop-burst duration up to ~35 ms per Jackson; syllable rate 4-8 Hz) and should not change.

problems.problem: A 2:1 downward expander at -45 dBFS is applied to a recording that will be edited. The rationale's own argument for shipping RNNoise off — 'a podcast is edited afterwards, offline denoising is strictly better than a real-time neural pass' — applies verbatim to the expander, and is not applied. Worse, the expander sits before a compressor with +5 dB makeup, so the gaps it attenuates are then re-amplified by up to 5 dB: on a typical USB condenser with room tone near -50 dBFS, net noise reduction in gaps is roughly 5 dB minus 5 dB of makeup, i.e. approximately nothing. What it does reliably achieve is modulating the breaths and word tails that the intent explicitly says to keep intact.
problems.corrected_value: {"enabled": false}  — or, if a floor is mandatory: {"enabled": true, "threshold_db": -55, "ratio": 1.5, "attack_ms": 5, "hold_ms": 200, "release_ms": 400}
problems.why: For an editor-bound capture, gating is the textbook case of a decision to defer: strip-silence and spectral denoise run offline, non-destructively, with the whole programme in view. Disabling it also removes the preset's self-admitted weakest number (a -45 dBFS constant that is only meaningful against a measured noise floor) rather than shipping it. If the product insists every input preset has a floor, -55/1.5 with 200 ms hold and 400 ms release sits below any plausible speech tail and cannot chatter, so it does no harm while doing very little.

problems.problem: +5 dB is derived to hit -19 LUFS mono / -16 LUFS stereo, which is a delivery spec for a finished file, not a spec for a capture node — and the intent line promises the opposite ('plenty of headroom left for the editor's own loudness pass'). It also bakes in a mono/stereo ambiguity the preset cannot resolve: if the virtual source is dual-mono the recorder measures -16 LUFS, if it takes one channel it measures -19. And any browser-based podcast recorder will re-level it with WebRTC AGC2 regardless.
problems.why: With the corrected 2:1/-16 compressor, +2 dB puts normal speech at about -22 dBFS RMS (~-21 LUFS mono) and peaks near -8 dBFS, i.e. 5 dB of headroom under the -3 ceiling and 3-5 dB of trivial gain for the editor to make up. Specify the target as short-term RMS in dBFS at the capture node, not LUFS, and still measure it against the same speech reference as the other five presets so the six stay A/B-comparable. Keep limiter_ceiling_db at -3: the reasoning for it is sound and it correctly becomes a door-slam catcher that never touches speech.

problems.problem: The filter order is left unstated ('Assume 2nd/4th-order Butterworth') while the entire low-end argument depends on which one it is. At 4th order an 80 Hz high-pass is -0.22 dB at 115.734 Hz, so the +1.5 dB body band is untouched — the 'division of labour' the rationale relies on. At 2nd order the same 80 Hz filter is -0.89 dB at 115.734 Hz and only -12.3 dB at 40 Hz, so the preset delivers +0.6 dB of net body instead of +1.5 while leaving most of the desk rumble in place. The preset's headline promise ('MORE body than Streaming') silently halves depending on an unspecified field.
problems.corrected_value: hpf_hz: 80 with an explicit hpf_order: 4 (24 dB/oct Butterworth). If the implementation is fixed at 2nd order, then hpf_hz: 60.
problems.why: A 2nd-order at 60 Hz is -0.30 dB at 115.734 Hz and -2.67 dB at 62.5 Hz, which restores the intended division of labour (body band clear, EQ band 0 left at 0.0 correctly) at the cost of weaker sub-60 Hz rejection — an acceptable trade for a preset whose stated job is body and whose output goes to an editor that can high-pass again. Do not ship '80' without the order, since the two readings differ by 0.67 dB in exactly the band the preset is built around.

problems.problem: 5 dB of ducking at the capture stage is irreversible, and the editor will de-ess again on top of it — every podcast mastering chain does. Double de-essing is what produces the lisp the rationale is trying to avoid, and the preset has no way to know the downstream pass exists. The 5 dB cap also sits at the top of the 3-6 dB working range the rationale itself cites, for the preset that should be at the bottom of it.
problems.why: 3 dB is inside the same cited 3-6 dB range, still catches the harshest sibilants (with threshold -24 and 3:1, a sibilant band peak at -15 dBFS asks for 6 dB and gets 3), and leaves the sibilant shape legible enough that the editor's own de-esser can finish the job. Keep split_hz 5500, ratio 3, attack 1 ms, release 60 ms — the reasoning for each is sound, and the refusal of azmarifdev's 3000 Hz split is correct.

problems.problem: 'Total added latency ~2 ms, well under the ~15 ms budget for self-monitoring' claims a budget the preset does not control. A talker monitoring themselves through this virtual source pays the full PipeWire capture-to-playback round trip — two graph quanta plus device latency, typically 10-40 ms at 48 kHz — before this chain contributes anything. The 15 ms budget is already spent by the transport, so the 2 ms figure is true and irrelevant, and stating it invites users to monitor through the processed node, which is the one thing they should not do.
problems.corrected_value: Replace with: 'Added algorithmic latency: 2 ms (limiter lookahead only); every other stage is zero-lookahead. Total monitoring latency is this plus the graph round trip (typically 10-40 ms) and is not controlled by the preset — monitor the microphone directly via hardware/interface monitoring, not through the processed source.'
problems.why: The claim as written is the only place the preset overstates what it controls, and the harness's own latency concern lands on the transport, not on the 2 ms. Stating the real constraint also removes any argument for shrinking the limiter lookahead below 2 ms, which would be the wrong fix.

preset.name: Discord
preset.intent: For voice calls into a client that already runs its own noise suppression, echo cancellation and AGC: hand Discord a clean, rumble-free, syllable-levelled signal with the consonants intact and plenty of headroom, and let the platform do the rest.
preset.rationale:
GOVERNING IDEA. Discord is not a delivery format, it is another processor. Its capture path is WebRTC-class: AEC + noise suppression (Krisp by default) + AGC1, which per the shipped config targets a peak 3 dB below full scale (target_level_dbfs = 3), applies up to 9 dB of digital compression gain, and hard-limits (audio_processing.h:314/319/323); AGC2's adaptive branch moves gain at most 3 dB/s. That settles the one real disagreement in the dossier — researcher 4 wanted the "strongest expander, 4:1 compression, luix-voice's -26 dB threshold with +6 dB makeup because call codecs punish dynamic range", researcher 6 wanted "process LESS". I side with researcher 6, and the reason is mechanical rather than aesthetic: an AGC that moves at 3 dB/s is a long-term level control and cannot touch syllable-to-syllable dynamics, so the sensible split of labour is that we do the fast work (3-6 dB of gain reduction per syllable) and leave long-term level to the AGC, which will renormalise whatever we send anyway. Every dB of makeup gain we add is a dB of noise floor the client's AGC then amplifies in the pauses — the documented cause of the pumping/breathing users blame on Discord. Hence the Discord preset is deliberately the least processed of the six except Studio/Natural.

HPF 90 Hz, 2nd-order Butterworth (12 dB/oct). Two researchers recommended 100 Hz for this preset; I went to 90 and here is why. Discord's own path already runs a 2nd-order Butterworth high-pass at 100 Hz on every mic — the WebRTC APM filter, whose shipped 48 kHz coefficients measure -3.54 dB @100 Hz, -6.21 dB @80 Hz, -1.01 dB @150 Hz (high_pass_filter.cc, read and verified numerically by researcher 2). Setting ours to 100 Hz stacks two 2nd-order filters at the same corner, giving roughly -7 dB at 100 Hz, which sits inside the adult male speaking fundamental (85-180 Hz) and thins exactly the voices it is meant to help. 90 Hz is inside Shure's published 70-90 Hz recommendation for spoken word and is iZotope's own worked example value, and it still does the job the pre-gate high-pass actually exists for: keeping desk rumble, HVAC and plosive LF out of the expander and compressor detectors, and out of the limiter's headroom. 2nd order rather than 4th because the two filters sum to a 4th-order-equivalent rolloff downstream anyway, and because a steeper filter buys nothing on a call while costing more phase distortion near the fundamental. Proximity boom — the real Discord complaint, since most users are on a headset boom mic a few cm from the mouth — is handled precisely at 115.7 Hz in the EQ instead, per Shure's own hardware precedent (the SM7B bass-rolloff switch is a broad tilt, about -3 dB at 200 Hz, not a steeper cut).

EXPANDER: -45 dBFS, 2.0:1, attack 5 ms, hold 150 ms, release 200 ms. Ratio 2.0 is Rane Note 155's explicit figure for downward expansion used as noise reduction; it is an expander, not a gate, so a fricative sitting 10 dB under the threshold loses 10 dB rather than being muted. That lands the effective depth in the -12 to -24 dB region that LSP (-24 dB default) and Calf (-24.26 dB) independently converge on, and that Fedora Magazine recommends explicitly as partial attenuation (-12 or -18 dB, never a full mute). Attack 5 ms: every tuned preset in the survey uses 1-5 ms; EasyEffects' 20 ms default clips word onsets. Hold 150 ms sits between the dossier's 70-150 ms speech figure and OBS's 200 ms default and spans inter-word gaps, which is the direct cure for chattering; release 200 ms matches the tuned presets (180-250 ms) and fades under the tail of a word instead of chopping it. Threshold -45 dBFS is the weakest number in this preset and I will say so: warning 9 of the dossier is right that a fixed dB threshold is meaningless without gain staging, and the surveyed presets differ by 26 dB on this control for exactly that reason. -45 assumes a normally gain-staged mic whose speech peaks land around -12 to -6 dBFS; it is chosen at the gentler end of the tuned range (-48 to -55) so that it errs toward leaving room tone in rather than chewing quiet fricatives. It should be replaced by a measured noise-floor offset when the port can measure one. Note also that Krisp runs downstream with its own VAD: stacking two tight gates means a word start must survive both, which is why this expander is deliberately shallow-ratio and slow-releasing rather than "strongest of the six". For the same reason the optional RNNoise stage should ship OFF in this preset — two neural suppressors in series produce artefacts neither produces alone, and Krisp resamples to its model rate and back regardless.

EQ, ten gains on the fixed ladder (band Q is 1.5976, 0.889 octave, and effectively constant-Q at any preset-sized gain, so these overlap and sum: three adjacent bands at +3 dB give about +4.1 dB, not +9).
62.5 Hz = 0.0. The task's constraint and the dossier agree, and the vendor's own 13 shipped .fac presets are 0 dB here without exception. The 90 Hz high-pass already leaves roughly -7 dB at 62.5 Hz, so a cut here is close to a no-op for rumble while its 0.889-octave skirt would pull about -1.8 dB out of 80 Hz per -3 dB of slider — thinning the voice we just decided to keep. Doubling the high-pass's job is precisely the mistake the constraint warns about.
115.734 Hz = -2.0. This band (85-157 Hz) is untouched by the 90 Hz high-pass and owns the male fundamental and the chest/proximity boom. It is the honest place to handle a close boom mic. -2.0 rather than researcher 5's -3.0 because that -3 was paired with a 100 Hz high-pass and mine is at 90, and because band 2 is also down 1 dB and the bands sum.
214.311 Hz = -1.0. Shure's own proximity answer is about -3 dB at 200 Hz; here half of it is enough because band 1 is already down and the two overlap. This band also carries the female fundamental, so a deeper cut would be a gendered defect.
396.85 Hz = -2.0. The mud/box core (250-500 Hz). Both independent tuned open-source voice presets landed on exactly -2 dB here. Mud is also the first thing a low-bitrate codec smears, so removing it is worth more on a call than anywhere else.
734.867 Hz = -1.0. Boxy/papery. Small: with 396.85 at -2 the composite across 300-900 Hz is already about -2.4 dB, and the dossier warns that anything past about -5 dB in this region makes the voice telephone-thin.
1360.79 Hz = 0.0. Nasal/honk plus the start of real intelligibility, two-sided and touchy; nothing in the sources justifies a move, and band 6's skirt already lifts it about +0.35 dB.
2519.84 Hz = +2.0. The presence and intelligibility core (1852-3429 Hz), and the single highest-value band for speech over a codec — Opus at a poor-connection bitrate spends its bits where the energy is, and consonant identity lives here. iZotope's stated limit for this region is that 1-2 dB is the normal move; Shure's own presence switch is about +3 to +4 dB and that is a manufacturer ceiling, not a starting point. +2.0.
4666.12 Hz = 0.0. Deliberately not boosted. This is the most damaging boost available on this ladder: it adds sibilance, and because the EQ sits ahead of the de-esser and compressor it makes both over-trigger, so the de-esser dynamically cancels the static boost — which sounds worse than not making the move.
8640.48 Hz = 0.0 and 16000 Hz = 0.0. Three independent reasons, and the third is Discord-specific. (a) On a cheap USB condenser this region is mostly self-noise, and the makeup gain plus the client's AGC would amplify that hiss in every pause. (b) Krisp resamples to its model's operational rate (often 32 kHz) and back, so content up here is discarded downstream regardless — a 16 kHz move in a Discord preset is close to pointless. (c) The device class that actually dominates Discord use is the Bluetooth headset, where HFP/mSBC capture is 16 kHz (Nyquist 8 kHz) and CVSD is 8 kHz; both of these band centres are then at or above Nyquist, where a peaking biquad is undefined. At 0 dB gain the band is a unity no-op and therefore safe; any non-zero value makes this preset's behaviour device-dependent on exactly the hardware its users own. I chose safety over a -1 dB hiss trim.
Net: a small low-mid tilt plus one +2 dB presence move, everything inside ±2 dB. The vendor's own presets on this ladder almost all live inside ±3 dB, and the ±12 dB range is a limit, not a working range.

DE-ESSER: split 6000 Hz, -20 dBFS, 3:1, max 4 dB, attack 1 ms, release 60 ms, split-band. 6000 Hz is Calf's own split default and Fedora Magazine's "good place to start"; it straddles male sibilance (5-6 kHz) and female (7-8 kHz) without reaching down into the 2519 Hz intelligibility band. I explicitly reject the 3000-5000 Hz split used by the Fifine-branded community preset: RODE puts sibilance at 4-7 kHz and FabFilter at 8-10 kHz, and a detector centred at 3 kHz ducks the consonants that make speech legible and produces an audible lisp. Threshold -20 dB is the modal tuned value (the range across genuinely retuned presets is -18 to -26; -18/3:1/6000/4500/+12/Wide is EasyEffects' factory default and its frequency of occurrence in the corpus is not evidence of tuning). Ratio 3:1 is what both tuned presets use. Max reduction capped at 4 dB, inside the 2-4 dB that most voices need and well under the 6 dB cap that prevents an outlier syllable turning /s/ into /th/. Attack 1 ms catches the sibilant onset; release 60 ms recovers before the following vowel (the 40-150 ms window). Split-band, not wide: Calf's own docs recommend Wide for a single voice, but Wide ducks the whole signal on every "s", and with a compressor immediately after it in this fixed order that reads as full-band pumping. I am picking against Calf's recommendation here and for the dossier's majority engineering view. On the fixed order EQ -> de-esser -> compressor, which inverts the community's 7-of-8 preference: the dossier says that if the order must stay, de-ess harder. I did not, and the reason is that the advice assumes a fast, heavy compressor that re-amplifies quiet passages including their sibilance. This compressor is 3:1 with a 20 ms attack, which barely engages on a sibilant burst; what follows the de-esser is mostly a static +4 dB of makeup, and static gain does not change the ess-to-vowel balance. Also, this preset adds no HF lift, so per the interaction rule the de-esser needs no compensating extra sensitivity.

COMPRESSOR: -18 dBFS, 3:1, 6 dB soft knee, attack 20 ms, release 150 ms. Threshold -18 is where OBS (-18.0) and Calf (0.125 = -18.06 dB) independently land. Ratio 3:1 is Rane's and RODE's stated spoken-voice figure and the modal value of the tuned presets; the real target, per Rane, is 3-6 dB of gain reduction on normal speech and about 0 on quiet passages, and threshold/ratio should be re-solved from that if the port ever measures input level. I did not take OBS's 10:1 default — at -18 dB that is a limiter wearing a compressor's name, defensible only for a Streaming preset. Knee 6 dB soft is unanimous (LSP -6 dB in compressor, expander and de-esser; Calf 9 dB); the sign convention here is positive-width, LSP's is negative, and the port must not map that naively. Attack 20 ms is the deliberate one: a stop-consonant burst is a transient of a few ms up to ~35 ms, so the 1-5 ms attack that consumer guides repeat lands the gain reduction on the burst itself and dulls exactly the 2-8 kHz energy that carries consonant identity. Rane's vocal figure is 25-100 ms, the tuned presets use 15-20 ms; 20 ms is the honest middle and matters more on a call than anywhere else, because a low-bitrate codec has already made consonants fragile. Release 150 ms is tied to syllable rate, not picked freely: the speech envelope's modulation spectrum peaks at 4-8 Hz with a dominant rate near 4.5-5 Hz, i.e. one syllable every 125-250 ms, so a shorter release recovers inside a syllable and audibly breathes on the noise floor, and a much longer one rides down a whole sentence. Note Rane's caveat that a release constant specified in dB/s is not wall-clock recovery time.

MAKEUP +4.0 dB. The TASCAM/Waves auto-makeup rule, 0.5 x |threshold| x (1 - 1/ratio), gives +6.0 dB for -18/3:1, which is the compensation for a 0 dBFS input. Real speech sees 3-6 dB of gain reduction, so half-compensation is nearer +3; the EQ is net slightly negative (four cuts totalling about -1 dB of broadband level against one +2 dB presence band), which adds roughly +1 back. That is +4.0, and it is computed net of the EQ contribution rather than hand-picked, which is what keeps the six factory presets loudness-comparable. I kept it at the low end of the dossier's +3 to +6 budget on purpose: Discord's AGC will renormalise the level anyway (so most of the makeup is wasted), while the noise floor it raises is not renormalised away but amplified during pauses. Against a -3 dBFS ceiling this should land short-term loudness near AES TD1008's -18 LUFS speech figure with about 15 dB of peak-to-loudness ratio, and comfortably above TD1008's -20 LUFS floor. That is a prediction, not a measurement: the dossier is explicit that per-preset makeup must be trimmed against a measured speech reference rather than derived on paper, and this number should be verified and adjusted on the real chain. Do not servo it from an integrated loudness measurement in real time — integrated loudness is defined over a programme and is not a control signal.

LIMITER CEILING -3.0 dBFS. Not -1.0, and this is a considered departure from the number everyone quotes. -1 dBTP is EBU R128's and AES TD1008's requirement for the last stage before one known encoder, and we are neither the last stage nor facing a known bitrate. Four documented reasons to sit lower: TD1008 says explicitly that the limiting threshold must go below -1.0 dBTP as bitrate falls, and Discord's Opus negotiates down to tens of kbps on a poor connection; TD1008 also documents up to 3 dB of gain reduction in a decode-side OS limiter when the encode side left insufficient headroom; libopus concedes the reconstruction problem structurally by shipping opus_pcm_soft_clip() to pull a decoded float signal back inside [-1,1]; and a cheap real-time brick wall without oversampling is measuring sample peak, not true peak, so the control should be labelled dBFS and given about 1 dB of extra margin rather than called "-1 dBTP compliant". The fifth reason is the Discord-specific one and the tidiest: the client's AGC targets a peak 3 dB below full scale. Handing it material that already peaks at -3 dBFS means its AGC has the least work to do in either direction and its own limiter never engages. -3 dBFS costs nothing perceptually because the far end normalises anyway. The limiter must remain the last gain-affecting stage — no makeup or output trim after it, which is the broken gain staging that spoiled two of the surveyed community presets. Target about 1 dB of gain reduction on normal speech; if this preset habitually drives the limiter harder than that, the makeup gain above it is wrong. Suggested lookahead 2 ms, which is enough for a plosive given the 90 Hz high-pass in front, and it is the only latency this preset adds: HPF, expander, EQ, de-esser and compressor all run with zero lookahead, so the chain costs about 2 ms. That matters because Krisp already costs roughly 10-25 ms downstream and self-monitoring degrades past about 15-20 ms.

WHAT THE DOSSIER DOES NOT COVER, STATED HONESTLY. (1) The three threshold values (-45, -20, -18 dBFS) are only meaningful relative to the user's capture gain; nothing in this chain normalises input, and the surveyed presets disagree by up to 26 dB on the gate threshold for exactly that reason. These are defaults for a normally gain-staged mic, not constants. (2) The predicted -18 LUFS landing point is arithmetic, not a measurement on this chain. (3) The claim that Discord enables Krisp, AEC and AGC by default is second-hand — the researcher could not retrieve Discord's own support article (Cloudflare bot-check). The structural claim that a WebRTC-class client applies AEC + NS + AGC with a limiter, and the specific numbers -3 dBFS target / 9 dB compression gain / 3 dB per second, are read directly from the WebRTC APM source and are solid; the Discord UI wording is not, and should not be repeated in user-facing copy without checking. (4) No independent measured frequency response exists for the Fifine-class mic on the test machine, so none of these EQ values are mic-compensation; they are voice-shaping moves that should survive any reasonable mic. (5) The dossier notes the ladder centres are per-preset in the .fac format rather than a hard constraint, so a mic preset could legally move band 8 to 6.3 kHz to cover the sibilance gap; I did not, because the derived Q comes from band count and min/max rather than from the actual centres, so the band would still be 0.889 octave wide and would still take presence or air with it, and because the slider labels should match between the music and microphone chains.
