critiques.overall:
TONE VERDICT: the shape is right, the low-end emphasis is in the wrong band.

I rebuilt the actual composite from the port's own filter design (crates/fxsound-dsp/src/biquad.rs `calc_parametric` + eq.rs Q = 1.5976 at 48 kHz) rather than trusting the arithmetic in the rationale. Three of its numeric claims check out: three adjacent +3 dB bands sum to +4.13 dB (it said ~4.1); the 90 Hz 2nd-order Butterworth is -7.24 dB at 62.5 Hz (it said ~-7); the 2519.84 band's skirt lifts 1360.79 by +0.38 dB (it said ~+0.35). One claim I want to flag as lucky rather than argued: the Q-warp in `calc_parametric` (Rule B, max_q = |boost|*3.3 + 0.2) only bites below |0.42| dB, so "effectively constant-Q at any preset-sized gain" is true here — but it stops being true if anyone later authors a 0.3 dB trim, which would silently widen to Q = 1.19.

Composite of the delivered ten bands (EQ only, dB): 62.5 -0.43, 115.7 -2.27, 214.3 -1.78, 396.9 -2.43, 734.9 -1.35, 1100 -0.30, 1360.8 +0.10, 1800 +0.78, 2519.8 +1.94, 3150 +1.28, 4000 +0.57, 4666.1 +0.35, 6300 +0.14, 8640 +0.06.

What is right, and I will not manufacture an objection about it:
- Not honky. The 1360.79 band is zero and the composite trough sits at 735-1100 Hz, so the nasal/honk region is the low point of the curve, not a bump. Megaphone tone needs a bandpass peak around 1-1.5 kHz; this is the opposite.
- Not harsh and not lispy. 4666.12 = 0 means the composite only reaches +0.57 dB at 4 kHz and +0.14 dB at 6.3 kHz, so the EQ hands the de-esser (split 6000) nothing it did not already have. The de-esser will not be chasing a boost the EQ made. This is the single best decision in the curve.
- The presence move is correctly sized. +2.0 at 2519.84 reads as +3.29 dB relative to the 734.867 Hz body, which is right at the Shure SM7B presence-switch precedent the rationale cites. Do not raise it: +3.0 makes the tilt 4.28 dB and puts +1.93 dB at 3150 Hz, which is hardness the 6 kHz de-esser cannot touch.
- The three zeros at 4666/8640/16000 are genuinely safe in this implementation, not just prudent: `calc_parametric` returns `BiquadCoeffs::UNITY` with `on: false` on an exact 0.0, so the Bluetooth/Nyquist argument holds literally — the section is bypassed, not designed.

What is wrong is the placement of the low cut, not its depth. The 115.734 Hz band is doing the job the high-pass already did, and the 214.311 Hz band is doing the job the 115.734 band should have. See the two corrections. With them applied the chain removes the same total boom energy but takes it from 200-250 Hz, where a boom mic's residual chest resonance actually lives after two cascaded 2nd-order high-passes, and returns 0.8 dB of male fundamental. The third correction is smaller and I would not block on it.

Does it fight the high-pass? Yes, at exactly one point, and by the preset's own standard. Everywhere else the two are well separated: at 214 Hz and above the 90 Hz HPF contributes under -0.2 dB, so bands 2-4 are working on clean air.

problems.problem: The rationale justifies HPF 90 instead of 100 Hz by refusing to stack filters at the fundamental — "roughly -7 dB at 100 Hz ... thins exactly the voices it is meant to help" — and then re-creates that stack with this band. It also asserts "this band (85-157 Hz) is untouched by the 90 Hz high-pass", which is false: the 90 Hz 2nd-order Butterworth is -1.35 dB at 115.7 Hz. Measured composite through our own chain: -3.62 dB at 115.7 Hz, -4.01 dB at 100 Hz. Add Discord's APM high-pass and the signal Discord's encoder sees is -5.55 dB at 115.7 Hz and -7.02 dB at 100 Hz — the exact number the preset rejected a 100 Hz corner to avoid.
problems.why: A male fundamental at 100-120 Hz loses 4 dB inside our own plugin before Discord touches it, and 7 dB by the time it is encoded. That is not proximity control, that is a thin voice, and it lands hardest on the low-pitched male speakers the preset claims to protect. Paired with the 214.311 correction the total boom reduction is preserved (composite avg 150-900 Hz goes -1.65 -> -1.94 dB, i.e. slightly more boom removed, not less) while 115.7 Hz recovers to -2.81 dB in our chain and -4.74 dB through Discord, and 100 Hz recovers to -3.32 / -6.33 dB. The shape also becomes monotone-corrective instead of a dip-bump-dip: the current curve dips to -2.27 at 115.7, recovers to -1.64 at 175, and dips again to -2.43 at 396.9, which is a wobble no engineer would draw by hand.

problems.problem: At -1.0 this band is the shallowest cut in a run of three, and it is sitting on the frequency where the residual boom actually survives. Between 175 and 300 Hz the current composite is flat at -1.64 to -1.78 dB — the band contributes shape worth only about 0.15 dB over its neighbours' skirts, so it functions as a pad, not a correction. Meanwhile the octave 130-250 Hz, which is what is left of proximity boom after our 90 Hz HPF and Discord's 100 Hz HPF have both run, is the least attenuated part of the low end.
problems.why: Proximity boom on a headset boom mic at 2-5 cm is a broad lift that the cited Shure precedent places at about -3 dB at 200 Hz, and the preset's own text quotes that figure — then applies half of it 90 Hz lower than Shure does. Swapping the emphasis (115.734 -> -1.0, 214.311 -> -2.0) puts the deepest cut at 214.3 Hz (-2.72 dB in our chain, -2.93 dB through Discord) where the boom is and where neither high-pass reaches, and it costs nothing in the female fundamental range the rationale worries about: 250 Hz moves from -1.69 to -2.37 dB, under a dB, and a female f0 at 200-255 Hz is the same missing-fundamental case that a call reconstructs perceptually. This is a lateral move in total energy, not a deeper cut.

problems.problem: Redundant. With 396.85 at -2.0 its skirt already puts 734.867 Hz at about -0.37 dB, and this band's own -1.0 takes the composite to -1.35 dB at 735 Hz, -1.43 at 630 and -1.78 at 500. The result is that the entire range 150-900 Hz sits inside a 1.6 dB window: the curve stops being tone shaping and becomes a broadband pad that makeup gain then adds straight back, which is why makeup had to be computed "net of the EQ contribution".
problems.why: This is the body of the voice, 500-800 Hz, and it is the region a small USB condenser is already weakest in. Zeroing it lifts 630 Hz by +0.76 dB, 735 Hz by +0.97 and 900 Hz by +0.68, and drops the 735->2520 Hz tilt from 3.29 dB to 2.35 dB, which is a safer place to be given that everything downstream (compressor makeup, then Discord's AGC with up to 9 dB of compression gain) re-amplifies whatever tilt we hand it. It also keeps the preset honest about its own stated principle of processing less: the 396.85 Hz cut is the mud fix and it survives untouched at -2.39 dB composite, while the boxiness argument for this band rests on a -0.5 to -1 dB difference that will not be audible on a 24-64 kbps Opus stream. I would not block the preset on this one; it is the difference between a good curve and a tighter one.

critiques.overall:
The topology reasoning is good and several choices are better-argued than the sources they come from: 2:1 downward expansion instead of a gate, the 20 ms compressor attack defended from plosive burst length rather than from consumer guides, release 150 ms tied to the 4-8 Hz syllable envelope, split-band de-essing at 6 kHz instead of the community's 3-5 kHz, the 4 dB reduction cap, and the refusal to boost 4666 Hz ahead of a de-esser. Those are all sound and I am not asking for changes to them.

The defects are not in the shapes, they are in the scales. Three of the four thresholds are absolute dBFS numbers borrowed from plugins whose detectors are not the same quantity, and the spec never says which quantity this chain uses. Concretely: (a) the compressor detector is unspecified, and peak-vs-RMS swings gain reduction on the same speech from ~0 dB to ~7.5 dB, so nothing downstream of it — makeup, limiter GR, the loudness prediction — is determined; (b) the de-esser threshold of -20 dBFS is a broadband-scale number applied to a >6 kHz split band that peaks 12-18 dB lower, so as written the de-esser almost never opens; (c) the +4 dB makeup lands the chain at roughly -22 LUFS short-term, below AES TD1008's -20 LUFS floor, not "comfortably above" it and not the -18 LUFS the rationale predicts.

Two real dynamic-interaction bugs, neither of which the rationale sees. The 150 ms gate hold and the 150 ms compressor release put a noise swell exactly in the phrase gap: speech stops, the compressor gives back its 4-5 dB of gain within 150 ms, and the expander has not begun closing yet (hold 150 + release 200 = 350 ms to full depth). That is the "breathing" the preset was designed to avoid, manufactured by its own two time constants. And because the 20 ms compressor attack deliberately does not catch plosives, the limiter is the only transient control in the chain, yet its release and lookahead exist only in prose, not as fields.

One rationale argument is mechanically wrong and should not survive into user-facing copy: "every dB of makeup we add is a dB of noise floor the client's AGC then amplifies" is false for a digital AGC, which is a servo — it subtracts whatever we add, leaving SNR unchanged. The low makeup value needs a different (and available) justification.

No lisp risk: split-band at 6000 Hz with a hard 4 dB cap cannot reach the 2519 Hz intelligibility band. The problem is the opposite — the de-esser is inert as specified. No gate chatter in the steady state either, provided the implementation really is a continuous expander; if it is a binary gate the single threshold will cycle.

Verdict NEEDS_CHANGES. Fix the detector specification first — findings 3, 4 and 7 are all downstream of it and should be re-derived, not applied blind, once the detector is pinned.

problems.problem: The spec gives threshold_db -18 with no statement of what the detector measures. The two cited corroborating sources are not measuring the same thing: OBS's -18 (compressor-filter.c) is a fast near-instantaneous/peak detector, while Calf's 0.125 and LSP's defaults are RMS sidechains. For speech with a 12-15 dB crest factor these differ by more than 10 dB at the same nominal threshold.
problems.corrected_value: Add "detector": "peak", "detector_ms": 2 to the compressor block (and the same field to gate and deesser).
problems.why: With a peak detector and vowel peaks arriving at -7 dBFS, GR = (1-1/3)x(-7+18) = 7.3 dB. With a 10 ms RMS detector the same vowel presents ~-19 dBFS, which is inside the 6 dB soft knee, giving roughly 0-1 dB GR. The rationale's own stated target is 3-6 dB. So the identical JSON produces either over-compression or no compression depending on an unwritten implementation choice, and makeup_db, limiter GR and the LUFS prediction are all undetermined until it is written down.

problems.problem: -20 dBFS is a broadband-scale threshold applied to a 6 kHz-and-up split band. That band's short-term level during a hot /s/ typically sits 12-18 dB below the broadband vowel peak, so with correctly gain-staged input (vowel peaks -6 to -8 dBFS) sibilant band level is about -20 to -26 dBFS. The detector rarely crosses -20 at all, and when it does it is 0-2 dB over.
problems.corrected_value: deesser.threshold_db: -30
problems.why: At 3:1, 2 dB over threshold yields 0.7 dB of reduction, so the preset ships a de-esser that does essentially nothing while the rationale claims the 2-4 dB most voices need. At -30: an average /s/ at -26 dBFS is 4 dB over, giving 2.7 dB reduction; a hot /s/ at -22 dBFS is 8 dB over and hits the 4 dB cap. That is exactly the stated 2-4 dB window. The cited -18 to -26 range from EasyEffects presets is not transferable, because those de-essers apply a sidechain bell boost (Calf's f2) ahead of the detector that this schema has no field for. If a sidechain gain field is added instead, keep -20 and set sidechain_gain_db to +10.

problems.problem: The predicted landing point of "-18 LUFS with about 15 dB PLR, comfortably above TD1008's -20 LUFS floor" does not follow from the chain. That arithmetic assumes output peaks sit at the -3 dBFS ceiling, which contradicts the preset's own instruction to target only ~1 dB of limiter GR.
problems.corrected_value: makeup_db: 6 (if compressor.threshold_db stays -18); keep 4 only if the threshold moves to -14 per the next finding. Either way restate the prediction as approximately -20 LUFS short-term, not -18.
problems.why: Trace it: input vowel peak -6 dBFS, EQ net about -1 on the vowel body, compressor (peak detector) -7 -> -14.3 dBFS, makeup +4 -> -10.3 dBFS. Vowel short-term RMS is roughly 12 dB under that, about -22 dBFS, so short-term loudness is about -22 LUFS. That is quieter than the -20 LUFS floor the rationale claims to clear, and at the quiet end of the preset's own stated gain-staging range (input peaks -12 dBFS) it lands near -25 LUFS. Every number in that sentence is off by 4-7 dB in the same direction.

problems.problem: -18 dBFS with a peak detector delivers 7-8 dB of gain reduction on normal vowel peaks, not the 3-6 dB the rationale sets as the target and attributes to Rane Note 155.
problems.corrected_value: compressor.threshold_db: -14 (peak detector). If the detector is RMS instead, -26.
problems.why: Solving the stated target backwards: for 4.5 dB GR at 3:1 on a vowel peak of -7 dBFS, threshold = -7 - 4.5/(1-1/3) = -13.75 dBFS. At -14 the vowel peak exits at -11.7 dBFS, and with the existing +4 makeup that is -7.7 dBFS, about -20 LUFS short-term — which simultaneously repairs the loudness deficit above without touching makeup_db. It also does what Rane actually asks for, roughly 0 dB GR on quiet passages: at the quiet end of the gain-staging range (peak -13) the compressor engages only 1 dB over threshold instead of 5.

problems.problem: Gate hold 150 ms and compressor release 150 ms are the same length, so at every phrase end the compressor's 4-5 dB of gain recovery happens entirely inside the window where the expander is still held open. Room tone is amplified by the recovered gain plus makeup for 150 ms before any attenuation begins, and the expander then needs another 200 ms to reach depth.
problems.corrected_value: gate.hold_ms: 100 (paired with the hysteresis field in the next finding)
problems.why: This is the pumping/breathing artefact the preset explicitly sets out to avoid, produced by its own two time constants rather than by Discord. With hold 100 ms the expander starts closing while the compressor is only about two thirds recovered, so the noise swell never reaches full amplitude. 100 ms still spans stop closures (50-100 ms) and the majority of inter-word gaps, and the chatter margin that the 150 ms figure was buying is better bought with hysteresis, which costs no speech. The alternative fix, compressor.release_ms 250, is worse: it breaks the syllable-rate derivation (200-220 ms period at 4.5-5 Hz) that the release value was correctly built on.

problems.problem: A single threshold with no close/reopen offset. The rationale argues this is an expander rather than a gate so it cannot chatter, but nothing in the JSON says the implementation must be a continuous-gain expander, and the field is literally named "gate".
problems.corrected_value: Add "hysteresis_db": 6 (open -45, close -51)
problems.why: Every gate the preset cites ships hysteresis precisely because a single threshold cycles: OBS uses open -26 / close -32 (noise-gate-filter.c), and the jtrv preset uses -3 dB. Sustained breath or fan noise sitting within a dB of -45 will cycle the stage on a 250-350 ms period (hold plus release), which is slow, in-band modulation of the noise floor and audibly worse than leaving the room tone up. 6 dB also makes the shortened hold above safe.

problems.problem: The rationale cites LSP's -24 dB and Calf's -24.26 dB as evidence that the effective depth lands in the -12 to -24 dB region, but those are range caps (a floor on total attenuation), not outcomes of a ratio. With ratio 2:1 and no cap, depth is unbounded: it equals whatever the threshold-to-noise-floor gap happens to be.
problems.corrected_value: Add "range_db": -20
problems.why: Depth = (ratio-1) x (threshold - noise floor). A quiet room at -70 dBFS gives 25 dB of attenuation, which is a dead, vacuum-like pause that Krisp's VAD then has to decide about, and is the full-mute behaviour Fedora Magazine warns against. A noisy room at -50 dBFS gives 5 dB, well under the claimed -12 minimum. A -20 dB cap makes the upper bound a property of the preset instead of a property of the user's room, which is what the cited defaults actually do.

problems.field: limiter (release and lookahead are prose-only, not fields)
problems.problem: Lookahead 2 ms appears only as a "suggested" value in the rationale and release is never given at all, yet because compressor.attack_ms is deliberately 20 ms, the limiter is the sole transient control in the chain and handles every plosive burst.
problems.corrected_value: Add "lookahead_ms": 2 and "release_ms": 50 to the limiter block.
problems.why: A plosive burst at input peak -6 dBFS escapes the 20 ms compressor attack entirely, picks up about +1 dB from the 2519 Hz EQ band and +4 dB of makeup, and arrives at the limiter around -1 dBFS — 2 dB over the -3 ceiling, rising to 3-4 dB if makeup goes to 6. If the limiter inherits a compressor-class release near 150 ms it ducks the vowel following every plosive by that amount, which is a per-syllable audible click-down and exactly the consonant damage the 20 ms attack was chosen to prevent. 50 ms recovers inside the burst-to-vowel gap; the 90 Hz high-pass means a release this fast cannot cause the LF distortion that normally argues against it.

problems.problem: 5 ms of attack with no lookahead means a word-initial stop consonant, arriving while the expander is at full depth after a pause, has its onset attenuated on a ramp.
problems.corrected_value: gate.attack_ms: 2
problems.why: A /t/ or /k/ burst is roughly 5-15 ms long, so a 5 ms ramp from about 20 dB down to unity attenuates the first third to half of the burst by an average of ~8-10 dB — softened word onsets, which is the specific failure the preset names and then does not avoid. 2 ms is inside the 1-5 ms range the rationale already endorses from the surveyed tuned presets and keeps the ramp well under the burst length. Adding lookahead would fix it too but costs latency the preset is right to guard, given Krisp's 10-25 ms downstream.

problems.problem: "Every dB of makeup gain we add is a dB of noise floor the client's AGC then amplifies in the pauses" is not true of a digital AGC. An AGC is a level servo: if we add 4 dB it applies 4 dB less, and the SNR at its output is identical either way. The argument as stated cannot justify the choice of +4.
problems.corrected_value: Replace the justification with: keep makeup low because the compressor's 20 ms attack leaves 12-15 dB of uncontrolled transient crest above the vowels, so added makeup is spent on limiter gain reduction of plosives rather than on loudness; and because a client-side analog/capture-gain AGC, if present, will turn hardware gain down in response to a hotter signal, which does cost real SNR.
problems.why: The stated mechanism is the load-bearing reason the preset is quieter than the sources it surveys, and it is wrong, so a later maintainer reading it will either propagate the error into user-facing copy (item 3 of the honesty section already flags Discord's own documentation as unverified) or correctly discard it and then raise makeup with no remaining constraint. The replacement reasoning supports the same conservative value and is checkable against the chain rather than against an unretrieved support article.

critiques.overall:
Character is right, staging is wrong. The judgement calls in this preset are mostly better than the sources it is arguing with: 2:1 expansion instead of a gate, 20 ms compressor attack instead of the 1-5 ms consumer figure, 0 dB at 4666 Hz, 0 dB at 62.5 Hz, a single +2 dB presence move, 6 kHz de-esser split rather than the 3-5 kHz community value, and a -3 dBFS ceiling aligned to AGC1's target_level_dbfs=3 — I tried to break the -3 and could not; it is the correct number for this destination. Two verified facts from the tree: derive_q(62.5, 16000, 10, 1.0) really is 1.59764 (0.8889 octave), and set_band_boost already bypasses any band with 2*f0 >= fs (crates/fxsound-dsp/src/eq.rs:276, test at :490), so rationale point (c) — "a peaking biquad is undefined above Nyquist, therefore 0 dB" — is factually void: on a 16 kHz HFP capture the 8640 and 16000 bands are bypassed whatever gain you write. The conclusion (0.0) still stands on reasons (a) and (b), so no value changes, but do not repeat the undefined-biquad claim.

What fails is level, not taste. The preset's own gain-staging assumption (speech peaks -12..-6 dBFS) run through its own compressor gives delivered peaks of -12..-10 dBFS, i.e. 7-9 dB below the AGC target the rationale spent a paragraph deriving. The AGC then supplies that gain at <=3 dB/s, which is exactly the swell-after-every-pause the preset was written to avoid, and its own claim of "about 1 dB of limiter gain reduction on normal speech" is unreachable by 7 dB. The same under-staging makes the de-esser inert: a -20 dBFS threshold on a >6 kHz band that peaks near -23 dBFS pre-makeup will never engage, so all the reasoning about split vs Wide and about de-essing before the compressor is currently moot. Fix makeup (+8) and the de-esser threshold (-28) and the chain does what the prose says it does.

The third real problem is that the rationale's most considered decisions are not in the JSON: filter order, de-esser mode, limiter lookahead, RNNoise off, and any bound on expander depth. The JSON is what ships; prose is not a parameter. Note also the AEC interaction the dossier misses entirely — this chain runs upstream of Discord's echo canceller, so every dB of time-varying gain we apply (expander, compressor) makes the echo path non-linear and slows AEC convergence for speaker users. That is an additional argument for bounding the expander and for keeping the compressor at 3:1 with a slow release, both of which this preset already does. With the eight corrections below I would ship it.

problems.problem: Under-delivers by 7-9 dB against the AGC target the rationale itself derives, and makes its own limiter-GR target unreachable. Work the preset's own numbers: input peak -12 dBFS -> compressor (-18, 3:1) gives 4 dB GR -> -16 -> +4 makeup = -12 dBFS delivered. Input peak -6 -> 8 dB GR -> -14 -> +4 = -10 dBFS. So delivered peaks are -12..-10 dBFS against an AGC whose target is -3 dBFS and a limiter ceiling at -3 that therefore never engages (the text claims 'target about 1 dB of gain reduction on normal speech'). The EQ contribution is also mis-estimated: the four cuts sit at 115-735 Hz where the long-term speech spectrum has its energy peak, so they remove nearer -1.5..-2 dB of broadband RMS, not -1.
problems.why: The argument that 'every dB of makeup we add is a dB of noise floor the AGC amplifies' is wrong in this direction, because gain is gain: whether we apply the missing 8 dB statically or AGC1 applies it with its digital compression gain, the far-end SNR is identical. The difference is that ours is constant and theirs moves at <=3 dB/s and re-adapts after every pause — which is the pumping the preset set out to prevent. Deliver at the target and the AGC has nothing to do. +8 is safe across the whole assumed staging range because the 3:1 compressor collapses a 9 dB input spread (-12..-3 dBFS peaks) into 3 dB of output spread: delivered peaks become -8..-5 dBFS, still under the -3 ceiling. Also correct the accompanying claim — with +8 the limiter should show 0 dB GR on normal speech and 2-4 dB on laughs and plosives; it is a safety catch, not a loudness stage. Predicted landing point moves from about -22..-25 LUFS (below AES TD1008's -20 LUFS floor, i.e. the preset currently misses its own stated target) to about -18..-20 LUFS.

problems.problem: Inert as staged. The de-esser sits pre-compressor and pre-makeup (fixed order EQ -> de-esser -> compressor, makeup after), so it sees raw capture level, while the -18..-26 dBFS values quoted from the EasyEffects corpus come from chains where the de-esser follows the compressor and its makeup. With the preset's own assumed staging (full-band speech peaks -12..-6 dBFS) the >6 kHz split band during an /s/ lands about 10-18 dB below the adjacent vowel peak, i.e. roughly -27..-19 dBFS with a median near -23. A -20 dBFS threshold is at or above the loudest sibilant on a normally gain-staged mic, so the stage does nothing except on unusually hot input.
problems.why: Threshold should sit near the median sibilant band level so the stage acts proportionally rather than all-or-nothing. At -28: a soft /s/ at -30 gets nothing, a median /s/ at -23 is 5 dB over and gets 3.3 dB GR at 3:1, a loud /s/ at -20 is 8 dB over and asks for 5.3 dB which the 4 dB cap trims — exactly the 2-4 dB most voices need. Anything below about -28 puts every sibilant against the cap, which degenerates into a static -4 dB HF shelf on consonants and costs intelligibility over a low-bitrate Opus stream. Keep max_reduction_db at 4. This assumes the port's detector is band-referenced (Calf convention, sidechain-filtered level compared against the threshold); if the port instead compares full-band level against the threshold, the number goes back to -20 and the field needs a documented convention in the schema.

problems.problem: Triple-stacked cut at the male fundamental. The rationale refuses to set the HPF to 100 Hz precisely to avoid stacking two 2nd-order filters at the male fundamental, then stacks an EQ cut into the same region and counts only its own HPF. Measured sum at 115.7 Hz: our 90 Hz 2nd-order Butterworth is -1.35 dB there, Discord's own 100 Hz Butterworth is about -2.4 dB (log-interpolated between the cited -3.54 dB @100 Hz and -1.01 dB @150 Hz), and the band adds -2.0 -> about -5.8 dB. At 100 Hz, which is the modal F0 for a lot of adult male speakers, the sum is -2.19 -1.7 (band skirt, 0.21 octave off centre at Q 1.5976) -3.54 = about -7.4 dB. That is deeper than the -7 dB at 100 Hz the text rejects as 'thinning exactly the voices it is meant to help'.
problems.why: -1.0 keeps the proximity-boom tilt (a boom mic a few cm from the mouth adds +6..+10 dB here, so a light cut plus two high-passes is still net corrective for the headset user the preset is aimed at) while limiting the worst case to about -4.8 dB at 115 Hz and -6 dB at 100 Hz for the desk-mic user who has no proximity lift to give away. It is also the robust choice under the rationale's own admitted uncertainty (item 3): the Discord-applies-its-own-HPF claim is second-hand, so the EQ cut should be sized to be tolerable both with and without that -2.4 dB. Shure's -3 dB at 200 Hz precedent is preserved by band 2, which stays at -1.0 and whose skirt reaches 200 Hz.

problems.problem: The expander is unbounded. The rationale claims the 2:1 ratio 'lands the effective depth in the -12 to -24 dB region that LSP (-24 dB default) and Calf (-24.26 dB) independently converge on', but those are hard floors on a range control, not the by-product of a ratio. With ratio 2 and no bound, a signal 30 dB under the -45 threshold is pushed 30 dB further down, so the residual room tone does not sit at a fixed attenuated level — it slides continuously with the input, which is precisely the noise-floor modulation that a downstream neural suppressor and AGC react badly to.
problems.why: A bounded floor makes the residual a steady, quiet room tone instead of a breathing one, which is what Krisp's VAD and AGC1's level estimator are built to sit on top of. 12 rather than the LSP/Calf 18-24 for a Discord-specific reason the dossier misses: this chain runs upstream of Discord's AEC, so every dB of time-varying gain we apply makes the echo path non-linear and slows the canceller's convergence for anyone on speakers rather than a headset. 12 dB of bounded depth plus Krisp downstream is ample; the deep expansion belongs in a Streaming or Recording preset where no AEC follows.

problems.problem: The rationale specifies 2 ms lookahead, calls it the only latency the chain adds and budgets the whole ~2 ms figure against Krisp's 10-25 ms, but there is no such field in the JSON. The port will use whatever its limiter defaults to. With zero lookahead a brick wall at -3 dBFS either clips the plosive it was put there to catch or needs a release short enough to intermodulate with low-frequency content.
problems.corrected_value: limiter_lookahead_ms: 2
problems.why: 2 ms is enough to catch a plosive given the 90 Hz high-pass ahead of it, and it is the number the rationale's own latency budget assumes. Latency on a live voice path has to be a declared parameter, not an aspiration in prose: self-monitoring degrades past about 15-20 ms and Krisp already spends most of that budget, so the port must not be free to pick 5 ms because that is its default.

problems.problem: Three load-bearing decisions exist only in the rationale. (a) 2nd-order Butterworth, argued explicitly against 4th order — the JSON carries only hpf_hz, so the port picks the order, and a 4th-order filter at 90 Hz would put about -2.8 dB at 115 Hz instead of -1.35 and blow the LF budget above. (b) Split-band de-essing, chosen against Calf's own Wide recommendation with a paragraph of reasoning about full-band pumping into the compressor — no mode field exists, so the port will take its default, which for a Calf-derived implementation is Wide, i.e. the exact behaviour the rationale argues against. (c) 'The optional RNNoise stage should ship OFF in this preset' — nothing in the JSON turns it off, and if it defaults on, two neural suppressors run in series.
problems.corrected_value: hpf_slope_db_oct: 12, deesser.mode: "split", rnnoise_enabled: false
problems.why: The emitted preset is the contract; prose does not survive into the runtime. Each of these three has a different default in the plausible implementations and each default is the opposite of what was argued for. Add the fields to the schema for all six presets, not just this one, so a preset is fully specified by its JSON.

problems.problem: The Nyquist safety argument was applied to the EQ and not to the de-esser. The preset reasons carefully that its users are on Bluetooth headsets where HFP capture is 16 kHz (mSBC) or 8 kHz (CVSD) — and on CVSD, Nyquist is 4 kHz, so a 6000 Hz crossover is undefined. Unlike the EQ, which already self-protects (crates/fxsound-dsp/src/eq.rs:276 bypasses any band with 2*f0 >= fs), nothing in the de-esser or in this JSON guards the split. On 16 kHz mSBC 6000 Hz is legal (Nyquist 8 kHz) and should stay.
problems.corrected_value: keep split_hz: 6000, and add the runtime rule: bypass the de-esser when split_hz > 0.45 * sample_rate (so it is active on 48 kHz and on 16 kHz mSBC, and bypassed on 8 kHz CVSD)
problems.why: Same class of bug the EQ already avoids, on the same device class the rationale identifies as dominant for Discord. A de-esser is pointless on an 8 kHz capture anyway, since the entire sibilance region is gone before the chain sees it; bypassing is both correct and free. Clamping the split downward instead would be wrong — at 8 kHz there is no legal split that does anything useful.

problems.problem: Single-threshold expander. The rationale says hold 150 ms is 'the direct cure for chattering', but hold only covers gaps shorter than 150 ms; a speaker whose level hovers near -45 dBFS at the end of a sentence crosses the threshold repeatedly at a rate hold cannot mask. Both tuned references cited do carry hysteresis (OBS -26/-32 open/close, jtrv -3 dB) and the preset drops it without argument.
problems.corrected_value: hysteresis_db: 3 (close threshold -48, open -45)
problems.why: 3 dB of hysteresis is the jtrv value and costs nothing: it does not change where speech opens the expander, only where it closes, so quiet word tails stay open instead of flickering. It matters more here than in the sources because the threshold is admitted to be the weakest number in the preset — hysteresis is what makes a mis-set threshold degrade gracefully rather than chatter, which is the right property while the port has no way to measure a noise floor.

preset.intent: For someone on a thin, bright USB condenser or a small dynamic worked at arm's length: adds chest and body below ~250 Hz, tilts the harsh 3-6 kHz presence peak down about 2 dB, and levels gently at 2.5:1 so the voice sounds fuller and rounder without sounding muddy, dull or obviously processed.
preset.name: Warm Voice
preset.rationale:
GENERAL POSTURE. The brief is "thin or harsh microphones": add body, tame a presence peak, do not create mud. That is a tone preset, not a dynamics preset, so every dynamics stage here sits at or below the gentle end of what the dossier's sources recommend, and all EQ work stays inside +2/-2 dB. FxSound's own 13 shipped presets on this exact ladder almost all live inside -4..+5 dB and its "Voice" preset (Installer/Resources/Factsoft/3.fac, read directly) keeps band 1 at 0 dB; manufacturers' own voicing switches (Shure SM7B) move 3-4 dB. A factory preset that moves a band 8 dB is broken on any mic other than the one it was tuned on.

HPF = 75 Hz. Sources cluster at 70-100 Hz: Shure 70-90, RODE 80, BOYA "start at 75, climb only if the room forces it", WebRTC's shipped capture filter is a 2nd-order Butterworth near 100 Hz. Warm Voice is the preset whose whole job is low-end weight, and the adult male fundamental runs to ~85 Hz, so it takes the bottom of that range rather than the middle; luix-voice, the most restrained real preset in the survey, also uses 75 Hz. I did not go lower: below ~70 Hz there is no speech, only desk rumble, HVAC and plosive energy, and that energy drives the gate and compressor detectors and eats limiter headroom without ever being heard. Order: 4th-order (24 dB/oct) is preferred — computed Butterworth residuals at 75 Hz are -7.3 dB at 62.5 Hz and only -0.13 dB at 115.734 Hz, i.e. it clears the rumble band while leaving the warmth band untouched. If the port's filter is fixed at 12 dB/oct the same 75 Hz gives -4.9 dB / -0.70 dB, which is still acceptable; the preset does not depend on the order. Latency: IIR, zero added samples either way. 300 Hz-style telephony cutoffs are not considered — G.712's 300-3400 Hz is a channel allocation, and ITU itself moved the low edge back down (G.722 50-7000, P.341 ~100-8000).

EQ. Verified against the port's own code: derive_q gives Q = sqrt(r)/(r-1) = 1.5976 for this ladder (r = 1.85175, 0.889 octave per band), and biquad.rs only widens Q when |gain| < 0.42 dB — so this EQ is constant-Q at every value used here, and a broad curve has to be authored across adjacent bands rather than with one big move. I simulated the composite of the ten peaking sections; the slider values and the resulting curve are:
  62.5 = 0.0 -> +0.39 composite (pure skirt from the band above)
  115.734 = +2.0 -> +2.12
  214.311 = +1.0 -> +1.05
  396.85 = -1.5 -> -1.44
  734.867 = -1.0 -> -1.28
  1360.79 = 0.0 -> -0.51
  2519.84 = -1.0 -> -1.48
  4666.12 = -2.0 -> -2.46
  8640.48 = -1.0 -> -1.79
  16000 = -2.0 -> -2.27
Shape: a +1.9 dB dome peaking near 130 Hz, zero crossing at ~285 Hz, a shallow -1.2 to -1.5 dB scoop through 400-800 Hz, and a slow downward tilt reaching -2.5 dB at 4.7 kHz. Mean gain over 100-8000 Hz is -0.66 dB, which the makeup gain compensates.
  Band 0 (62.5 Hz) = 0.0 deliberately, and this is the one number I most want on the record. The HPF has already removed that band (-7.3 dB at 62.5 Hz), so a cut there does nothing about rumble; what it would do, because the bell is 0.889 octave wide, is pull -1.8 dB out of 80 Hz and -0.9 dB out of 100 Hz — thinning exactly the body this preset exists to add. Boosting it would re-import what the HPF just removed and spend limiter headroom on inaudible content. It is also free: biquad.rs bypasses a section whose gain is exactly 0.0. FxSound's own 13 factory presets leave this band at 0 dB without exception.
  Band 1 (115.734 Hz) = +2.0 is the actual "warm" control — its span (85-157 Hz) is the male fundamental, and the 75 Hz HPF leaves it essentially intact. +2 matches luix-voice's +2 dB bell at 130 Hz and sits just under azmarifdev's +3 dB shelf at 90 Hz chosen for exactly this mic class (thin FIFINE-type condensers). I stopped at +2 rather than +3 because the band already sums with band 2.
  Band 2 (214.311 Hz) = +1.0. Body and the female fundamental region. The generic vocal-EQ literature cuts here as "boom", and Shure's own bass-rolloff switch is about -3 dB at 200 Hz — but that switch exists to fight proximity effect on a mic worked at 2-3 inches, which is the opposite of this preset's target. For a thin source +1 is the right sign; +2 on both bands (one researcher's suggestion) would have summed to a ~+2.6 dB plateau running right into the 250-350 Hz mud core, which the brief forbids.
  Band 3 (396.85 Hz) = -1.5 and band 4 (734.867 Hz) = -1.0. This is the part that keeps the low-end lift from reading as mud: mud is 250-500 Hz and box/papery is 400-800 Hz, and both independent open-source voice presets cut -2 dB somewhere in 220-425 Hz. Spread over two adjacent bands at a smaller value each, per the ladder's overlap, rather than one deep cut — past about -5 dB at 396 Hz the voice goes telephone-thin.
  Band 5 (1360.79 Hz) = 0.0. Nasal/honk above, intelligibility below; two-sided and touchy, and it already sits at -0.5 dB from its neighbours' skirts.
  Bands 6 and 7 (2519.84 = -1.0, 4666.12 = -2.0) are the "tames a presence peak" move. Harshness on cheap bright condensers sits at 3-5 kHz, straddling the 3429 Hz crossover between these two bands, so the cut is weighted onto band 7 (whose span is 3429-6350 Hz) and only lightly onto band 6. Band 6 is the intelligibility core — iZotope's guidance for 1.5-5 kHz is that 1-2 dB is the normal move, and ISO 226 says the ear is most sensitive here — so -1 dB is a tilt, not a scoop; cutting it hard would produce the dull result users "fix" by boosting air, which then feeds the de-esser. Net across the presence region is -1.5 to -2.5 dB, roughly the inverse of the SM7B's own +3-4 dB presence switch, which is the closest thing to a manufacturer-sanctioned magnitude for this move.
  Bands 8 and 9 (8640.48 = -1.0, 16000 = -2.0). The target mic class is described by reviewers as brittle and bright with apparent onboard top-end lift, and FIFINE's own published figures (-80 dBFS equivalent noise, 78 dB S/N) put an audible hiss floor up there; +5 dB of makeup downstream makes that hiss louder, not quieter. Above ~12 kHz there is essentially no speech harmonic content at all — only hiss, breath and codec artefacts. Small cuts, not boosts. On an HFP/mSBC Bluetooth mic (16 kHz capture) band 9 is at Nyquist and band 8 near it; the implementation should bypass bands above ~0.4x the sample rate, and this preset loses nothing when it does.
  What the EQ deliberately does NOT do: de-ess. Sibilance centres on 5-9 kHz, which lands on the 6350 Hz crossover between bands 7 and 8; neither band can reach it without taking presence or air with it, and a static cut cannot track an intermittent event. That is the de-esser's job.

GATE (downward expander) = -48 dBFS, 2.0:1, 5 / 150 / 250 ms. Ratio 2.0 is Rane Note 155's stated figure for noise reduction by expansion, and every source agrees a hard gate on speech is wrong: an infinite-ratio gate chatters when the signal hovers at threshold and amputates voiceless fricatives and plosive tails, which sit only a few dB above room tone. At 2:1 a fricative 6 dB under the threshold is pulled down 6 dB, not muted. Attack 5 ms is the unanimous value among the tuned presets (EasyEffects' 20 ms default and Obscurely's 20 ms clip word onsets; every tuned preset uses 1-5 ms). Hold 150 ms sits in the 70-200 ms window the gate literature gives for speech and spans inter-word gaps, which with the 250 ms release (jtrv's value) is the anti-chatter mechanism this schema gives me — there is no hysteresis field, so hold has to carry that load, and I would not ship this preset with hold at 0. Threshold -48 dBFS is the weakest number in the preset and I will say so plainly: it is only meaningful relative to the mic's noise floor, which is why two reputable presets differ by 26 dB (jtrv -50, luix -55, azmarifdev -50, Barisozyurek -48 versus OBS's -26 on a different gain-staging assumption). -48 is the median of the tuned Linux presets. Threshold should ultimately be derived from a short noise-floor measurement, and the UI should expose it. One interaction the fixed stage order forces: the gate sits before the compressor, so it cannot see the noise floor that the compressor's gain reduction plus +5 dB makeup will raise by roughly 6-10 dB; -48 dBFS is chosen with that downstream gain in mind rather than against the raw input. If RNNoise is enabled the expander should be softened further, since two suppressors in series on a word start is one too many. Latency: zero, no lookahead.

DE-ESSER = split 6000 Hz, -18 dBFS, 3:1, 4 dB maximum reduction, 1 ms attack, 60 ms release, split-band. 6 kHz is Calf's split default and the value that actually means "crossover above which gain is reduced"; it straddles male sibilance (5-6 kHz) and female (7-8 kHz), which a single fixed preset has to do. I did not take azmarifdev's 3 kHz split: that is inside the intelligibility region and produces an audible lisp — RODE puts sibilance at 4-7 kHz and FabFilter at 8-10 kHz, and nobody credible puts it at 3 kHz. Threshold -18 dBFS is deliberately less sensitive than the tuned presets' -20 to -26: those presets lift the HF (jtrv +2 dB at 10 kHz, azmarifdev +2 dB at 9 kHz) whereas this one cuts 4666 by 2 dB and 8640 by 1 dB, so the detector sees a quieter sibilant band and the threshold must be offset upward by about that amount or the de-esser double-counts the EQ. Ratio 3:1 is the universal value. The 4 dB reduction cap is the guard against lisping (guides put typical sibilant GR at 2-4 dB and recommend capping at 6); a warm preset that has already tilted the top down needs less. Attack 1 ms catches the sibilant onset (this is the one stage that should be fast — unlike the main compressor, its whole job is the transient); 60 ms release is inside the 40-150 ms window and short enough to recover before the following vowel. Split-band, not wide: Calf's docs recommend Wide for a single voice, but Wide ducks the full signal on every "s", and with a compressor immediately downstream in this fixed order that reads as full-band pumping. I picked Split for that reason. Latency: zero, detection is feed-forward with no lookahead. Note the ordering caveat honestly: the fixed chain de-esses before the compressor, whereas 7 of the 8 surveyed presets with both stages de-ess after it, because a compressor re-amplifies the sibilants you just removed. The dossier's advice for keeping the fixed order is to de-ess harder; I have instead kept it gentle and relied on the EQ's 4666/8640 cuts to do the static part, because over-de-essing is the worse failure and this preset is tonally dark up top already. If the stage order is ever revisited, moving the de-esser after makeup is the better design.

COMPRESSOR = -18 dBFS, 2.5:1, knee -6 dB, attack 25 ms, release 200 ms. Ratio 2.5 sits between Calf's 2:1 default and the 3:1 that Rane and RODE both give for gentle spoken word; Warm Voice is the round-sounding preset, not the loud one, and Rane's "severe" territory starts around 10:1 (which is OBS's default and is a limiter wearing a compressor's name). Threshold -18 dBFS is the strongest convergence in the dossier — OBS -18.0, Calf -18.06, jtrv -18 — and with 2.5:1 it produces roughly 4-6 dB of gain reduction on speech peaking near -8 to -10 dBFS, which is exactly Rane's stated target of 3-6 dB on normal speech and ~0 dB in quiet passages. Attack 25 ms is Rane's lower bound for vocals (25-100 ms) and is chosen against the common "1-5 ms for vocals" advice: a stop-consonant burst is a transient of a few ms up to ~35 ms, so a 1-5 ms attack compresses the burst itself and dulls exactly the 2-8 kHz energy that carries consonant identity — the failure people then try to fix with HF boost, which feeds the de-esser. 25 ms lets the consonant through and clamps the vowel behind it. Release 200 ms is tied to syllable rate, not picked freely: the speech envelope's modulation spectrum peaks at 4-8 Hz (one syllable per 125-250 ms), so a much shorter release recovers inside each syllable and pumps the noise floor between words, and a much longer one rides down a whole phrase. Rane gives 100-500 ms for vocals; jtrv uses 200 ms. Attack and release both cost zero latency — this is envelope timing, not lookahead. knee_db = -6.0 uses the LSP sign convention that every preset in the survey uses: it means a 6 dB-wide soft knee spanning -24..-18 dBFS, so compression fades in below the threshold and the transition between compressed and uncompressed syllables is inaudible. If the port's field is ever defined as a positive knee width, this value is +6.0 with the same meaning; the sign must be pinned in code, not inferred.

MAKEUP = +5.0 dB, and this number is a starting value that must be trimmed by measurement, not shipped as authored. Derivation: the compressor gives about 4.3 dB of average gain reduction at this threshold/ratio on speech peaking near -10 dBFS (the signal-independent TASCAM/Waves rule, 0.5 x |threshold| x (1 - 1/ratio), gives 5.4 dB for a 0 dBFS input), and the EQ's mean gain over 100-8000 Hz is -0.66 dB, so +5.0 dB restores the level roughly to where it entered while leaving the peaks slightly lower than unity. That puts output peaks around -10 dBFS, i.e. about 7 dB below the ceiling, so the limiter stays a safety net catching plosive leftovers and door slams rather than a loudness tool — AES TD1008 recommends about 1 dB of limiting as the maximum starting point. Two things I am explicitly not claiming: that this lands the chain at any particular LUFS (that depends on the user's input gain, which the chain cannot know), and that the six presets are loudness-matched by construction. They are not, and they must be: measure each factory preset on one common speech reference, target -18 LUFS short-term for speech (AES TD1008's published speech distribution loudness, deliberately ~2 LU below the music figure because speech at equal BS.1770 loudness is perceived 2-3 dB louder), and trim each preset's makeup so they land within 0.5 LU of each other and Studio/Natural lands within 0.5 LU of bypass. Mind the channel-count reference while doing it: -16 LUFS stereo equals -19 LUFS mono, not the reverse, and getting it backwards is a silent 3 dB error on every preset. Do not servo this value from an integrated loudness measurement in real time — integrated loudness is a programme measure, not a control signal; use short-term (3 s) for the meter and keep makeup static.

LIMITER CEILING = -3.0 dBFS. -1 dBTP is the genuine standard (EBU R128 §m, AES TD1008 §4, Spotify, Apple) but it assumes you are the last processing stage before one known encoder, and a virtual microphone is neither. Downstream of this chain sit, in some combination: a VoIP client's AGC (WebRTC's shipped config targets -3 dBFS, applies up to 9 dB of digital compression gain and then hard-limits), an Opus encode that may drop to tens of kbps — precisely the regime where TD1008 says to go below -1 dBTP because peak overshoot grows as bitrate falls — and OBS's own limiter, which defaults to a -6 dBFS threshold. TD1008 also documents up to 3 dB of gain reduction in a decode-side OS limiter when the encode side left insufficient headroom. -3 dBFS buys margin against all three and costs nothing perceptually because every one of those consumers renormalises. It is also honest about measurement: unless the limiter oversamples 4x per BS.1770 Annex 2, this number is sample-peak dBFS, not dBTP, and a -1 dBFS sample-peak limiter routinely leaks above 0 dBTP — so the UI should say dBFS and the extra 2 dB partly pays for that error. Lookahead should be 2 ms, not the 5 ms LSP ships: lookahead is added latency 1:1, and the 75 Hz high-pass has already defused most plosive energy, so 2 ms is enough. Total chain latency is then about 2 ms (HPF, gate, EQ, de-esser and compressor all add zero), or about 12 ms with RNNoise's fixed 10 ms frame — inside the ~15 ms budget beyond which self-monitoring becomes distracting. Note the schema has no lookahead field, so that value has to be set in the limiter stage itself.

TWO CHAIN-LEVEL DEFECTS THIS PRESET'S NUMBERS ASSUME WILL BE FIXED. First, the planned order puts optional RNNoise after the brick-wall limiter. Nothing should follow the limiter: RNNoise is spectral gain modification, and AES TD1008 §7B states that filtering removes programme energy and can raise the peak (their square-wave case is +2.1 dB), so "filtering (if used) should ideally occur before the peak limiter". Zero of the nine surveyed presets do what is planned; five put denoise first. RNNoise belongs before the gate, where it also makes the gate's threshold decision easier. Until that moves, the -3 dBFS ceiling is not actually enforced at the output when RNNoise is on. Second, makeup gain is the last gain-affecting stage before the limiter and nothing may be applied after it — two surveyed presets break exactly this rule and their ceilings mean nothing.

WHAT IS NOT SOURCED. The ten EQ gains are not copied from any shipped preset: no open-source project ships a graphic preset on this ladder, and all the real voice curves are parametric with centres and band types this ladder cannot express. They are my mapping of an agreed four-move voice shape (body lift 90-130 Hz, mud cut 220-425 Hz, presence move 2-4 kHz, top-end handling 8-16 kHz) onto the fixed centres, inverted in sign where the target mic class calls for it, with the composite simulated at the port's real Q of 1.5976 so the summed curve — not the slider values — is what was designed. The gate threshold is a median of community presets and is gain-staging dependent. Everything else traces to the manufacturer, standards or plugin-source numbers cited.

preset.name: Studio
preset.intent: The honest reference: a level-matched, flat-EQ chain with only a gentle high-pass, light 2:1 levelling and a safety limiter, so a user can A/B the raw microphone against the processed one and hear processing rather than loudness.
preset.rationale:
PURPOSE CONSTRAINS EVERYTHING. This preset's job is to be the A/B reference. Three dossier sources independently warn that a reference preset which is even 1-2 dB louder than dry makes users conclude "processing sounds better" when they are only hearing level (EasyEffects survey warning 9; loudness-standards warning 12; EQ-ladder warning 11). So every value below is chosen for "least processing that is still a product default", and the whole preset is subordinate to one acceptance test: short-term (3 s) loudness of the processed path must sit within +/-0.5 LU of the dry path on the same speech take. If it does not, makeup_db is wrong, not the rest.

HPF 75 Hz. A dedicated high-pass is kept (not bypassed) because it is the one stage that earns its place even in a reference: it removes desk rumble, HVAC, handling noise and DC that are inaudible on laptop speakers but drive the compressor detector and eat limiter headroom. 75 Hz is the gentlest value the sources support: Shure says 70-90 Hz for spoken word, BOYA says start at 75 Hz and only climb to 100/150 Hz when the room forces it, RODE and nearly every community preset say 80 Hz. Male speaking fundamentals run down to ~85 Hz (arXiv 1709.07552; Wikipedia Voice frequency), so 75 Hz is below every user's fundamental — 100 Hz would cost a deep male voice ~3.5 dB at its fundamental (WebRTC's shipped 2nd-order coefficients measure -3.54 dB at 100 Hz), which is exactly the tonal change a reference must not make. 2nd-order Butterworth (12 dB/oct) is the well-trodden choice and is literally what WebRTC ships on every VoIP capture path; it also costs zero added latency. I deliberately did NOT take research-4's 60 Hz suggestion for Studio: below 75 Hz the filter stops defusing plosive LF, and the dossier's own interaction note (D) is that the HPF is what lets the limiter run with minimal lookahead. 300 Hz is rejected outright — G.712's 300-3400 Hz is a telephone channel allocation, not an intelligibility finding, and ITU itself moved back down (G.722 50-7000 Hz, P.341 ~100-8000 Hz).

EQ: ten zeros. Non-negotiable for this preset. Independent supporting evidence beyond the brief: I checked the vendor's own 13 shipped .fac files in this repo — band 1 (62.5 Hz) is 0.0 dB in all 13, and 11 of 13 keep every band inside -2..+3 dB. Note also that 62.5 Hz is left at 0 rather than cut: the 75 Hz 2nd-order high-pass already gives about -5.7 dB at 62.5 Hz, and because this ladder is effectively constant-Q at Q=1.598 (0.889 octave; the port's Q-widening rule only engages below ~0.42 dB of gain, biquad.rs:29-38,127-134), a -3 dB move at 62.5 Hz would also pull 80 Hz down ~1.8 dB — thinning the voice's real bottom end while removing rumble the HPF already removed. That is the doubling the constraints forbid, and it is declined deliberately.

GATE: OFF, and inert if enabled. The brief specifies gate off for this profile, and the reasoning holds independently: an expander is the one stage whose correct threshold depends entirely on the user's own noise floor and mic gain, which a factory constant cannot know (the dossier's two reputable presets differ by 26 dB on this single number). A reference preset that intermittently ducks room tone is not a reference. ratio is set to 1.0, which per the stated constraint means no expansion — so the stage is inert on two counts, enabled=false and unity ratio, and cannot silently colour the A/B if a future UI ignores the enable flag. The remaining numbers are parked at defensible values so that a user who turns it on gets something sane rather than the factory-default trap: threshold -50 dBFS (jtrv -50, azmarifdev -50, luix -55 — the tuned presets; the -24 dB LSP/EasyEffects default and Calf's -18 dB are generic dynamics defaults that will chop speech), attack 5 ms (every tuned preset uses 1-5 ms; the 20-25 ms defaults clip word onsets), hold 100 ms (spans inter-word gaps; Rane/SoS/Wikipedia all name hold as the direct cure for chattering, and OBS's voice-tuned gate ships 200 ms), release 200 ms (100-250 ms consensus; long enough to fade under a word tail).

DE-ESSER: OFF. With the EQ flat there is no HF lift for it to correct, and the dossier is explicit that the de-esser and the 4666/8640 Hz region are coupled (interaction E): presets with HF lift need the de-esser proportionally more sensitive, so a preset with zero HF lift needs it least. Leaving it off also removes its detector filters and its contribution to latency, and removes the risk of the named failure mode (over-de-essing to a lisp) in the one preset where a user is listening for fidelity. Parked values if enabled: split 6000 Hz (Calf's own split default, and the compromise between male 5-6 kHz and female 7-8 kHz sibilance — this is also precisely where the fixed EQ ladder cannot help, since 5-9 kHz lands on the band 7/8 crossover at 6350 Hz), threshold -18 dB (Calf default, and the low end of the -18..-22 range in tuned presets), ratio 3:1 (jtrv, MateusRodCosta, Calf, and RODE/mastering.com all agree), max_reduction 4 dB (typical de-essing is 2-4 dB on most voices; capping well under the 6-9 dB ceiling is the guard against lisping), attack 1 ms (sibilance is a short burst; unlike the main compressor the de-esser must catch it), release 80 ms (inside the 40-150 ms window so the band recovers before the next vowel). I am NOT adopting split mode vs wide mode here since the schema has no such field; if the implementation exposes one, use split — Calf recommends Wide, but Wide ducks the whole signal on every "s" and, with a compressor after it, produces audible full-band pumping.

COMPRESSOR: threshold -18 dBFS, ratio 2:1, knee 6 dB, attack 25 ms, release 200 ms.
- Threshold -18 dBFS is the strongest numerical convergence in the whole dossier: OBS ships -18.0 and Calf ships 0.125 linear = -18.06 dB. LSP's -12 dB is 6 dB hotter and is a generic default.
- Ratio 2.0 is the gentlest ratio any source treats as real compression: Calf's shipped default, Rane's "gentle" end (2:1-3:1), the bottom of RODE's stated 2:1-4:1 for vocals, and research-4's own Studio/Natural recommendation. Everything above 3:1 belongs to the working presets, not the reference. With this threshold, knee and ratio, normal speech peaking around -10 dBFS sees ~4 dB of gain reduction and mid-level syllables around -14 dBFS see ~2 dB — the gentle end of Rane Note 155's stated target of 3-6 dB GR on normal speech, which is the authoritative way to set a threshold rather than picking a dB number blind.
- knee_db = +6.0 means a 6 dB-wide soft knee starting below the threshold, i.e. numerically identical to LSP's -6 dB and close to Calf's +9.03 dB. SIGN CONVENTION DECLARED, NOT INHERITED: I grepped this repo and the port has no compressor, de-esser, gate or limiter yet (only the playback leveller in crates/fxsound-dsp/src/leveller.rs), so there is no existing convention to follow. This schema field is a bare number, so I define positive = knee width in dB. Anyone wiring this to an LSP-style plugin must negate it; the dossier's warning 3 is that mapping knee naively is a real bug source. Soft knee matters more here than in any other preset: it is what makes the transition between compressed and uncompressed syllables inaudible, which is the whole point of a transparent reference.
- Attack 25 ms is chosen against the loudest bad advice in the field. Rane Note 155 gives 25-100 ms for vocals; the two best-tuned open-source mic presets use 15 and 20 ms; consumer blogs say 1-5 ms. A stop-consonant burst is a transient of a few ms up to ~35 ms (Jackson, Columbia EE), so a 1-5 ms attack clamps the burst itself and dulls exactly the 2-8 kHz energy that carries consonant identity. 25 ms sits at the bottom of Rane's vocal range and above the tuned-preset middle — deliberately the slowest of the six presets, because passing transients untouched is what "natural" means.
- Release 200 ms is tied to syllable rate, not picked freely: the speech envelope's modulation spectrum peaks at 4-8 Hz with a dominant rate near 4.5-5 Hz, i.e. one syllable every 125-250 ms. Shorter than that and the compressor recovers inside each syllable and you hear breathing on the noise floor; much longer and it rides down a loud sentence and buries the next one. 200 ms is jtrv's value and sits mid-window. Note Rane's definition caveat: release is specified in dB/second, so actual recovery = (gain reduction x release setting)/10 dB — a "200 ms" constant is not 200 ms of wall clock once 4 dB has to unwind. This is a documentation point for the implementer, not a reason to change the number.

MAKEUP +1.5 dB — PROVISIONAL, AND THE DOSSIER DOES NOT COVER IT. No surveyed preset has a separate makeup stage at all, so there is no number to cite; this is reasoning plus a measurement procedure. The TASCAM/Waves auto-makeup rule (0.5 x |threshold| x (1 - 1/ratio)) would give +4.5 dB here, and that is WRONG for this preset: it compensates the reduction a 0 dBFS signal would receive, but speech spends most of its time below the knee, so applying it would ship the reference 3 dB hot and destroy the A/B. The actual short-term loudness loss of 2:1 compression at -18 dBFS on speech is roughly 1-1.5 dB, so +1.5 dB is the centre of that estimate. It is net of the EQ because the EQ contributes exactly 0 dB. REQUIRED BEFORE SHIP: measure the chain's short-term loudness against the dry path on a real speech take and trim this value to land within +/-0.5 LU; do not hand-pick it. Do not servo it from an integrated (BS.1770-gated) measurement in real time — integrated loudness is defined over a programme and is not a control signal; makeup stays static per preset. For orientation only, the published speech distribution figures are -18 LUFS (AES TD1008 Table 1), -16 LKFS +/-1 (Apple Podcasts) and -16 LUFS stereo / -19 LUFS mono (Google) — and note the brief's "-16 mono / -19 stereo" is inverted: duplicating mono into two channels ADDS 3.01 LU under BS.1770, so it is -16 stereo / -19 mono. For Studio the target is not a LUFS number at all, it is parity with dry; the LUFS figures matter for the other five presets.

LIMITER CEILING -3.0 dBFS. The sources conflict and I am taking the streaming-standards side over the community-preset side. The community presets sit at -1.0/-1.5 dB and research-4 suggested -1.0 for Studio; -3.0 is correct here for four citable reasons. (1) -1 dBTP is the standards' requirement for a signal about to hit ONE known encoder as the LAST processing stage (EBU R128 section m; AES TD1008 section 4) — a virtual microphone is neither: Discord's Krisp/AGC, OBS's own limiter (which itself defaults to -6.0 dBFS threshold) and the receiving client's decoder all sit after us. (2) TD1008 section 7B is explicit that the threshold must go BELOW -1.0 dBTP as bitrate drops, and Discord's Opus negotiates down to tens of kbps. (3) TD1008 documents up to 3 dB of gain reduction in a decode-side OS limiter when the encode side left insufficient headroom. (4) This is a dBFS sample-peak ceiling unless the implementation oversamples 4x per BS.1770 Annex 2 — a non-oversampled brick wall at -1 dBFS routinely leaks above 0 dBTP, so the label must stay dBFS and carry ~1 dB extra margin. Against all that, -3 dBFS costs nothing perceptually here because the receiver normalises, and it costs nothing at all in this preset specifically: with +1.5 dB of makeup and speech peaking near -10 dBFS after 2:1 levelling, the limiter should essentially never engage. It is a door-slam catch, not a loudness tool — TD1008 recommends ~1 dB of limiting as a maximum starting point and warns that more is worse than occasional clipping. Also load-bearing: nothing may apply gain after the limiter. Two surveyed presets break exactly this (Obscurely limits at -14 dB then adds +10 dB after; MorrisAboveThis limits at 0 dBFS then trims -1.1 dB after) and their ceilings mean nothing as a result.

LATENCY BUDGET. With gate and de-esser off, this preset's added latency is the limiter's lookahead and nothing else: the HPF and the ten EQ biquads are zero-latency IIR sections, and the compressor runs without lookahead. Recommend 1.5-2 ms lookahead (jtrv ships 2 ms; LSP's 5 ms default is 5 ms of mic latency for no benefit here) — the 75 Hz high-pass has already removed the plosive LF excursion that would otherwise demand a long window, which is the dossier's interaction D. Total added latency under 2 ms, which is the quietest possible answer for a path the speaker may monitor.

TWO THINGS THE IMPLEMENTATION MUST GET RIGHT THAT THIS SCHEMA CANNOT EXPRESS.
1. RNNoise must be OFF for this preset (it is a reference; a neural denoiser is the opposite of transparent, and it alone would add 10 ms — five times the rest of the chain). Separately, the planned chain's placement of RNNoise AFTER the brick-wall limiter is a defect, not a style point: AES TD1008 section 7B states that filtering "should ideally occur before the peak limiter" because removing programme energy raises peaks (their square-wave example is +2.1 dB), and zero of the nine surveyed presets put denoise last. It belongs before the gate, or at worst immediately before the limiter.
2. Studio is NOT bypass — it still has the high-pass, 2:1 levelling and a limiter. Ship a real, loudness-matched bypass toggle for the A/B and say so in the UI, rather than letting users believe this preset is the unprocessed signal.
