critiques.overall:
The EQ curve itself is SOUND and I will not manufacture an objection to it. Ten zeros on this ladder is not merely defensible, it is stronger than the rationale claims: biquad.rs:113-116 returns BiquadCoeffs::UNITY with on:false for an exact 0.0 dB band, and the `on` field's own doc says such a section is "skipped entirely rather than run at unity" — so the flat ladder is ten bypassed sections, not ten unity biquads. No phase shift, no coloration, no CPU. Nothing is honky (734.9/1360.8 at 0), nothing is boomy (62.5/115.7 at 0), nothing is harsh or lispy (4666/8640 at 0, de-esser off, and with no HF lift there is nothing for a de-esser to correct). No single band is doing too much because no band is doing anything. The rationale's constant-Q numbers check out exactly: derive_q(62.5, 16000, 10, 1.0) = 1.5977 at r = 1.8518 (0.889 oct), and Rule B un-warps Q above (1.5977-0.2)/3.3 = 0.4236 dB, so the "~0.42 dB" figure is right and the argument that a -3 dB cut at 62.5 would drag 80 Hz down ~1.8 dB is right. Declining that cut is the correct call. The refusal to micro-trim is also right for a reason the rationale does not give: any trim under 0.42 dB would trip Rule B and become a much wider, lower-Q bump than intended, so 0.0 is the only honest value on this ladder.

Every tone problem in this preset therefore lives outside the EQ, in the two stages that colour the spectrum without a gain slider. First, the 75 Hz high-pass is the single largest tonal deviation in the whole chain and the rationale understates it: at 12 dB/oct it takes 2.06 dB off an 85 Hz fundamental, not ~0 dB. A preset whose entire acceptance test is transparency cannot carry a 2 dB dip on a deep male voice, and band 1 cannot fix it (a +2 dB peak at 62.5 Hz with Q=1.6 delivers only ~+1 dB at 85 Hz while restoring the rumble at 62.5 the filter was there to remove) — so the corner must move, not the EQ. Second, the compressor detector is full-band, and with the EQ flat it is the 115-400 Hz vowel energy that drives gain reduction: every stressed vowel pulls the 2519/4666/8640 Hz consonant bands down with it by 3-4 dB, which reads as the processed path being slightly duller than dry. That is exactly the tone difference an A/B is supposed to be free of, and the repo already ships the fix as a convention (leveller.rs:55, SIDECHAIN_HPF_HZ = 120.0). The 75 Hz signal-path filter does not substitute for it: at 200 Hz it is 0.16 dB down.

Two arithmetic slips in the rationale, corrected below. Neither changes a conclusion but both are load-bearing for the next reviewer. Unrelated to tone but worth one line: the rationale's "the port has no compressor, de-esser, gate or limiter yet" is not accurate — effects/dynamic_boost.rs is a look-ahead peak limiter with LOOK_AHEAD_SECONDS = 0.00075 and a permanent -0.3 dBFS ceiling. That is playback, not capture, but it is evidence against the recommended 1.5-2 ms capture lookahead: this codebase's own limiter does the job in 0.75 ms.

problems.problem: The high-pass is the only stage in this preset that changes tone, and its cost is understated. The rationale says "75 Hz is below every user's fundamental", implying ~0 dB, but a 2nd-order Butterworth at 75 Hz measures -2.06 dB at 85 Hz (r=1.1333, |H|^2 = r^4/(1+r^4) = 0.6226) and -1.19 dB at 100 Hz. A corner being below a fundamental does not make the filter transparent there — at 12 dB/oct you are still on the skirt a third of an octave up. For the five working presets that is free; for the one preset whose stated acceptance test is transparency against dry, a 2 dB dip on a deep male fundamental is the single largest colour in the chain, larger than anything the compressor does, and it is precisely the 'thin' failure mode. It cannot be repaired on the ladder: a +2 dB peak at 62.5 Hz (Q=1.5977, half-bandwidth 0.444 oct) sits 0.443 oct from 85 Hz and so delivers only about +1 dB there, while adding a full +2 dB at 62.5 Hz where the filter was deliberately removing rumble. The fix has to be the corner.
problems.corrected_value: hpf_hz: 60 (Studio only; keep 75-80 for the other five presets). At 60 Hz the 85 Hz fundamental loses 0.96 dB instead of 2.06 dB, 100 Hz loses 0.52 dB instead of 1.19 dB, and 62.5 Hz sits at -2.66 dB instead of -4.87 dB. The cost is 3.4 dB less rejection at 40 Hz (-7.8 dB vs -11.3 dB) and 3.9 dB at 20 Hz (-19.1 dB vs -23.0 dB), which is inaudible content whose only real harm was feeding the detector — and that harm is removed outright by the 120 Hz detector high-pass in the next finding. This is also the value research-4 suggested for Studio and it was declined on the strength of the overstated transparency claim.
problems.why: A reference preset is allowed exactly one job: sound like the microphone. 2 dB at the fundamental is well above the ~0.5 dB threshold at which listeners start calling a voice thinner, and it lands on the one region users are most sensitive to in their own voice. The stated reason for preferring 75 over 60 ("below 75 Hz the filter stops defusing plosive LF" and "the HPF is what lets the limiter run with minimal lookahead") is a detector/headroom argument, not a tone argument, and it is better served by filtering the detector than by filtering the programme.

problems.problem: The compressor detector is full-band and nothing in the schema or rationale conditions it. With the EQ flat, broadband level is dominated by the 115-400 Hz vowel region (bands 2-4), so gain reduction is triggered almost entirely by low-mid energy and then applied to the whole spectrum. Every stressed vowel therefore ducks the 2519.84 / 4666.12 / 8640.48 Hz consonant bands by the same 3-4 dB, even though those bands contributed almost nothing to the trigger. The audible result is a processed path that is consistently a shade darker and duller than the dry path, and it tracks the talker's vowels — the exact tonal artefact an A/B is designed to expose. The 75 Hz signal-path high-pass does not substitute for detector conditioning: it is only 0.72 dB down at 115.7 Hz and 0.16 dB down at 200 Hz, so it leaves untouched the band that actually drives the detector. The rationale's claim that the HPF's job is to stop LF from "driving the compressor detector" is true only for sub-75 Hz rumble, which is not what dominates speech.
problems.corrected_value: Add a detector-path (side-chain) high-pass at 120 Hz, one-pole, matching the house convention already in this repo: leveller.rs:55 SIDECHAIN_HPF_HZ = 120.0, with the coefficient helper at leveller.rs:202 (high_pass_alpha, rc/(rc+dt)). Signal path stays unfiltered above the 60 Hz programme high-pass. If the schema cannot express it, ship it as a fixed internal constant on the capture compressor rather than a preset field, exactly as the leveller does.
problems.why: The rationale states there is "no existing convention to follow" for the dynamics stages. That is true for the knee sign but false for the detector: the vendor's own levelling block, ported verbatim in leveller.rs, high-passes its detector at 120 Hz and splits tonality at 180/1200 Hz. Following it costs nothing, removes vowel-driven spectral ducking, and makes the compressor's 3-4 dB of gain reduction track speech loudness rather than speech pitch — which is also what makes the +/-0.5 LU parity test reproducible across male and female talkers instead of only the one you measured on.

problems.problem: Two filter magnitudes in the tonal argument are wrong. (1) "the 75 Hz 2nd-order high-pass already gives about -5.7 dB at 62.5 Hz" — the correct value is -4.87 dB. The linear magnitude at that point is 0.5704, and 5.7 appears to be that figure read as dB. (2) "100 Hz would cost a deep male voice ~3.5 dB at its fundamental (WebRTC's shipped 2nd-order coefficients measure -3.54 dB at 100 Hz)" conflates two different measurements: what a filter does at its own corner versus what it does at an 85 Hz fundamental. A 2nd-order Butterworth at 100 Hz is -3.01 dB at 100 Hz by definition, and -4.65 dB at 85 Hz.
problems.corrected_value: (1) "-4.9 dB at 62.5 Hz" in place of "-5.7 dB". (2) "a 100 Hz corner costs a deep male voice 4.7 dB at an 85 Hz fundamental (and 3.0 dB at 100 Hz, its own corner)" in place of the WebRTC-sourced 3.54 dB figure.
problems.why: Both errors point the same way — they make the chosen 75 Hz corner look gentler at 62.5 Hz than it is, and make the rejected 100 Hz corner look gentler at the fundamental than it is — so correcting them does not overturn the choice to reject 100 Hz, it strengthens it while simultaneously weakening the case for 75 over 60. The 62.5 Hz figure is the specific number the decision to leave band 1 at 0.0 dB rests on, and the next reviewer will check it.

critiques.overall:
DYNAMICS VERDICT: the topology and the time constants are right; the *levels* are not pinned down, and that is what breaks the preset's own acceptance test.

What passes, with the arithmetic:
- Compressor will not pump or squash. 2:1 with T=-18 and a 6 dB knee gives GR = 0.5·(x+18) above the knee: 4.0 dB at a -10 dBFS peak, 2.0 dB at -14, 0 dB below -21. Max GR on speech ~4 dB is inside Rane 155's 3-6 dB target. Nothing here can squash.
- Attack 25 ms is correct and is the strongest single choice in the preset. Stop-burst transients (a few ms to ~35 ms) pass essentially untouched, so consonant identity in 2-8 kHz survives. The 1-5 ms consumer advice would dull exactly that.
- Release 200 ms = one syllable period at the 4.5-5 Hz modulation peak, so gain motion is ~2-4 dB at syllable rate. With only 4 dB of GR and a soft knee this is gentle, not pumping. I would not change it; 300 ms would ride the phrase instead of the syllable and be marginally more transparent, but 200 ms is defensible and I am not counting it as a defect.
- Limiter cannot be driven into constant reduction — provably. Steady-state output peak = x - 0.5(x+18) + 1.5 = 0.5x - 7.5 dBFS, so reaching a -3 dBFS ceiling needs x = +9 dBFS input. Impossible. The limiter can only ever catch transients faster than the 25 ms attack (door slam, desk knock, hard plosive), which is exactly what a safety catch should do. Corollary the rationale should own: because the limiter never engages on speech, the whole -3 vs -1 dBFS argument is audibly moot in *this* preset — it costs nothing and buys nothing here, so keep -3.
- Gate will not chatter and will not clip consonants: it is off, and if enabled, 5 ms attack opens ahead of any onset and 100 ms hold spans inter-word gaps. The one real risk if a user enables it is that -50 dBFS sits below many real desktop noise floors (a room+USB-mic floor of -45 dBFS is common), in which case it simply never closes — harmless, not chatter. The schema has no hysteresis field, so hold is the only chatter defence; 100 ms is enough.
- De-esser will not lisp. Ratio 3:1 with a 4 dB cap means the cap binds at 6 dB over threshold, so max reduction is hard-bounded well under the 6-9 dB lisp region.

What fails: the preset's entire loudness-parity claim rests on an undeclared detector convention. The rationale carefully declares the knee sign convention but never says whether threshold_db is peak-domain or RMS-domain, and that single omission swings GR from ~3 dB to ~0 dB — six times the ±0.5 LU budget the preset says it is subordinate to. The only detector precedent in this repo (leveller.rs: a six-buffer RMS ring with a 120 Hz sidechain HPF) is RMS, so an implementer following house style will get the wrong branch. With an RMS detector, vowel RMS sits ~9-11 dB under vowel peaks, i.e. ~-20 dBFS when peaks hit -10, which is inside the lower knee: GR ≈ 0.04 dB. The compressor then does nothing and the preset ships +1.5 dB of naked gain — the reference preset becomes 1.5 LU LOUDER than dry, which is precisely the failure mode (warnings 9/12/11) the whole design is built around. Fix the detector declaration and the makeup number and the preset is sound.

problems.problem: The GR arithmetic in the rationale (4 dB at -10 dBFS, 2 dB at -14) only holds for a peak/instantaneous-envelope detector. The schema and rationale never declare peak vs RMS detection, and the only precedent in this repo is RMS (crates/fxsound-dsp/src/leveller.rs uses a six-buffer RMS power ring with a 120 Hz sidechain high-pass). With an RMS detector, voiced speech RMS sits 9-11 dB below its peaks, so a take peaking at -10 dBFS has vowel RMS near -20 dBFS — inside the lower half of the 6 dB knee (-21..-15), where GR = 0.5·(x+21)²/(2·6) = 0.04 dB. The compressor becomes inert and the stage contributes only makeup gain. The rationale declares a knee sign convention (a ~0.5 dB issue) but not this one (a 3 dB issue). Note also that OBS's -18.0, cited as convergence, is a peak-domain envelope on fabsf(sample); Calf's 0.125 is read under a selectable detection mode — the two cited sources are not commensurable until this is fixed.
problems.corrected_value: Declare peak-domain detection explicitly in the preset ("threshold_db is peak dBFS") and keep threshold_db = -18. If the implementation uses RMS detection instead, threshold_db = -26 (so ~-20 dBFS vowel RMS sits 6 dB over threshold and yields the intended ~3 dB GR).
problems.why: Without the declaration, the same JSON produces either ~3 dB of levelling or ~0 dB, a 3 dB swing on a preset whose stated acceptance test is ±0.5 LU. The RMS branch silently converts the reference preset into a pure +1.5 dB gain stage, which is the exact bias the preset exists to avoid.

problems.problem: +1.5 dB is inconsistent with the preset's own gain-reduction figures and fails its own ±0.5 LU acceptance test in either detector branch. Short-term loudness is energy-dominated by vowel nuclei, which are exactly the -14..-10 dBFS region the rationale itself shows taking 2-4 dB of GR; with a 200 ms release that reduction also persists across the following consonants. Loudness-weighted GR on real speech at the stated operating point is therefore ~2.5-3 dB, not the asserted 1-1.5 dB, so the processed path lands 1.0-1.5 LU UNDER dry. (In the RMS-detector branch the error flips sign: GR ≈ 0, so the processed path lands 1.5 LU OVER dry — the disqualifying direction.) Second defect in the same field: makeup is a static gain compensating a level-dependent GR, and the preset never states the input level it is calibrated at. A quiet talker peaking at -25 dBFS gets no compression at all and hears the processed path +1.5 LU louder; a hot talker at -5 dBFS gets 6.5 dB GR and hears it 3-4 LU quieter. Parity is only ever true at one input level.
problems.corrected_value: makeup_db = 2.5, and add the calibration level to the preset text: "calibrated for speech peaking -12 ±3 dBFS; parity holds within that window only." Keep the mandate to trim by measurement. If ship-time measurement is not possible, makeup_db = 0.0 is the safer default, because erring quiet biases the A/B against processing rather than for it.
problems.why: The preset declares itself subordinate to a single acceptance test — ±0.5 LU versus dry — and +1.5 dB misses it by 1-1.5 LU at the very operating point the rationale uses for its own GR numbers. Undeclared calibration level means the error is unbounded across users.

problems.problem: Self-contradiction inside one paragraph. The rationale states the parked values exist "so that a user who turns it on gets something sane", and then sets ratio = 1.0, which by the stated constraint means no expansion. Enabling the gate therefore changes nothing: threshold, attack, hold and release are all inert behind a unity ratio. The double-inertness is defensive coding against a hypothetical UI that ignores enabled=false, but it is bought by breaking the parked-value promise — and a gate that appears enabled while doing nothing is a worse user-facing failure than the one it guards against (the user concludes the gate is broken, or raises threshold until it chops speech).
problems.corrected_value: gate.ratio = 2 (gentle downward expansion), with gate.enabled left at false. Use enabled=false alone as the inertness mechanism; if a UI is found that ignores it, that is a UI bug to fix, not a preset value.
problems.why: ratio=1 makes every other gate field in this preset dead data, and contradicts the stated reason those fields carry tuned values at all.

problems.problem: The parked value will not engage — the de-esser's failure mode here is the opposite of lisping. In a split-band de-esser the detector sees the ~6 kHz-and-up band, and sibilance in that band runs 10-15 dB below vowel peaks: for a take peaking at -10 dBFS full-band, the /s/ band peaks around -20 to -25 dBFS. A -18 dB threshold is never crossed, so a user enabling this stage gets 0 dB of reduction and concludes the de-esser does not work. Calf's -18 default is a full-band-ish factory number, not a tuned split-band value. The problem compounds if the de-esser sits after the compressor and makeup, where speech peaks are ~-12.5 dBFS.
problems.corrected_value: deesser.threshold_db = -26 (band sibilance at ~-20 dBFS then sits 6 dB over threshold, which at ratio 3 gives exactly the intended 4 dB, right at the max_reduction cap). Also record which side of the compressor the detector sits on, since it moves this number by the GR amount.
problems.why: ratio 3 and max_reduction 4 dB are internally consistent with each other (the cap binds at 6 dB over threshold) but only matter if the threshold is ever crossed; -18 dB makes the whole stage a no-op when enabled.

problems.problem: The declared convention itself is fine and welcome (positive = total knee width in dB), but the provenance claim attached to it is wrong and will mislead whoever ports it. LSP's and Calf's knee parameters are half-widths applied symmetrically about the threshold (the knee region runs threshold×knee … threshold÷knee), so LSP's -6 dB is a 12 dB-wide knee spanning -24..-12 dBFS, not a 6 dB one. An implementer copying LSP's -6 dB on the strength of "numerically identical" doubles the knee width. The audible cost is small — at -14 dBFS a 12 dB knee gives 2.08 dB GR versus 2.0 dB for a 6 dB knee, and above -12 they converge — but the sign-convention paragraph is presented as the authoritative mapping note and should not carry a factual error.
problems.corrected_value: Keep knee_db = 6.0 as total width, and correct the note to: "equivalent to LSP knee = -3 dB and Calf knee ≈ 1.41, since those are half-widths about the threshold; negate and halve when mapping."
problems.why: The rationale explicitly flags naive knee mapping as a known bug source (warning 3) and then supplies a mapping that is off by a factor of two in the direction it warned about.

problems.problem: +1.5 dB static makeup is derived from feeding SAMPLE-PEAK dBFS into the static compression curve. The rationale's own worked example ("speech peaking around -10 dBFS sees ~4 dB of gain reduction") is arithmetically correct for the curve but wrong for the signal: with attack_ms 25 the detector tracks the syllable envelope, not sample peaks. Speech with a 10-14 dB crest factor that sample-peaks at -10 dBFS has a 25 ms-averaged envelope around -20 to -24 dBFS on its loudest syllables — at or below the knee floor (-21 dBFS for a 6 dB knee centred on -18). Loudness-weighted GR is then ~0-0.7 dB, not 4 dB, so +1.5 dB of makeup is ~1-1.5 dB of net level gain. That is the exact failure the whole rationale is built to avoid (its own warnings 9/11/12), it lands outside the stated ±0.5 LU acceptance test, and it is gain-dependent: at a hot -3 dBFS peak setting GR really is ~2-3 dB and +1.5 is roughly right, while at a conservative -20 dBFS peak setting GR is 0 and +1.5 dB is pure loudness. No static constant can satisfy the parity test across user gain settings, so the default must fail safe.
problems.corrected_value: makeup_db: 0.0
problems.why: 0.0 is the only value that cannot manufacture a false preference: a reference that is at most a fraction of a dB quieter than dry never makes a user conclude "processing sounds better" when they are hearing level. The measurement procedure the rationale already specifies stays, but it should only ever be allowed to raise this number after a measured loss is demonstrated, and Studio is the one preset where it will measure ~0. Keep threshold_db at -18 (it is correct as a safety-net threshold for a reference), but delete the claim that this chain delivers Rane Note 155's 3-6 dB GR on normal speech — it delivers under 1 dB on normal speech, which is right for this preset's purpose and is precisely why makeup must be 0.

problems.problem: ratio 1 is chosen as belt-and-braces ("inert on two counts") but it silently defeats the stated second goal for the parked values — that "a user who turns it on gets something sane rather than the factory-default trap". Per the schema's own stated convention, ratio 1 means no expansion, so a user who flips enabled to true gets a stage that does literally nothing at any threshold. threshold -50 / attack 5 / hold 100 / release 200 are well chosen and then made unreachable. This trades a real usability failure for a hypothetical bug (a UI that ignores enabled), and if that bug existed it would be a bug worth fixing in the UI, not worth papering over in six preset files.
problems.corrected_value: gate.ratio: 2.0 (keep enabled: false, threshold_db: -50, attack_ms: 5, hold_ms: 100, release_ms: 200)
problems.why: 2:1 downward expansion is the gentle end used by tuned speech gates and matches the LSP/EasyEffects gate default family; it gives roughly 6 dB of floor reduction for a floor 6 dB under threshold, which is audible as noise control without the chattering of a hard gate. enabled: false already guarantees Studio's A/B is uncoloured; the parked values then do the job they are documented to do.

problems.problem: 75 Hz is a good centre, but the schema carries no filter order and the whole justification depends on one ("2nd-order Butterworth, 12 dB/oct"). At 2nd order, 75 Hz costs -2.1 dB at 85 Hz, -0.9 dB at 100 Hz and -0.2 dB at 130 Hz — already the single largest tonal difference in a preset advertised as tonally neutral, and more than the rationale implies when it says 75 Hz is "below every user's fundamental". If the implementation ships a 4th-order low cut (24 dB/oct, a very common default and what several of the surveyed plugins expose), the same 75 Hz costs -4.1 dB at 85 Hz and -1.8 dB at 100 Hz, which is an audible thinning of a deep male voice in the reference path and larger than the 100 Hz/-3.5 dB case the rationale explicitly rejects.
problems.corrected_value: hpf_hz: 75 with the order pinned to 2 (12 dB/oct Butterworth) in the preset schema or the engine; if the engine's high-pass is fixed at 4th order, hpf_hz: 55
problems.why: 55 Hz at 4th order gives -1.0 dB at 85 Hz and -0.3 dB at 100 Hz, i.e. it restores the same tonal honesty the 75 Hz/2nd-order choice was picked for, while keeping ~-17 dB at 30 Hz for rumble and plosive LF — enough to keep the compressor detector and the limiter headroom clean, which is the interaction (D) the rationale relies on.

problems.problem: The ship gate is specified as "short-term (3 s) loudness of the processed path within ±0.5 LU of the dry path". Short-term LUFS on speech swings by several LU between 3 s windows depending on which syllables and pauses land inside them, so a single 3 s comparison has more measurement noise than the ±0.5 LU tolerance it is being asked to resolve. The rationale correctly rejects integrated loudness as a real-time control signal, then uses the weaker statistic for an offline calibration where integrated is exactly the right tool.
problems.corrected_value: Match BS.1770 gated INTEGRATED loudness of dry vs processed over the same ≥30 s speech take to within ±0.5 LU; use the 3 s short-term trace only as a secondary check that no window drifts beyond ±1.0 LU
problems.why: Integrated loudness is gated and defined over a programme, which is what an offline per-preset calibration is; it is stable to well under 0.5 LU on a 30 s take, so it can actually resolve the tolerance. The short-term trace then catches the different failure — a release constant that makes the processed path wander even when its average matches.

critiques.overall: The architecture is right and most of the numbers are well defended. EQ at ten zeros, gate and de-esser off, ratio 2:1, knee 6 dB with the sign convention declared rather than inherited, attack 25 ms chosen against the 1-5 ms consumer advice, release 200 ms tied to the 4-5 Hz syllable rate, sub-2 ms latency, the -3 dBFS ceiling defended against -1 dBTP on the grounds that a virtual mic is not the last stage before one known encoder, the "nothing may apply gain after the limiter" rule, the RNNoise-before-the-limiter correction, and the "Studio is not bypass, ship a real loudness-matched bypass" note are all correct and correctly reasoned for this destination. I verified the three repo claims: crates/fxsound-dsp/src/eq.rs:30 has the F10 table exactly as stated, eq.rs:396 confirms the 10-band Q of 1.5976, and crates/fxsound-dsp/src/ contains only biquad/eq/leveller/spectrum/engine — there is indeed no existing compressor, gate, de-esser or limiter convention to inherit, so declaring the knee sign is the right call. One value defeats the preset's entire purpose: makeup_db +1.5 comes from reading sample-peak dBFS off the static curve, and with a 25 ms envelope detector this chain removes well under 1 dB of loudness from normal speech, so the "honest reference" would ship about 1-1.5 dB louder than dry — the precise illusion the rationale spends three paragraphs warning about. Set it to 0.0. The other three are cheap: give the parked gate a usable ratio, pin the high-pass order that the 75 Hz argument silently assumes, and calibrate against gated integrated loudness rather than a single 3 s short-term window.
